0.title: In the Beginning: The Book of Origins
0.overview:
Genesis is the book of beginnings — and every beginning in the Bible finds its root here. The creation of the cosmos, the dignity of humanity as image-bearers of God, the catastrophe of the fall, the first promise of redemption, the flood and new creation, the scattering of nations, and then the extraordinary narrowing of God's redemptive focus onto one man, one family, one people through whom all the families of the earth will be blessed (12:3). To read Genesis is to stand at the headwaters of everything that follows in Scripture.

The book divides naturally into two great movements. The primeval history (chapters 1–11) moves from creation to catastrophe to new beginning — from the garden of Eden to the tower of Babel — tracing the spread of sin and the persistence of grace. The patriarchal history (chapters 12–50) follows Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph, tracing the covenant God makes and keeps across four generations in spite of every human failure. Throughout both movements, one thread holds everything together: the seed of the woman (3:15), the promise that will not be extinguished, the line that leads through flood and famine and fratricide and exile to the One who crushes the serpent's head.

Genesis is also the fountainhead of the Bible's great typological stream. Adam is the type of the One to come (Romans 5:14) — and where Adam fails, Christ succeeds. The sacrifice of Isaac on Moriah (chapter 22) is the most luminous prefiguration of Calvary in the Old Testament: a father, a son, a mountain, a substitute, and the word of the LORD: "The LORD will provide." Joseph — rejected by his brothers, sold for silver, condemned unjustly, exalted to the right hand of power, and the savior of the very brothers who betrayed him — is the most sustained type of Christ in Genesis, and one of the most beautiful in all of Scripture.

The theological lens throughout this commentary is Reformed and christological, drawing especially on Timothy Keller's Genesis sermon series at Redeemer Presbyterian Church, John Calvin's Commentary on Genesis, Derek Kidner's Genesis (Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries), Bruce Waltke's Genesis: A Commentary, and Gordon Wenham's Genesis (Word Biblical Commentary). The governing conviction is that Genesis is not a problem to be defended but a gift to be received — and that every page, rightly read, leads to Jesus Christ, in whom all the promises of God find their Yes and Amen (2 Corinthians 1:20).

1.title: In the Beginning, God

1.overview:
The first verse of Genesis is the most momentous sentence ever written: "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth." Before the cosmos, before time, before anything — there was God. Creation is not God (pantheism), and matter is not evil (dualism) — it is the good gift of a God who exists in glorious self-sufficiency and chooses to bring another into existence out of pure generosity.

The sovereign creative word — "and God said" — echoes ten times through the chapter, each time calling something new into existence. The same Word that spoke at creation became flesh in Jesus Christ (John 1:1–3; Col. 1:16). Creation is a trinitarian act: the Father creates, the Spirit hovers, the Son is the Word through whom all things are made.

The climax is the creation of humanity in the image of God (imago Dei, vv.26–27). Unlike every other element of creation, humanity is made not by divine command but by divine deliberation — "Let us make" — and is stamped with the divine likeness. This image is not a faculty but a relational and vocational reality: humanity is made to represent God in the world and rule the creation as vice-regents under his lordship. The chapter closes with the Creator's own verdict: "it was very good."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Creation Days One through Three
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis opens not with argument but with proclamation: God created. The majestic, measured cadence of the creation account — God speaks, it is so, God sees that it is good, evening and morning — establishes the sovereignty, goodness, and rationality of the Creator before any human being appears. Days one through three bring order out of formlessness: light separated from darkness, waters above from waters below, dry land distinguished from sea, and the earth clothed with vegetation.
verseByVerse.theology: Creation ex nihilo — from nothing — is the foundational theological claim of verse 1. God does not shape pre-existing matter; he speaks reality into existence. The Spirit hovering over the waters anticipates the new creation theology of the New Testament (2 Cor. 5:17; John 1:1–3). The repeated 'it was good' is a moral and aesthetic verdict, not merely utilitarian: the created order reflects the character of its Creator. Wenham notes the symmetrical structure of days 1–6 (days 1–3 form the domains; days 4–6 fill them) reveals intentional, literary artistry that signals theological purpose.
verseByVerse.examples: Waltke observes that the creation account is simultaneously polemical — countering ancient Near Eastern cosmogonies where chaos gods battle — and doxological, inviting worship of the Creator. Kidner notes that 'formless and void' (tohu wabohu) is the antithesis of everything God will accomplish: purposeful order from purposeless chaos. This is the pattern of all God's redemptive work — creating order, beauty, and life where there was only darkness and void.

verseByVerse.quote: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ten Hebrew words, and every one of them carries weight. There is no scene to set here, and that is the first thing to feel: no stage, no backdrop, no dark room waiting for someone to find the switch. Before this sentence there is no "before." Time starts inside it. Whatever picture is forming in your mind of what things were like beforehand — empty space, a waiting silence, a vast nothing stretching away — take it away. There was no space to be empty. There was God, and nothing else at all.

The verb is bara, to create. In the Hebrew Bible it never once takes a human subject. Men shape, carve, build, weave, assemble; only God baras. It is not a bigger word for making. It names a different kind of act altogether — the kind that needs no material, no workshop, no supplier. "The heavens and the earth" is a Hebrew way of saying everything by naming the two ends of it, the way we say "young and old" and mean the whole town. Genesis opens with a claim so wide that nothing is left standing outside it.

Three questions are settled before anyone can raise them. The universe is not eternal; it had a start. It is not divine; the sun you squint at and the sea you swim in are things God made, not powers to be appeased. And it is not an accident; it came from a will, not from a collision. Scripture never argues for any of this. It states it in one line and then builds on it for sixty-five books.

The New Testament comes back to this verse and puts a face on it. "In the beginning was the Word... All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made" (John 1:1–3). The one through whom the galaxies were flung out is the man who fell asleep in the back of a fishing boat because he was tired. In him all things hold together (cf. Col. 1:16–17; Heb. 1:2–3). The beginning had a Beholder, and the Beholder has a name, and the name has scars.

verseByVerse.quote: The earth was without form and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first description of the world God has made is not flattering. It is tohu wabohu — formless and empty, a pair of words chosen for their sound as much as their sense, like saying "waste and void." Not evil, not a mistake, not the wreckage of some earlier war among the gods. Simply unfinished: a house with no rooms and nobody living in it. The whole chapter will now do two things to that condition. Days one to three give it form. Days four to six fill it. God is not embarrassed by raw material.

Then the sentence turns. "And the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters." The verb translated hovering appears again in Deuteronomy 32:11 of an eagle fluttering over its nest, and the picture it gives is not of a bird circling a meal but of a parent over the young — close, attentive, poised to act. Over a dark and shapeless deep, the posture of God is not distaste. It is brooding care.

Take the measure of that if your own life is at the formless stage. Not ruined, just not yet anything — the years that have produced no visible shape, the prayers that have not landed, the long stretch where nothing is finished. Genesis 1:2 is the verse for it. The state of the world one sentence before the first word of God was exactly that, and the Spirit was already over it. What came next was not repair. It was light.

The New Testament reads this scene forward without hesitation. The God who brooded over the dark deep is the God who "has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor. 4:6), and the man who is in Christ is called, in so many words, a new creation (2 Cor. 5:17). The same Spirit, the same darkness, the same speech.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let there be light," and there was light. And God saw that the light was good. And God separated the light from the darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Creation happens by speech. No struggle, no sweat, no raw material dragged in from somewhere else, no rival to be beaten down first. God says it and it is. The gap between his intention and the fact is nothing at all. Every other creator in the ancient world had to fight for his world or build it out of something; the God of Genesis opens his mouth.

Which is why the word of God is treated everywhere else in Scripture as the most powerful thing there is. It is a word that makes worlds, and it is the same word that stills a storm with two syllables, that calls a four-day corpse out of a tomb by name, that told a paralysed man to pick up his mat. In the end that word did not stay a word. "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14).

A fair question arrives immediately: how is there light on day one when the sun is not made until day four? The text is not embarrassed by this and neither should we be. Light is a created thing, not a by-product of the sun; the sun is one lamp among many, hung later in the fixture. And the ordering makes a point the ancient reader could not miss — the nations around Israel worshipped the sun, so Genesis has God make light without it, and puts the sun in its place as a fitting three days late. At the far end of the Bible the same note is struck again: the city has no need of sun or moon, "for the glory of God gives it light" (Rev. 21:23).

"And God saw that the light was good." This is the first verdict ever pronounced, and it is an aesthetic and moral one at once. God is not merely efficient. He looks at what he has made and he likes it.

verseByVerse.quote: God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And there was evening and there was morning, the first day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God names what he makes. In the ancient world naming was an act of authority — you named your children, your servants, your territory — so this is not labelling but lordship. Day and Night belong to him because he called them that. And then the refrain that will beat through the whole chapter like a drum: "And there was evening and there was morning, the first day."

Notice the order. Evening first, then morning. Hebrew days begin at sunset, which is why the Sabbath starts on Friday evening; but the pattern also says something the rest of Scripture will keep saying. The dark comes first and the light comes after. That is the shape of the week, of the exile, of Friday and Sunday, and of every believer's dying. God's ordinary sequence is not light fading into dark but dark giving way to light.

Here is where a reader usually stops and asks the honest question: are these six ordinary days? Christians who love this book and hold it to be true have answered differently, and it is better to say so plainly than to pretend there is no discussion. Some read six consecutive twenty-four-hour days, the plain sense of "evening and morning" and the ground of the Sabbath command in Exodus 20:11 — R. C. Sproul came to this position late in life and said so openly. Others read the days as a literary frame: three domains formed, then the same three filled in the same order, with day seven left deliberately without an evening. Derek Kidner and Bruce Waltke argue along these lines, and note that the sun which measures a day is not made until day four.

What the text itself insists on is not in dispute between them, and it is what a reader most needs. One God made everything. He made it by speaking. He made it in order, and the order was good. Whatever length the days were, they were his, and they ran to a plan. Hold the certainty tightly and the timetable loosely, and do not let a question the text does not settle become a wall between believers who both bow to it.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let there be an expanse in the midst of the waters, and let it separate the waters from the waters." And God made the expanse and separated the waters that were under the expanse from the waters that were above the expanse. And it was so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Day two divides the waters. A raqia — expanse, something beaten out thin like hammered metal — is set in the middle of the deep, and water is now above it and below it. This is the sky as anyone standing in a field sees it: a vast overhead from which rain falls, holding back an ocean that would otherwise come down all at once. The Bible describes the world the way it looks to a person standing in it, as we still do when we say the sun rose at half past six. That is not primitive science; it is ordinary speech, and it is how the flood account will talk when the windows of heaven are opened (7:11).

The theological point is the one that matters, and it is about water. In the imagination of every nation around Israel the sea was the enemy — chaotic, divine, ravenous, the thing the gods had to defeat before anything could be built. Genesis has God divide it as calmly as a man drawing a curtain. There is no battle in this chapter. What terrifies the neighbours is, in this account, plumbing.

"And it was so." The phrase lands like a gavel. God does not propose, suggest or attempt. Between the saying and the being there is no interval and no possibility of failure — which is the ground under every promise he ever makes afterwards, including the ones still outstanding.

verseByVerse.quote: And God called the expanse Heaven. And there was evening and there was morning, the second day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The expanse is named Heaven, and the second day closes. And something is missing. Every other day carries the verdict "God saw that it was good" — day three and day six get it twice — but not day two. Not once.

The likeliest explanation is structural rather than mysterious: day two's work is unfinished. A sky with nothing in it is a room with no furniture. Not until day five, when the birds are given the expanse and the fish the waters below, does the domain made here receive its verdict — and on that day the "good" comes for both. Gordon Wenham makes this case, and it fits the architecture of the chapter exactly.

There is a habit of mind to learn from an unfinished day. God is not in a hurry to pronounce a thing good before it is done, and he is entirely comfortable ending a stage of his work with the verdict withheld. Anyone in the middle of something unfinished — a marriage being rebuilt, a faith being slowly put back together, a child not yet home — is living in a day two. The silence is not disapproval. The week is not over.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let the waters under the heavens be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear." And it was so. God called the dry land Earth, and the waters that were gathered together he called Seas. And God saw that it was good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Day three, and the last separation: the waters gather, the dry land comes up out of them. This is the third time God has divided something — light from dark, water from water, and now land from sea. Order, in Genesis, is made by putting things in their places and keeping them there.

Once more the sea is put in its place and named. The nations around Israel told stories in which the sea-god had to be killed before the world could exist. Genesis says God gathered it into one place and called it Seas. Later Scripture keeps the image and makes it thunderous: God shut in the sea with doors and said, "Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed" (Job 38:8–11). The chaos is not God's rival. It is God's tenant, and he set the fence.

So it is a deliberate thing when, centuries later, a Galilean carpenter stands up in a boat in a killing storm and speaks to the water as though it belonged to him. The disciples ask exactly the right question: "Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?" (Mark 4:41). Genesis 1 has already answered it. The sea obeys the voice that gathered it.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let the earth sprout vegetation, plants yielding seed, and fruit trees bearing fruit in which is their seed, each according to its kind, on the earth." And it was so. The earth brought forth vegetation, plants yielding seed according to their own kinds, and trees bearing fruit in which is their seed, each according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Notice who does the work. God does not manufacture plants; he says, "Let the earth sprout vegetation," and the earth sprouts it. The ground is handed a share in the making. This is a small thing with a long reach: God delights to work through what he has made rather than around it, so that the wheat in the field is no less his gift for having come up through soil, rain and a farmer's labour.

"Each according to its kind" tolls three times in two verses. Creation is not a blur; it is furnished with distinct, stable, reproducing kinds, each carrying its own seed and therefore its own future. Christians who take this book with full seriousness have disagreed about how much biological weight the phrase can bear, and the argument is not settled by a verse that was not written to settle it. What the verse is doing is plain enough: it is saying that the living world is ordered, not random, and that its ordering came from God.

And the seed is the quiet marvel here. Every plant is made carrying inside itself the means of its own multiplication, so that the provision is not a delivery but a supply line — abundance built into the structure of things before anyone existed to eat it. Long afterwards the Lord Jesus would take that ordinary buried seed, the one his Father wrote into the third day, and use it to explain his own death (John 12:24).

verseByVerse.quote: And there was evening and there was morning, the third day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Day three ends, and it has been the fullest day so far — two works, two verdicts of "good." That is not accidental. Day six will also carry two works and a double portion of blessing, and the correspondence is one of the clearest signs that this chapter is built with great care.

Lay the six days out in two columns and the design shows itself. Days one, two and three make three domains: light and dark, sky and sea, land. Days four, five and six fill exactly those domains in the same order: lights for the day and night, birds and fish for sky and sea, animals and man for the land. Empty becomes full; formless becomes formed. The two problems named in verse 2 are answered in order, and the chapter closes the circle it opened.

None of this is decoration. It tells the reader what kind of God is at work here — not a force but a mind, not a spasm of energy but an architect who finishes what he starts in the order he intended. The universe is not a mess that happens to contain some order. It is a building.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–31 — Creation Days Four through Six: Lights, Living Creatures, and the Image of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second triad of creation fills the domains established in days one through three. The lights fill the sky and govern time; sea creatures and birds fill the waters and expanse; land animals and finally humanity fill the earth. The account builds to its climax in the creation of the human being in the image of God — male and female — entrusted with dominion over the whole creation. God's final verdict on the completed creation is not merely 'good' but 'very good.'
verseByVerse.theology: The image of God (imago Dei) in verse 26–27 is the theological summit of Genesis 1. Human beings are not the product of chance or the plaything of capricious deities but the intentional creation of God, bearing his image and entrusted with his delegated authority over creation. The image involves rationality, morality, relationality, and the capacity for dominion — reflecting God's own character as one who orders, names, evaluates, and rules. The creation of male and female together as image-bearers establishes the equality of the sexes in dignity before any distinction in role is introduced.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller's 'The Reason for God' and his Genesis sermons are essential here: he argues that Genesis 1 presents the cosmos as a temple — structured, ordered, God-filled — with humanity as the priests who serve within it. Waltke notes that the creation mandate (be fruitful, multiply, fill, subdue, have dominion) is the first word God speaks to humans, defining their purpose before any prohibition appears. Dominion is stewardship, not exploitation: humans rule on God's behalf, accountable to the Creator whose image they bear.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let there be lights in the expanse of the heavens to separate the day from the night. And let them be for signs and for seasons, and for days and years, and let them be lights in the expanse of the heavens to give light upon the earth." And it was so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Day four fills the domain made on day one. Lights are set in the expanse to separate day from night and to serve "for signs and for seasons, and for days and years." Their job is given in the same breath as their making: they are clocks and calendars and lamps. They mark the harvest, the festival, the Sabbath, the year. Time in the Bible is not a neutral river we are all floating down; it is measured out by fixtures God hung for the purpose.

And they are creatures. That is the sharpest edge of the passage. In Babylon and Egypt the sun and moon were gods with names, temples and priests, and the educated world read the sky for destiny. Genesis gives them a job description instead of a title. What the neighbouring empires worshipped, Israel was told to use for working out when to plant barley.

The instinct that reads the sky for fate has not died; it has only got a column in the newspaper. When a person checks a horoscope before a decision, something is being consulted that was made on the fourth day for the purpose of telling us the season. Isaiah is scornful about it precisely because it is such a small thing to be afraid of (Isa. 47:13–14). Lift your eyes to the stars and worship, by all means — but worship past them.

verseByVerse.quote: And God made the two great lights—the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night—and the stars. And God set them in the expanse of the heavens to give light on the earth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And God made the two great lights" — and the text refuses to name them. Sun and moon had names everywhere in the ancient world, and the names were the names of gods. Genesis calls them the greater light and the lesser light, as one might say the big lamp and the small one, and hands them the humblest verb available: they are made, and then they are set. Placed. Like furniture.

Then comes one of the most astonishing clauses in Scripture, and it is over before you notice it: "and the stars." That is all. Every sun in every galaxy, every one of the hundred billion in the Milky Way and the hundred billion galaxies beyond it — vast, ancient, unimaginably hot, and thrown into the sentence as an afterthought at the end of a list. The empires of Mesopotamia built a science and a religion out of those points of light. Moses gives them three words and moves on.

It is a deliberate flattening, and it does not diminish the stars; it enlarges God. Set the whole night sky beside him and it fits in a subordinate clause. He knows their number and calls them each by name (Ps. 147:4), and not one of them has ever been anything other than his handiwork, lit and hung and kept burning for the purpose of giving light on a small planet where he intended to place his image. The heavens do not compete with the glory of God. They declare it (Ps. 19:1).

verseByVerse.quote: to rule over the day and over the night, and to separate the light from the darkness. And God saw that it was good. And there was evening and there was morning, the fourth day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lights rule and separate — and the verb "rule" is a royal one. They govern their domains, but they govern under authority, the way a steward runs a household that is not his. Everything in Genesis 1 that exercises power does so on loan.

"And God saw that it was good." Day four fills the domain of day one, and the regularity it establishes is not merely useful; it becomes a pledge. After the flood God will bind himself to it: "While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, shall not cease" (8:22). Jeremiah will point at the fixed order of day and night and say that God's covenant with David is exactly that unbreakable (Jer. 33:20–21).

So the sunrise is a sermon, and it preaches every morning without being asked. The reader who has just had the worst night of his life will find the light coming up over the roofs at the usual time, on the usual schedule, because the God who keeps the fourth day keeps his word. Faithfulness is not something God does on special occasions. It is the ordinary condition of the universe, and it can be seen from any window.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let the waters swarm with swarms of living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth across the expanse of the heavens." So God created the great sea creatures and every living creature that moves, with which the waters swarm, according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Day five fills the sky and the sea. And the word chosen for it is a word of sheer excess: "Let the waters swarm with swarms of living creatures." Not populate — swarm. Anyone who has seen a shoal turn all at once, or a cloud of starlings fold in on itself over a winter field, has seen the fifth day doing exactly what it was told.

Then the sentence does something pointed. "So God created the great sea creatures" — the Hebrew is tanninim, the sea monsters, the dragons of the deep that in the surrounding mythologies were the primeval enemies of the gods, with names and battles and a whole literature of terror attached. Here they are on the list. Between "swarm" and "every winged bird," without a raised voice, the monsters are simply things God made. What the nations feared, Genesis files under wildlife.

And the abundance is the point to carry away. God did not make one adequate fish. He made a world stocked past the point of usefulness, full of creatures no human being would see for four thousand years, colours at the bottom of the ocean where there is no light to show them off. This is not a minimal God meeting a specification. This is an artist who could not stop, and the same extravagance turns up later in a Father who kills the fattened calf and a Saviour who makes a hundred and twenty gallons of good wine for a wedding that had already drunk its fill.

verseByVerse.quote: And God blessed them, saying, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters in the seas, and let birds multiply on the earth." And there was evening and there was morning, the fifth day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first blessing in the Bible is spoken over fish and birds. Let that land. Before there is a human being to bless, before covenant or promise or law, God turns to the creatures of sea and sky and says, in effect, flourish. "Be fruitful and multiply and fill." The same words will be said to humanity six verses later and to Noah after the flood (9:1).

A blessing in Scripture is never a warm sentiment. It is a word that carries power to do what it says — which is why Jacob will wrestle all night for one and why Esau, having lost his, cannot simply be given another. Here the blessing installs fruitfulness into the creatures themselves. Their multiplying is not mere biology; it is obedience to a word spoken over them on the fifth day and never withdrawn.

So the creation is given a share in its own filling. God could have made every fish that would ever live in a single afternoon. Instead he made some, blessed them, and let them carry the work forward — which is the way he still tends to do things, entrusting his purposes to creatures who will finish them, and getting the glory for both the gift and the fruit of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds—livestock and creeping things and beasts of the earth according to their kinds." And it was so. And God made the beasts of the earth according to their kinds and the livestock according to their kinds, and everything that creeps on the ground according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Day six begins on the ground. Livestock, creeping things, wild beasts — the three categories cover the range from the ox in the yard to the beetle under the stone to the lion on the ridge. And again the earth is invited into the work: "Let the earth bring forth living creatures."

Hold that phrase, because in the next chapter it will matter enormously. The man will be formed of dust from the same ground (2:7). Whatever else the image of God turns out to mean, it does not mean that human beings are made of finer stuff than the animals. We share their material entirely. A doctor and a vet study much the same chemistry. The dignity that is about to be announced does not rest on our being biologically special; it rests on something said over us by God.

"And God saw that it was good." The verdict comes, and yet the day is not over. A world of oceans, forests, birds and beasts, all of it good, and God is not finished. Something is still missing from a creation that looks complete — and it is not a better animal.

verseByVerse.quote: Then God said, "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. And let them have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over the livestock and over all the earth and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth." So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rhythm breaks. Nine times God has said "Let there be" and it was so. Now he says, "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness," and the sentence turns inward before it turns outward. Everything else was commanded into being. This one is deliberated over.

Who is the "us"? Three answers are offered. Some take it as a plural of majesty, a royal we — though Hebrew does not otherwise use one. Some take it as God addressing a heavenly court of angels — though the very next verse says God made man in his own image, not in theirs, and angels create nothing. And the church has long heard in it the first faint sound of the God who is one and yet not solitary, the same God the New Testament will name as Father, Son and Spirit. Genesis alone would not prove the Trinity. But a reader who knows John 1 and Colossians 1 finds this verse pointing where he has already been taken.

"Image" translates tselem, and its ordinary use is concrete: a statue of a king, set up in a province he ruled but could not visit, so that everyone walking past could see whose territory this was. That is the job. A human being stands in the creation as the visible marker of an invisible King. The image is not a part of you — not the soul as opposed to the body, not intelligence, not moral sense — it is what you are and what you are for.

The text will not let this go. Verse 27 says it three times in a single breath, and then adds five words that levelled the ancient world: "male and female he created them." Both. Equally. Before any word about roles, before marriage, before the fall, the man and the woman stand on the same ground, bearing the same image, holding the same dignity from the same God.

Take the measure of that against what is broken now. The dignity of a person does not rest on productivity, so the man who has just been made redundant has not lost any of it. It does not rest on cognition, so the woman in the late stages of dementia who no longer knows her daughter's name is not less an image-bearer than the daughter weeping by the bed. It does not rest on independence, on beauty, on usefulness, on being wanted, or on having been born yet. It rests on a decision God made on the sixth day and has never revised. James says this is exactly why cursing a man is such a serious business: he is made "in the likeness of God" (James 3:9). Run the test on yourself. Think of the person you find hardest to value — the one who irritates, or costs, or frightens you. Genesis 1:27 was written about them.

And there is one more turn, the one the whole Bible is going towards. The image was defaced in Eden, not erased but cracked through. So the Son came, who is himself "the image of the invisible God" (Col. 1:15), not stamped with the likeness but the thing itself; and those who are his are being changed into that same image, from one degree of glory to another (2 Cor. 3:18; Rom. 8:29). What Adam was made to be, Christ is. What Christ is, his people will be.

verseByVerse.quote: And God blessed them. And God said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over every living thing that moves on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first words God ever addresses to a human being are a blessing and a job. "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion." Not a warning, not a rule, not a threat — a commission. Before there is any prohibition in the Bible there is a vocation.

Two verbs have taken a beating, and they deserve a straight answer. Kabash (subdue) means to bring under control, and radah (have dominion) means to rule as a king rules. Critics have said, not unreasonably, that these words have been used to justify strip-mining the planet. But the ruling described here is modelled on God's own, and his rule in this chapter has consisted entirely of ordering, filling, providing and delighting. He has not consumed a thing. A viceroy who wrecks the province is not doing his king's will loudly; he is doing his own, and he will answer for it. The image-bearer who leaves a river dead behind him has misread his job description, not obeyed it.

Which makes ordinary human work far more dignified than most people who do it suspect. Farming, engineering, teaching, cooking, coding, keeping accounts, raising children — all of it is the sixth-day mandate being carried out. The world was made good but not finished; it was given to us as a garden to tend and a raw creation to build a civilisation out of. There is no sacred-secular divide in Genesis 1. A person who cleans a hospital ward well on Monday morning is doing something God commissioned before he commanded anyone to pray.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Behold, I have given you every plant yielding seed that is on the face of all the earth, and every tree with seed in its fruit. You shall have them for food. And to every beast of the earth and to every bird of the heavens and to everything that creeps on the earth, everything that has the breath of life, I have given every green plant for food." And it was so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before God says a single "you shall not," he says, "Behold, I have given." The whole seed-bearing world is handed over as food, to humans and animals alike, with a wave of the hand across "the face of all the earth." The Bible's first note about the human condition is not restriction. It is a full table.

Get the order right and half the Christian life falls into place. The reader who thinks of God primarily as the one who forbids has begun at chapter 2, verse 17, and skipped this. The prohibition in the garden is one tree; the gift is every other tree in it. Whatever a person believes about God will be governed by which of those two facts he heard first.

The diet given is vegetarian, for people and beasts together, and permission to eat meat does not arrive until after the flood (9:3). Something in the original arrangement was gentler than the world we know, and the prophets expect it back: the wolf and the lamb grazing together, and nothing hurting or destroying in all God's holy mountain (Isa. 65:25; 11:6–9). The blood-soaked food chain we take for the natural order is a parenthesis between two versions of peace, and it is the parenthesis that will end.

verseByVerse.quote: And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good. And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good." Six times the verdict has been "good" on a piece of the work. Now it is passed on the whole, with the image-bearer standing in it, and the word is raised. Very good. Not adequate. Not a promising start. Exactly what he wanted.

Everything the Christian faith says about evil depends on this sentence. Suffering, cruelty, disease and death are not original equipment. They are not part of the design, not the necessary cost of a material world, not God's shadow-side. They are intruders in a house that was pronounced very good before they arrived — which is why the Bible can promise their removal without promising the removal of the world. God does not intend to rescue us from matter. He intends to rescue matter.

So hold this against the grief you are actually carrying. Whatever it is — the diagnosis, the funeral, the ruined body, the ruined family — Genesis 1:31 gives you permission to call it wrong. It does not belong here. Your instinct that this is not how things are meant to be is not sentimentality; it is an accurate memory of the sixth day, and a true anticipation of the last one, when the dwelling place of God is with man and he wipes away every tear (Rev. 21:3–4).

And the chapter ends where it began, with God. He spoke, and there was light. He divided, and there was order. He filled, and there was life. He looked, and there was joy in the looking. Every atom in existence came out of that voice, and the same voice would one day be heard saying "Lazarus, come out," and "Father, forgive them," and "It is finished." The Maker of the heavens and the earth is very good, and everything he touches he means to make so.

1.theology:
The Trinity in Creation. Genesis 1 contains seeds the New Testament flowers. The Spirit hovers (v.2); God speaks his Word (v.3); the Father creates (v.1). John 1:1–3 identifies the creative Word with the eternal Son: "All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made." Colossians 1:16 and Hebrews 1:2 confirm: the universe was made through and for Christ. Creation is a trinitarian act.

The Image of God and Human Dignity. The imago Dei (vv.26–27) is the theological foundation of every claim about human dignity — not achievement, intelligence, beauty, or utility, but the image of God stamped on every human being from conception. This is why the taking of human life is an assault on God himself (Gen. 9:6). In an age of competing accounts of human value, Genesis 1:27 remains the most radical claim ever made: every person bears the image of the Creator of the cosmos.
1.examples:
Then: Israel's neighbors had elaborate creation myths — the Babylonian Enuma Elish featured warring gods and humanity created as divine slave labor. Genesis 1 is a quiet, majestic polemic: one God, sovereign speech, ordered goodness, humanity as image-bearers rather than slaves. The chapter was simultaneously theological and political — a declaration that Israel's God alone is Creator and Lord.

Now: Contemporary cosmology traces the universe to a beginning (the Big Bang), confirming what Genesis asserted millennia ago. But science cannot tell us whether the beginning had a Beholder. Genesis answers with the confidence of revelation. And the imago Dei cuts against every modern reductionism — the person reduced to their productivity, genome, or social utility has had their image-bearing dignity denied. The church holds the most radical account of human worth available in the contemporary marketplace of ideas.

2.title: The LORD God Formed the Man
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them.<sup>2</sup>And on the seventh day God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done.<sup>3</sup>So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it God rested from all his work that he had done in creation.<sup>4</sup>These are the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created, in the day that the LORD God made the earth and the heavens.<sup>5</sup>When no bush of the field was yet in the land and no small plant of the field had yet sprung up—for the LORD God had not caused it to rain on the land, and there was no man to work the ground,<sup>6</sup>and a mist was going up from the land and was watering the whole face of the ground—<sup>7</sup>then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and there he put the man whom he had formed.<sup>9</sup>And out of the ground the LORD God made to spring up every tree that is pleasant to the sight and good for food. The tree of life was in the midst of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.<sup>10</sup>A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden, and there it divided and became four rivers.<sup>11</sup>The name of the first is the Pishon. It is the one that flowed around the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold.<sup>12</sup>And the gold of that land is good; bdellium and onyx stone are there.<sup>13</sup>The name of the second river is the Gihon. It is the one that flowed around the whole land of Cush.<sup>14</sup>And the name of the third river is the Tigris, which flows east of Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.<sup>15</sup>The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it.<sup>16</sup>And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, "You may surely eat of every tree of the garden,<sup>17</sup>but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die."<sup>18</sup>Then the LORD God said, "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him."<sup>19</sup>Now out of the ground the LORD God had formed every beast of the field and every bird of the heavens and brought them to the man to see what he would call them. And whatever the man called every living creature, that was its name.<sup>20</sup>The man gave names to all livestock and to the birds of the heavens and to every beast of the field. But for Adam there was not found a helper fit for him.<sup>21</sup>So the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon the man, and while he slept took one of his ribs and closed up its place with flesh.<sup>22</sup>And the rib that the LORD God had taken from the man he made into a woman and brought her to the man.<sup>23</sup>Then the man said, "This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man."<sup>24</sup>Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.<sup>25</sup>And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.
2.overview:
Where Genesis 1 surveys creation from the cosmic perspective, Genesis 2 zooms in — camera descending from the heavens to settle on a garden, a man formed from dust, the breath of God filling his lungs. The change of divine name is significant: chapter 1 uses Elohim (God, the transcendent Creator); chapter 2 introduces YHWH Elohim (the LORD God), the covenant name that will define all of Israel's subsequent relationship with this God. The Creator is not merely a force but a Person who walks in gardens and calls for conversation.

The garden of Eden is not merely a pleasant park but a sacred space — a temple-garden where God dwells with humanity. The man's vocation to "work it and keep it" (v.15) uses the same Hebrew verbs (abad and shamar) used later for priestly service in the tabernacle (Num. 3:7–8). Adam is simultaneously a gardener and a priest — his work is worship and his worship is work.

The creation of woman is the chapter's climax. "It is not good that the man should be alone" (v.18) — the first "not good" in Genesis — reveals that even paradise without community is incomplete. Marriage is the first human institution, established before the fall. Paul calls it a "profound mystery" that images Christ's union with the church (Eph. 5:31–32) — and Jesus upholds its creational authority when asked about divorce (Matt. 19:4–6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — The Seventh Day and the Garden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The creation account concludes with the Sabbath rest of God — the first holy time in Scripture — and then zooms in to tell the story of human origins with vivid particularity. Chapter 2 is not a contradiction of chapter 1 but a complementary close-up: where chapter 1 gives the cosmic panorama, chapter 2 gives the intimate portrait of the man formed from dust and the woman formed from his side, placed in a garden designed for abundance and communion with God.
verseByVerse.theology: The Sabbath rest of God (vv.1–3) is the theological and temporal crown of creation: God rests not from exhaustion but in sovereign completion, blessing the seventh day as a pattern for human life and worship. The garden of Eden is not merely paradise but a sanctuary — the place where God walks with his image-bearers in unhindered communion. The two trees at the center — life and the knowledge of good and evil — represent the two dimensions of the human condition: dependence on God for life, and the question of moral allegiance. The prohibition of the tree of knowledge is not arbitrary but constitutive of the creature-Creator relationship.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller on Genesis 2: the garden is a temple, Eden is the innermost sanctuary, and Adam is the priest-king who serves within it. Wenham notes that the terms used for Adam's work in the garden — 'to work' (abad) and 'to keep' (shamar) — are the same terms used for priestly service in the tabernacle (Num. 3:7–8; 8:26). Human vocation begins as priestly: maintaining and guarding the sacred space of God's presence.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them. And on the seventh day God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus the heavens and the earth were finished." The word is a builder's word. It will come back when the tabernacle is completed (Exod. 40:33) and when the temple is (1 Kings 7:51), because Genesis is describing the same kind of moment: a house made ready for its owner. "And all the host of them" — a military word, the ranks of stars and creatures drawn up in order, everything present and accounted for.

Then the sentence nobody would have dared invent: "and he rested." The Hebrew verb is shabath, which does not mean to recover but to stop. God was not tired. Isaiah says so flatly — the Creator of the ends of the earth "does not faint or grow weary" (Isa. 40:28). This is not a man collapsing into a chair on Friday evening. It is a craftsman putting down his tools because the work is done, and there is nothing left that needs doing.

And something is missing from the seventh day. Six times the refrain has closed a day — "and there was evening and there was morning." Here it simply stops. The seventh day is never shut. The writer to the Hebrews notices the open end and builds a whole argument on it: there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, and the one who enters it has rested from his works as God did from his (Heb. 4:9–10). The seventh day is still running, and there is a door into it.

verseByVerse.quote: So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it God rested from all his work that he had done in creation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first thing in the Bible that God makes holy is not a place, a person or an object. It is a stretch of time. There is no temple yet, no altar, no priest, no nation; there is a day, blessed and set apart, and the whole later apparatus of holy things will be built on that pattern. God begins his sanctifying work with the calendar.

Which tells you what he thinks a human being is for. The man made on day six wakes on day seven into a day with no assignment in it. Before he has produced anything at all, he is given a day whose entire content is God. His first full day is a holiday, and he did not earn it, because at that point he had not worked an hour.

Run that against your own week. If the work stopped tomorrow — the job gone, the usefulness gone, nothing to show anyone — would there be anything left of you? The Sabbath was given to answer that question in advance, and the answer is that a person's worth is not the output of a person's labour. God rested first, and he was not resting from exhaustion but from completion. He is teaching his image-bearers to do the same, and later he will bind it into the Ten Commandments with this very verse as the reason (Exod. 20:11).

And there is a rest deeper than a day off. When the Son of God had finished the work his Father gave him he said, "It is finished," and then he rested — on a Sabbath, in a tomb, from a work that could not be added to. Everyone who trusts him stops trying to earn what has already been completed (cf. Heb. 4:9–10; Matt. 11:28).

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created, in the day that the LORD God made the earth and the heavens. When no bush of the field was yet in the land and no small plant of the field had yet sprung up—for the LORD God had not caused it to rain on the land, and there was no man to work the ground, and a mist was going up from the land and was watering the whole face of the ground—
verseByVerse.commentary:
"These are the generations of..." — elleh toledot. This little formula is the spine of the whole book. It appears eleven times, and each time it introduces not the origin of the thing named but what came out of it. Genesis is built as a series of these panels: the heavens and the earth, then Adam, Noah, Shem, Terah, Ishmael, Isaac, Esau, Jacob. The book is not a scrapbook. It is a line being narrowed, from the whole cosmos down to one family.

And the name of God changes here. Chapter 1 said Elohim thirty-five times — God as the sovereign power. Now, for the first time, comes "the LORD God", Yahweh Elohim. When your Bible prints LORD in capitals it is standing in for the personal covenant name, the name given to Moses at the bush (Exod. 3:14). The Creator of galaxies has a name, and he is about to walk in a garden in the cool of the day.

Readers are often told that chapter 2 is a second and contradictory creation story, with the order muddled. Look again at what verse 5 actually says: there was no bush of the field and no small plant of the field — cultivated growth, the sort that needs rain and a farmer — and neither had arrived yet, "for the LORD God had not caused it to rain on the land, and there was no man to work the ground." This is not a rival timetable. It is a camera moving from the whole cosmos down to one patch of dry ground where a garden is about to be planted, and it tells us in passing that the world was made waiting for a gardener.

verseByVerse.quote: then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two halves of a sentence, and the whole of what a human being is sits between them.

"The LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground." The verb is a potter's word — it is used of a craftsman with wet clay under his thumbs. And the wordplay is impossible to miss in Hebrew: adam (man) is taken from adamah (ground). Earthling from earth. Every atom in your body was borrowed from the topsoil, and one day it goes back (3:19). This is the great deflater of human pride, and it comes before any mention of sin. Kneel down and take a handful of dirt; that is the raw material God chose.

"And breathed into his nostrils the breath of life." Now look at the posture. Everything else in creation was made at a distance, by a word spoken across the void. This one is made face to face, close enough for breath. God kneels in the dust of his own world and puts his mouth to the mouth of a clay figure. There is nothing else like it in the chapter, and nothing else like it in the literature of the ancient world.

"And the man became a living creature" — a nephesh chayyah, a living being. Not a soul poured into a body, as though the body were packaging. The dust plus the breath equals the person. Which is why Christianity has never believed that salvation means escaping the body; the promise is a body raised (1 Cor. 15:42–44). And it is why the last Adam did not come as a spirit but as a man of the same dust, and why "the last Adam became a life-giving spirit" (1 Cor. 15:45). On the evening of the resurrection he stood in a locked room and breathed on his disciples (John 20:22). The same act, and the second time it made something that will never go back to the ground.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and there he put the man whom he had formed. And out of the ground the LORD God made to spring up every tree that is pleasant to the sight and good for food. The tree of life was in the midst of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God plants a garden. Not a warehouse, not a factory floor, not a bare sanctuary — a garden, in a region called Eden, a name that means delight or luxury. And the trees are described in two ways, in this order: "pleasant to the sight and good for food." Beautiful first, useful second. God was not merely provisioning a species. He was making a place a man would like being in.

That order says something about God worth resting on. He did not have to make the world beautiful. Chlorophyll works in any colour. Sunsets could have been grey and functional. The fact that a thing can be both nourishing and lovely is a fingerprint left deliberately, by a God who is not merely competent but generous.

Then the two trees, both "in the midst of the garden." The tree of life is not magic; it is a sacrament, a visible pledge of a life God gives. And the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is not a booby trap. To "know good and evil" in Hebrew idiom is to decide for yourself what is good and what is evil — to be the one who draws the line rather than the one who receives it. The forbidden tree does not offer information. It offers autonomy.

Keep an eye on the tree of life, because Scripture does. It stands guarded at the end of chapter 3, disappears for a thousand pages, and reappears in the last chapter of the Bible, growing on both banks of the river in the middle of the city, its leaves for the healing of the nations (Rev. 22:2). What was closed in Eden is not lost. It is held in trust.

verseByVerse.quote: A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden, and there it divided and became four rivers. The name of the first is the Pishon. It is the one that flowed around the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold. And the gold of that land is good; bdellium and onyx stone are there. The name of the second river is the Gihon. It is the one that flowed around the whole land of Cush. And the name of the third river is the Tigris, which flows east of Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four rivers and a short geography lesson, and readers usually skim it. Two of the rivers are still on the map — the Tigris and the Euphrates run through modern Iraq — and two, the Pishon and the Gihon, cannot now be traced. The flood is likely to have redrawn the land beyond recognition. The passage is telling us that Eden was a real place in a real world, not a myth set nowhere.

But the detail that is easy to miss is the shopping list: gold, and it is good gold; bdellium, an aromatic resin; onyx stone. Those are not random minerals. Gold and onyx are exactly what the tabernacle and the priest's breastpiece will be made of (Exod. 25:7; 28:9–20), and the fragrant resin belongs with the holy incense. Eden is being described in the vocabulary of a sanctuary — which is why a river runs out of it to water the world, exactly as Ezekiel sees a river running out from under the temple threshold, deepening as it goes and turning the Dead Sea fresh (Ezek. 47:1–12).

So the garden is the first temple, and the last one looks like it. In the city at the end of Revelation there is a river of the water of life flowing from the throne, and no temple building at all, because the whole place has become what Eden was: the ground where God and his people are at home together (Rev. 22:1–3).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the sentence that settles what work is. "The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it." This is before the serpent, before the fruit, before the curse. Labour is not a punishment for sin. It is part of what humanity was made for on a morning when everything was still very good.

Which is a relief to anyone who has quietly suspected that Monday is the consequence of Adam's mistake. What the fall introduced was not work but the sweat, the thorns and the frustration of it (3:17–19). The work itself was already there, given by God to a man in a perfect world, because a person with nothing to do is not a person at rest but a person diminished.

The two verbs matter. Abad (work, serve) and shamar (keep, guard) are ordinary agricultural words — but they turn up together again in the law as the technical description of what the priests do in the tabernacle: to serve it and to guard it (Num. 3:7–8). Adam is not just a gardener. He is a priest in a sanctuary, and his cultivating is a form of worship. The man who does his job honestly, for God, in a world God made, is doing something closer to liturgy than he thinks (cf. Col. 3:23).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, "You may surely eat of every tree of the garden, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Notice the proportions before anything else. "You may surely eat of every tree of the garden" — the Hebrew doubles the verb for emphasis, eating you shall eat, a lavish and unrestricted grant. Then one exception. Every tree but one. The first divine command to a human being is overwhelmingly a permission.

Get this backwards and the whole Christian life sours. The serpent's entire strategy in the next chapter will be to reverse the ratio — to make one prohibition look like a fence around a life, when in fact it is a single peg in a field. Any picture of God that leads with what he forbids has begun reading at verse 17 and skipped verse 16.

And the prohibition is not arbitrary. The tree is the one place in the world where the man can say: I will decide what is good, and I will not be told. God does not hide it, does not fence it, does not remove it. Love that cannot be refused is not love, and obedience that has no alternative is not obedience. The tree is the door standing open, marked.

"In the day that you eat of it you shall surely die." Adam ate and lived another nine hundred years, so what happened? Everything the Bible means by death happened at once, in stages. The relationship died that afternoon — they hid in the bushes from the God who came looking for them. The body began to die from that day, and it took its time. And a further death lay behind both, the one Jesus called the second death. Sin does not always kill quickly. It always kills.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — The Creation of Woman and the First Marriage
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The creation of Eve completes the image of God in humanity and establishes marriage as the foundational human institution. God's declaration that "it is not good" for man to be alone is the first 'not good' in Scripture — interrupting the rhythm of 'it was good' from chapter 1 to underscore that human beings are inherently relational. The woman is not an afterthought but the completion of what the man could not be alone.
verseByVerse.theology: The creation of woman from Adam's side establishes both her equality (same flesh, same nature, image-bearer equally) and her distinctiveness (formed differently, described as helper and complement). The marriage covenant — leaving, cleaving, becoming one flesh — is the human institution that most directly reflects the divine image's relational nature. Jesus will later appeal to this text (Matt. 19:4–6) as the permanent basis of marriage, and Paul will read it as a type of Christ and the church (Eph. 5:31–32).
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes that 'helper' (ezer) is not a term of subordination — it is used of God himself as Israel's helper (Ps. 121:2). The woman is a helper in the sense of completing what is lacking — providing what the man cannot provide for himself. Keller observes that the nakedness without shame (v.25) describes a state of perfect transparency and trust between the man and woman, which sin will shatter and redemption will ultimately restore.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD God said, "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six times in chapter 1 God looked at what he had made and said it was good. Once he raised it to very good. Now, in a world with no sin in it, God looks at something and says it is not good — and it is a man on his own. "It is not good that the man should be alone."

Which means loneliness is not a symptom of the fall. It was diagnosed before there was anything wrong with the world. The ache a person feels in an empty house is not a character flaw or a lack of spiritual maturity; it is the God-given signal of a creature made in the image of a God who is himself never solitary. He does not scold Adam for the ache. He goes to work on it.

"A helper fit for him." The English word helper has done a lot of damage, because it sounds like an assistant, a junior, a pair of extra hands. The Hebrew is ezer, and its most frequent use in the Old Testament is of God himself: "The LORD is my helper; I will not fear" (Ps. 118:6–7; cf. Ps. 121:2). It is a word for the one who comes with strength to supply what you cannot supply yourself. And "fit for him" is literally corresponding to him — his counterpart, facing him, his equal and his opposite number, neither his echo nor his rival.

The remedy God gives here is marriage, and the chapter is going there. But notice what the diagnosis is: aloneness. Marriage answers it for many, and never completely for anyone. The unmarried reader has not been left out of Genesis 2:18 — he has been told, by God, that his need for others is real and named, and that the answer to it is a people, which is precisely what God is building (cf. Ps. 68:6; Mark 3:34–35).

verseByVerse.quote: Now out of the ground the LORD God had formed every beast of the field and every bird of the heavens and brought them to the man to see what he would call them. And whatever the man called every living creature, that was its name. The man gave names to all livestock and to the birds of the heavens and to every beast of the field. But for Adam there was not found a helper fit for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God brings the animals to the man "to see what he would call them," and the man names every one. This is the image of God at work: the God who named Day and Night in chapter 1 hands the naming of the creatures to his viceroy and stands back to watch. It is delegated authority exercised in real freedom — whatever the man called it, "that was its name." God did not correct him once.

But the parade has a second purpose, and it is not zoology. "But for Adam there was not found a helper fit for him." One after another they come, and one after another they are magnificent and wrong. He is looking down a line of living creatures, every one of them made by the same hands that made him, and finding no face at his own level in the whole of creation.

God knew this before the first animal was led up. The search was staged so that the man would feel the lack before he was given the gift, and would therefore recognise it when it came. That is a pattern God has never given up. He lets his people arrive at the end of their own resources first — the barren womb, the empty jar, the four days in the tomb — because a gift received after the search has failed is received as a gift and not as a discovery.

verseByVerse.quote: So the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon the man, and while he slept took one of his ribs and closed up its place with flesh. And the rib that the LORD God had taken from the man he made into a woman and brought her to the man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God puts the man to sleep. The one human being alive is unconscious while the most important thing in the chapter happens to him. He contributes nothing, witnesses nothing, and wakes to find the answer to his loneliness standing in front of him. Every good thing in Scripture comes to people like this.

The word usually translated rib, tsela, means side; everywhere else in the Old Testament it is architectural, the side of the ark or the side chamber of the temple. And the verb in verse 22 is not made or formed but banah, built. The woman is built from the man's side — not from his head to rule him and not from his feet to be walked on, as the old preachers said, but from his side, from under his arm, near his heart. The picture is of two halves of one structure.

Then the last clause, and it is the tenderest thing so far: God "brought her to the man." He does not leave them to find each other. He conducts her, like a father walking a bride up an aisle at the first wedding, where God gives away the bride he has just made. Marriage begins as something God does, not something two people arrange.

Christians have long noticed the shape of this, and it is not fanciful: a bridegroom falls into a deep sleep, his side is opened, and out of the wound comes a bride he did not have before. On a hill outside Jerusalem another bridegroom slept the deeper sleep, and a soldier opened his side with a spear (John 19:34), and out of that came a people. Paul quotes this passage, then says plainly that he is speaking about Christ and the church (Eph. 5:31–32).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the man said, "This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first recorded human words are a poem. Not a request, not a complaint, not a survey of the property — a shout of recognition with a rhythm in it. "This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh."

"At last" carries the weight of the whole failed parade. He has looked at every living creature on earth and found nothing that answered him, and now he looks up. The Hebrew opens with something like a cry: this one, this time, this is it. Whatever else marriage has become in a tired world, its first note in Scripture is astonishment.

"Bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh" is not romantic language in Hebrew; it is covenant language, used later of a family binding itself to a king (2 Sam. 5:1). He is saying: this is my own kin, my own kind, my own people. Then the naming — ishshah from ish, woman from man, a wordplay that survives even into English. He names her as he named the animals, but the name he gives her is his own.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore." The narrator steps out of the story to tell the reader what all of it was for. One man, one woman, brought together by God — and from that single event comes the pattern for every marriage since. Three verbs carry it.

Leave. A new household is founded, and the old one loosens its claim. This is the striking verb, since in that culture the son brought his wife into his father's house, not the reverse. The word means to forsake. It does not mean dishonouring parents; it means that a man's first loyalty on earth has moved. More marriages are strangled by a cord never cut than by any dramatic sin.

Hold fast. The word is used of glue and of a soldier's hand welded to his sword in battle (2 Sam. 23:10), and it is used of Israel clinging to the LORD (Deut. 10:20). It is a covenant word, not a feeling word. It describes what you do when the feeling is not there — which, in every long marriage, is a great many Tuesdays.

One flesh. More than the body, though certainly not less: a shared life, shared name, shared money, shared shame, shared future. And note the tense in the account itself — this is stated as fact before the fall, before children, before any law about marriage exists. Marriage is not a religious invention. It is written into creation, which is exactly why the Lord Jesus reached past every rabbinic argument of his day and settled the divorce question by quoting this verse: "What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate" (Matt. 19:4–6).

And then Paul goes further than anyone would dare who had not been taught it. He quotes Genesis 2:24 word for word, and says: "This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church" (Eph. 5:31–32). Marriage was never the point. It was the picture. From the beginning God was sketching, in the most ordinary and universal human arrangement, the one thing he had always intended to do — leave the glory of heaven, take a bride who could not be worthy of him, and hold fast to her for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed." That is the last sentence before everything goes wrong, and it is a description of a state most people alive have never known for an hour.

Nakedness here is more than clothing. It is total exposure with nothing to hide and no wish to hide it — fully seen and fully welcome, at the same time. No performance, no impression management, no version of himself that he shows her and no version she keeps back. Nothing in either of them needed covering, because there was nothing in either of them that could not bear the light.

Test it against the way you actually live. There is almost certainly something you would not want said aloud in a room of people who know you — something from years ago, or something from last week. That instinct to cover is not native to being human. It is three verses away, and it arrives the moment sin does: they sewed fig leaves together, and they hid (3:7–8). Shame is not humility. It is the wound the fall left in the place where openness used to be.

And it is the wound the gospel is aimed at. To be known completely and loved anyway is what the human heart has been trying to get back to ever since this verse, and it is exactly what God offers — the one who searches the heart and knows everything there is to find has, in Christ, already dealt with all of it (cf. Ps. 139:1–4; Rom. 8:1). There will be a garden again, and a people in it with nothing to hide.

2.theology:
The Garden as Temple. Eden is the original sacred space — the place where heaven and earth overlap, where God walks with humanity. The imagery recurs in the tabernacle (gold, cherubim, guarded entrance) and temple. Revelation 21–22 closes the canon with the new Jerusalem as a garden-city in which the temple is the Lord God himself: God and humanity dwelling together without barrier, the original vision of Eden fully restored and surpassed.

The Second Adam. Paul's argument in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15 turns on the contrast between Adam and Christ. Adam, formed from dust, given every permission, faced one prohibition, failed, and brought death to all. Christ, the eternal Son who took on flesh, faced every temptation the first Adam faced, obeyed perfectly, and brought life to all in him. The garden of Gethsemane is the counter-garden of Eden: where Adam chose his will over God's, Christ prayed "not my will, but yours be done."
2.examples:
Then: The garden-temple imagery was immediately legible to an Israelite audience familiar with the tabernacle. The cherubim guarding Eden's entrance (3:24) matched the cherubim woven into the tabernacle veil. The gold and onyx of Eden (2:11–12) matched the temple's materials. The man's priestly vocation prepared Israel to understand the priesthood as a restoration project — attempting to restore, through ritual, the access to God's presence lost at the fall.

Now: The theology of work in Genesis 2 is urgently needed in a culture that either deifies career (finding identity in productivity) or denigrates it (work as mere necessity). Genesis 2 says: work is a gift before it is a burden, a vocation before it is a job. And the chapter's account of gender and marriage — the complementarity of male and female, the one-flesh covenant, the goodness of embodiment — flows from creation design, not cultural construction. To recover a theology of Genesis 2 is to recover a theology of the human person.

3.title: The Fall
