Have you eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?"<sup>12</sup>The man said, "The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit of the tree, and I ate."<sup>13</sup>Then the LORD God said to the woman, "What is this that you have done?" The woman said, "The serpent deceived me, and I ate."<sup>14</sup>The LORD God said to the serpent, "Because you have done this, cursed are you above all livestock and above all beasts of the field; on your belly you shall go, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life.<sup>15</sup>I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel."<sup>16</sup>To the woman he said, "I will surely multiply your pain in childbearing; in pain you shall bring forth children. Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you."<sup>17</sup>And to Adam he said, "Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you, 'You shall not eat of it,' cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life;<sup>18</sup>thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you; and you shall eat the plants of the field.<sup>19</sup>By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, till you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return."<sup>20</sup>The man called his wife's name Eve, because she was the mother of all living.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them.<sup>22</sup>Then the LORD God said, "Behold, the man has become like one of us in knowing good and evil. Now, lest he reach out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat, and live forever—"<sup>23</sup>therefore the LORD God sent him out from the garden of Eden to work the ground from which he was taken.<sup>24</sup>He drove out the man, and at the east of the garden of Eden he placed the cherubim and a flaming sword that turned every way to guard the way to the tree of life.
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the hinge of all human history — the chapter that makes every other chapter in the Bible necessary. Without the fall, there is no need for a flood, a covenant, a law, a temple, a sacrifice, a prophet, a Messiah, a cross, or a resurrection. Every subsequent movement of Scripture is a movement of redemption, and redemption only makes sense in light of what is lost here.

The serpent's strategy is a masterpiece of misdirection. He begins not with a command but with a question: "Did God actually say?" — casting doubt on the divine word, then on the divine motive. The lie is plausible. "You will be like God" — and they already were, made in his image. The serpent offers a counterfeit of what they already possess. This is the anatomy of every temptation: the distortion of a good thing into a god-thing.

But before any judgment is announced, God speaks the first gospel — the protevangelium of verse 15: the seed of the woman will crush the serpent's head. And before expelling them from the garden, God clothes them with skins — the first sacrifice, the first covering of shame by divine grace. The gospel is embedded in the fall itself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Temptation and the Fall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 3 is the hinge of all Scripture — the pivot between creation's goodness and the fallen world we inhabit. The serpent's strategy is subtle: not a frontal assault on God's existence but a quiet questioning of his goodness. Eve is drawn into dialogue, then doubt, then desire, then action. Adam stands passively by and eats. In a moment, the entire fabric of human life with God is torn. The nakedness and hiding that follow are the symptoms of a rupture that touches every dimension of existence.
verseByVerse.theology: The fall narrative reveals the anatomy of sin: the serpent distorts God's word ('Did God actually say?'), denies God's judgment ('You will not surely die'), and substitutes a counterfeit promise ('You will be like God'). Eve evaluates the fruit by three criteria — good for food, pleasant to the eyes, desired to make one wise — which John will recognize as the world's three temptations (1 John 2:16). The essence of the fall is not eating fruit but the human creature asserting autonomy from the Creator, claiming the right to determine good and evil independently of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller on Genesis 3: the serpent's lie is not that there is no God but that God cannot be trusted — that his commands are restrictions rather than gifts, and that humans can flourish better on their own terms than on his. This is the lie at the heart of every sin: that God is withholding something good. The hiding in the garden is the first evidence of a guilty conscience — conscience is the echo of God's law written on the heart, producing shame and fear before the God whom sin has offended.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the serpent was more crafty than any other beast of the field that the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, "Did God actually say, 'You shall not eat of any tree in the garden'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Now the serpent." No introduction, no explanation of where he came from. The chapter opens with a creature already in the garden and already hostile, and Genesis simply does not tell us how evil got into a world God had called very good. That silence is deliberate and it should be respected. Scripture explains what sin is and what God has done about it; it never offers a tidy account of its origin, because there is no explanation that would not, in the end, excuse it.

What we are told is that he is a beast "that the LORD God had made" — a creature, not a rival power, not a dark god of equal weight. Whatever else this chapter is, it is not a battle between two equals. Later Scripture identifies the voice behind the animal plainly enough: "that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world" (Rev. 12:9; cf. John 8:44).

And now watch the first sentence Satan ever speaks to a human being, because his method has not changed since. "Did God actually say...?" It is not an assertion. It is a question, and a friendly-sounding one, and it does three things at once. It puts God's word up for discussion. It exaggerates the restriction into something monstrous — "any tree in the garden," when God had forbidden exactly one. And it never mentions the generosity at all.

The attack is not aimed at her behaviour. It is aimed at her picture of God. Get a person to believe that God is essentially a withholder — a being whose default posture is No — and the disobedience follows almost as a matter of course. Which is why the most dangerous question you will ever be asked is not "is this wrong?" but "is God really good?"

verseByVerse.quote: And the woman said to the serpent, "We may eat of the fruit of the trees in the garden, but God said, 'You shall not eat of the fruit of the tree that is in the midst of the garden, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
She answers, and she is trying to defend God. That is the sad thing about this exchange: she is not on the serpent's side. But three small slips have already crept into her reply, and together they show the ground shifting under her feet.

God's word was lavish — "you may surely eat of every tree of the garden," the verb doubled for emphasis. She reports it flatly: "we may eat." The generosity has gone. Then she adds a clause God never spoke: "neither shall you touch it." Nobody had said that. It is the instinct that builds a fence around the fence, and it always makes God look harsher than he is. And finally she softens the penalty. God said, "you shall surely die," doubling the verb again; she says "lest you die," as if it were a risk rather than a certainty.

Less generous, more restrictive, less serious. That is what happens to God's word in the hands of someone who has begun listening to a second voice about it, and it happens without any conscious decision to distort anything. Nothing here is a lie yet. It is drift.

Which is a reason to know what God has actually said, in his own words, rather than the general impression of it you carry around. The version of Scripture a person defends under pressure is the version he has been feeding on, and vague recollection is no defence at all. The Lord Jesus, tempted in a wilderness rather than a garden, answered every approach with a text quoted exactly (Matt. 4:4, 7, 10).

verseByVerse.quote: But the serpent said to the woman, "You will not surely die. For God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the question becomes a flat contradiction: "You will not surely die." The serpent takes the precise words of God — the doubled verb, "dying you shall die" — and negates them syllable for syllable. This is the moment a suggestion becomes a lie, and Jesus put his finger on exactly this verse when he called the devil "a liar and the father of lies" (John 8:44).

But the second half is more dangerous than the first, because it is nearly true. "For God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil." Their eyes will indeed be opened (v.7). They will indeed come to know good and evil (v.22, from God's own lips). The most effective lies are not fabrications; they are accurate facts wired to a false motive.

And the false motive is the sting: God is holding out on you. He knows. He has information he is not sharing and a status he is protecting, and the rule is there to keep you small. The serpent turns the one prohibition in a world of gifts into evidence of a mean streak in God.

Two things are already spoiled before any fruit is eaten. She is invited to doubt God's honesty and to doubt God's goodness, and the appeal is to become "like God" — which is bitterly funny, because Genesis 1:27 says she already is. She was made in his image. She is being offered, as a prize, something she already possessed as a gift, on terms that will cost her everything.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"So when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate." Three appetites, and none of them is evil in itself. Food is good. Beauty is good — chapter 2 said God made the trees "pleasant to the sight" for that very reason. Wisdom is good; Proverbs will spend nine chapters recommending it. Sin is almost never a desire for something bad. It is a good desire pursued outside the will of God.

John seems to have this verse open in front of him when he writes of "the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life" (1 John 2:16) — the same three, still working. And they worked in a wilderness too: turn these stones to bread, throw yourself down and be seen, take the kingdoms without the cross. The second Adam heard all three and did not eat.

Then the phrase that changes the shape of the whole Bible: "and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate." With her. Not away at the far end of the garden, not off working. Beside her, through the entire conversation, silent. The one who had received the command directly from God (2:16–17), the one appointed to work and keep — that is, to guard — this sanctuary, watches a creature contradict his Maker and says nothing.

Which is why the New Testament, when it names the guilty party, does not name Eve. "Sin came into the world through one man" (Rom. 5:12); "in Adam all die" (1 Cor. 15:22). The passive silence of the one who should have spoken is not a lesser failure than the active reaching of the one who was deceived. There is a whole world of ordinary Christian cowardice in the words who was with her.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked. And they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then the eyes of both were opened." The serpent kept his word — and this is what the promised enlightenment amounted to. They were promised the knowledge of gods and they got the knowledge of their own nakedness. Every temptation overpromises and underdelivers, and the receipt always arrives afterwards.

Yesterday they were naked and not ashamed (2:25). The nakedness has not changed; the seeing has. Something in them now recoils from being known, and the first instinct of fallen humanity is not to repent but to cover. Fig leaves are sewn together — the first manufacturing in history, and it is the manufacture of concealment.

Every human being has a version of the fig leaf, and most of us wear several. The carefully edited account of a difficult year. The competence that is worn where the fear is. The busyness that keeps anyone from asking the real question. The religious performance that would collapse if someone saw the private life behind it. What you are covering with, you already know; the point of this verse is that the covering never works, and that it began here.

Notice too what leaves are: temporary. They wilt within a day. Before this chapter ends, God will replace them with something that had to die first (v.21).

verseByVerse.quote: And they heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden. But the LORD God called to the man and said to him, "Where are you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And they heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day." The phrasing implies a habit. This was not the first time; it was the usual hour, the ordinary appointment, and it is the loveliest picture in the chapter — God walking, at the breeziest part of the day, in a garden he made, to be with people he loves.

And they hide behind trees. Consider how absurd that is, and then consider how familiar. Nothing was hidden; the hiding was for their sake, not his. And yet they did it, because guilt does not make a person want to be found. It is the same instinct that keeps a man out of church for a year after a sin nobody knows about, or leaves a prayer unprayed because the one thing he cannot bear is to turn towards God with it.

"But the LORD God called to the man." He does not leave. He does not withdraw in disgust and let them work out the consequences. He comes into the garden and he calls, and the entire Bible is in that verb — a God who comes looking. Sin makes people run from God; grace is God walking towards them anyway.

"Where are you?" He is not lost, and neither are they. This is the first question in the Bible, and it is not a request for information; it is an invitation to come out. God begins the interrogation of the human race by giving the guilty man an opening to speak. Long afterwards a Saviour would tell a story about a father who scanned the road, and would say of himself that the Son of Man came "to seek and to save the lost" (Luke 19:10). The seeking started here.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself." He said, "Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Adam answers, and every word of it is true, and all of it is evasion. "I heard the sound of you... I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself." He names the fear. He names the nakedness. He names the hiding. He does not name the sin.

Sit with that, because it is the most common shape of half-repentance. A man will confess to being stressed, or ashamed, or distant, or struggling — all true, all painful to admit, and all of it downstream of the one thing he has not said. It is possible to be genuinely miserable about the consequences of sin and never once mention the sin.

So God asks two questions that close the escape route. "Who told you that you were naked?" — that is, where did this new self-consciousness come from, and whose voice have you been listening to? And then, with no room left: "Have you eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?" It is a yes-or-no question about a specific act.

And it is asked by a God who already knows the answer. He is not gathering evidence; he is drawing out a confession, which is the only thing that could do Adam any good. God never asks a question because he needs the information. He asks because the man needs to hear himself say it (cf. 1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.quote: The man said, "The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit of the tree, and I ate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit of the tree, and I ate." Follow the pointing finger. It goes first to his wife — the woman he had sung a poem about one chapter ago, the one he called bone of his bones. She is now "the woman." And then it travels further, and it lands on God: the woman whom you gave. The gift he had wept for gratitude over is now the evidence for the prosecution, and the Giver is in the dock.

Three words at the end are all that remain of an honest answer: "and I ate." True, and buried at the end of a sentence built to make sure nobody hears it.

This is what sin does to love. Twenty-four hours earlier these two stood naked in front of each other with nothing to hide; now, under pressure, he will hand her over to save himself. Every marriage that has curdled into blame is running this verse again. And the deeper move is the one aimed upward — the suggestion that if God had arranged things differently, none of this need have happened. Very few people say that out loud. A great many have thought it in a hospital corridor.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD God said to the woman, "What is this that you have done?" The woman said, "The serpent deceived me, and I ate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God turns to the woman and asks a question with grief in it: "What is this that you have done?" And she does the same thing her husband did, one step down the chain: "The serpent deceived me, and I ate."

Notice that it is true. Paul says so explicitly — she was deceived (1 Tim. 2:14). Unlike Adam's answer, hers is not a distortion of the facts. And it changes nothing, because deception is not the same as innocence. Being lied to does not remove responsibility for what you did after believing the lie. The buck has now been passed twice, and there is nobody left to pass it to; the serpent is not asked anything at all.

But notice also what both of them do get right, and it is the only hopeful thing in the paragraph: each one ends with the same two words. "And I ate." Under all the deflection, the confession is there. God has extracted from both of them the sentence that makes forgiveness possible. Excuses do not cancel the admission buried inside them, and God is patient enough to wait for it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–24 — The Curse and the Expulsion from the Garden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The consequences of the fall are pronounced in three stages: curse upon the serpent, consequences for the woman, consequences for the man and the ground. But embedded in the curse on the serpent is the first gospel proclamation — the protoevangelium — the promise that the seed of the woman will crush the serpent's head. Judgment falls, but within the judgment is the seed of redemption.
verseByVerse.theology: The curses describe the distortion of creation's good structures: the serpent's domain is diminished, the woman's pain in childbearing and her marital relationship are disordered, the man's work becomes toil against a resistant ground, and death — already threatened — becomes the inevitable end. But these are distortions, not destructions: childbearing still happens, work still produces food, marriage still exists. Sin has corrupted but not annihilated creation's goodness. The expulsion from the garden preserves the terrible mercy of verse 22: access to the tree of life in a fallen state would mean eternal life in sin — the expulsion is judgment that contains grace.
verseByVerse.examples: The protoevangelium (v.15) is the seed from which all Messianic prophecy grows. Waltke traces the 'seed' theme through Genesis (Seth, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, David) to its fulfillment in Christ, who is the seed of the woman born under the law (Gal. 4:4) who crushed the serpent at the cross (Col. 2:15; Rom. 16:20). Calvin calls v.15 the mother of all promises — the first ray of gospel light in the darkness of the fall.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD God said to the serpent, "Because you have done this, cursed are you above all livestock and above all beasts of the field; on your belly you shall go, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life. I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God does not ask the serpent a question. There is no interrogation, no invitation to explain — only sentence. "Cursed are you." This is the first time the word curse appears in Scripture, and it falls first on the tempter.

"On your belly you shall go, and dust you shall eat." Snakes do not literally eat dirt; this is the language of total defeat, the posture of a beaten enemy licking the ground before a conqueror (cf. Ps. 72:9; Isa. 49:23). The creature who offered to raise humanity to the level of God is put on his face in the dust that humanity was made from.

And then verse 15, which the church has called for centuries the protoevangelium — the gospel before the gospel, the first promise of a Saviour, spoken in a curse on the devil rather than in a comfort to the man and woman, who are standing there listening in. "I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring."

God himself will start the war. Left to themselves the human race had just made peace with the serpent; God breaks that alliance by sovereign act, and the first sign of grace in a fallen world is that people begin to hate the thing they had agreed with. Then the singular appears: "he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel." Out of the woman's line, one will come. The wounds are not equal — a crushed head against a struck heel — but neither is painless. The serpent-crusher will be hurt in the crushing.

Everything after this page is the tracing of that offspring: through Seth, and Noah, and Abraham, and Judah, and David, and finally to a woman in Nazareth. Paul knew exactly where it was going: "God sent forth his Son, born of woman" (Gal. 4:4), and "the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet" (Rom. 16:20). On a Friday afternoon the heel was struck through with an iron nail, and by that wound the head was broken (cf. Col. 2:15; Heb. 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: To the woman he said, "I will surely multiply your pain in childbearing; in pain you shall bring forth children. Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman's sentence touches the two relationships in which she was most to find joy: her children and her husband. "I will surely multiply your pain in childbearing." Not invent — multiply. The bearing of children remains a blessing; it is now a blessing that costs blood. Every labour ward is a place where the goodness of creation and the damage of the fall are visible in the same hour.

"Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you." This is one of the harder lines in Genesis, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a shrug. The same two words — desire and rule — appear again four verses later in the next chapter, where sin's "desire is for" Cain and he must "rule over it" (4:7). There the desire is a desire to master, and the ruling is a struggle to hold down. Read the two together, and the sentence describes a war: she will strain against him, and he will answer with domination.

Which means this is a description of the wreckage, not a job description. God is not commanding husbands to rule; he is telling a woman what the fall has done to the one-flesh union of 2:24, where two equals faced each other. Every marriage that has settled into a cold contest of wills is living inside this verse — and every husband who has ever used a Bible to justify pushing his wife around has mistaken a curse for a command.

And there is a rescue, not merely a diagnosis. The New Testament sends husbands to a different model altogether — not rule but the cross: "Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her" (Eph. 5:25). Grace does not merely forgive Genesis 3:16. It works backwards through it.

verseByVerse.quote: And to Adam he said, "Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you, 'You shall not eat of it,' cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you; and you shall eat the plants of the field.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Because you have listened to the voice of your wife." The charge is not that he took her advice; it is that in the one moment he had been given a command directly by God, he took his instructions from somewhere else. He had the word. He chose the other voice.

And then the curse itself is aimed past him: "cursed is the ground because of you." God does not say cursed are you — that was said to the serpent. The man is not cursed; his world is. And that is a mercy hiding inside a judgment, because a cursed man could not be redeemed, while a cursed ground can be restored.

"Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you." The world will now resist the work it was made for. Every gardener knows this and so does every teacher, nurse, parent and administrator: things do not simply go well. They have to be fought for, and the ground pushes back. Frustration at work is not a personal failing or a sign that you are in the wrong job; it is Genesis 3:18, and it is universal.

Paul says the whole creation was "subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope" — and that it is groaning, like a woman in labour, for the day it is set free (Rom. 8:20–22). Even the thorns were given in hope. Which is why it is not an accident that when the Son of God took the curse on himself, they pressed a crown of thorns onto his head.

verseByVerse.quote: By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, till you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread." Not by the sweat of his hands — his face. The picture is of a man labouring hard enough that it runs down his forehead, and the food he gets for it is bread. Bare sufficiency, hard won.

"Till you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return." The sentence God pronounced in 2:17 has arrived, and it is spoken with an awful symmetry. The word for man was adam and the word for ground was adamah; he was lifted out of it and he is going back into it. Death in the Bible is not natural. It is a returning, an undoing of the making.

Every funeral you have ever attended is this verse being read out loud, which is why the old burial service says earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust. And every human strategy for avoiding it — the diet, the surgery, the frantic photographs, the refusal to make a will — is an argument with Genesis 3:19 that nobody has ever won.

Except one. The last Adam went into the ground too, and he did not stay in it, and the promise attached to him is not that his people will avoid the dust but that they will come out of it: "we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven" (1 Cor. 15:49). Death is the last enemy, and it is an enemy that has already been served notice (1 Cor. 15:26).

verseByVerse.quote: The man called his wife's name Eve, because she was the mother of all living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man has just heard that he is going to die. And the next thing he does is give his wife a name that means life. "Adam called his wife's name Eve, because she was the mother of all living."

This is faith, and it is the first act of it in the Bible. He has heard verse 15 — that from her offspring a deliverer will come — and he takes God at his word before there is a single piece of evidence. Standing in the wreckage of everything he had, under sentence, with the ground already turning against him, he looks at the woman he had blamed an hour ago and calls her Life.

There is also a repair in it. His last words about her were an accusation (v.12). Now he names her, and names her in hope. Something has changed in the man between verse 12 and verse 20, and what changed was that God made a promise.

Faith always looks like this: not a feeling of optimism but a decision to treat God's word as more solid than the facts in front of you. He had a death sentence in his ears and he named his wife after a future he could not see.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them." Read it slowly, because in twenty words the gospel is sketched for the first time.

They had made their own covering, and it was leaves — free, immediate, costing nothing, and inadequate. God rejects it, without comment, and replaces it. His covering is skin, and skin comes off an animal, and an animal that gives up its skin has died. Somewhere just outside the frame of this verse is the first death in the Bible, and it is not the death of the guilty. Blood is shed in Eden so that shame can be covered, and it is God who does the killing and God who does the clothing.

Everything in the sacrificial system is here in seed. The whole book of Leviticus is an expansion of Genesis 3:21 — that sin is covered at the cost of a life, that the sinner does not provide the covering, that God does. And when the last sacrifice was made, it was made by God out of himself: "for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Cor. 5:21).

And watch the verb, because God does not hand them the garments. He clothes them. The Judge kneels down in front of the condemned and dresses them with his own hands. That is the God of the Bible, three verses after the curse — sentence pronounced in full and mercy administered personally, and neither one softening the other.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD God said, "Behold, the man has become like one of us in knowing good and evil. Now, lest he reach out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat, and live forever—" therefore the LORD God sent him out from the garden of Eden to work the ground from which he was taken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, the man has become like one of us in knowing good and evil." The serpent's promise came true, and it is the emptiest victory in history. They know good and evil now — not as God knows them, from above and untouched, but as a man knows a disease he has caught.

Then God speaks a sentence he never finishes: "Now, lest he reach out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat, and live forever—" The line breaks off. What is on the other side of that dash is too grim to say: a human race fixed for ever in its ruined state, sin made permanent, no death and therefore no end to it and no way back.

So the expulsion is not only a punishment. It is a rescue. To be shut out of the garden means the fall is not final. It means the story can still go somewhere. Death, the sentence of verse 19, turns out to stand between us and something worse — an unending life in a body and a heart like this one.

"Therefore the LORD God sent him out from the garden of Eden to work the ground from which he was taken." Even the exile keeps his vocation. The work of 2:15 goes with him out of the gate, harder now and among thorns, but not cancelled. Grace leaves a man something to do.

verseByVerse.quote: He drove out the man, and at the east of the garden of Eden he placed the cherubim and a flaming sword that turned every way to guard the way to the tree of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"He drove out the man." The verb is violent; it is used later of driving out the nations from Canaan. The gate is shut, and it is shut hard.

And the guard set on it is not a fence but cherubim with a flaming sword turning every way. Cherubim in Scripture are the creatures associated with the immediate presence of God — they are embroidered on the tabernacle curtain and carved over the ark, above the mercy seat. Their appearance here says what the whole Old Testament will keep saying: a sinner cannot simply stroll back into the presence of a holy God. The way to the tree of life is barred by a sword, and it is barred on God's initiative.

Which makes the last chapters of the Bible almost unbearable to read, if you have this verse in mind. The tree of life reappears, and there is no sword and no guard, and the gates of the city "will never be shut" (Rev. 21:25; 22:2). What happened in between? The sword did not vanish. It fell — on the one who stood in the sinner's place, so that the way in was opened by the same blade that had closed it (cf. Zech. 13:7; Heb. 10:19–20).

Chapter 3 ends with a locked garden and a drawn sword, and the whole rest of Scripture is God's work to get his people back in. He did not open the gate by lowering the standard. He came through it himself, from the inside, and took the sword.

3.theology:
The Anatomy of Sin. Genesis 3 gives the Bible's most complete account of how sin operates. It begins with doubt about the word of God (v.1), moves to distrust of the character of God (vv.4–5), leads to autonomous action against the will of God (v.6), and produces shame, fear, and broken relationship (vv.7–13). Keller identifies the root as the displacement of God from the center of life — the claim, in practice if not theory, that I am a better judge of my good than my Creator is.

The Protevangelium and Redemptive History. Verse 15 is the seed from which all of redemptive history grows. Every subsequent act of God in Scripture — the call of Abraham, the exodus, the Davidic covenant, the prophets, the incarnation — is an unfolding of this one promise. The enmity between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent is the great conflict structuring all of history, and its resolution is the cross and resurrection. To read Genesis 3 without verse 15 is to miss the point of the chapter entirely.
3.examples:
Then: Ancient Near Eastern creation-and-fall narratives — the Gilgamesh epic, the Adapa myth — portrayed sin as a cosmic accident or work of rival gods. Genesis 3 subverts them all: sin is the free act of human creatures endowed with the image of God. The curse on the ground (v.17) and painful childbirth (v.16) were daily realities for ancient Israel; Genesis 3 explained not just that these things are hard but why, and with the implication that the curse can be reversed.

Now: The fall answers what every philosophy and therapy system eventually confronts: what is wrong with us? Not ignorance, not environment, not psychology — but moral rebellion against the Creator, a structural disorder of the will requiring not improvement but redemption. The gospel begins with Genesis 3's diagnosis: we are not basically good people who occasionally do bad things, but fallen image-bearers who need a new creation. And it ends with Genesis 3's promise: the seed of the woman has come, and the serpent's head is crushed.

4.title: Am I My Brother's Keeper?
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain, saying, "I have gotten a man with the help of the LORD."<sup>2</sup>And again, she bore his brother Abel. Now Abel was a keeper of sheep, and Cain a worker of the ground.<sup>3</sup>In the course of time Cain brought to the LORD an offering of the fruit of the ground,<sup>4</sup>and Abel also brought of the firstborn of his flock and of their fat portions. And the LORD had regard for Abel and his offering,<sup>5</sup>but for Cain and his offering he had no regard. So Cain was very angry, and his face fell.<sup>6</sup>The LORD said to Cain, "Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen?<sup>7</sup>If you do well, will you not be accepted? And if you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is for you, and you must rule over it."<sup>8</sup>Cain spoke to Abel his brother. And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him.<sup>9</sup>Then the LORD said to Cain, "Where is Abel your brother?" He said, "I do not know; am I my brother's keeper?"<sup>10</sup>And the LORD said, "What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood is crying to me from the ground.<sup>11</sup>And now you are cursed from the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand.<sup>12</sup>When you work the ground, it shall no longer yield to you its strength. You shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth."<sup>13</sup>Cain said to the LORD, "My punishment is greater than I can bear.<sup>14</sup>Behold, you have driven me today away from the ground, and from your face I shall be hidden. I shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth, and whoever finds me will kill me."<sup>15</sup>Then the LORD said to him, "Not so! If anyone kills Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold." And the LORD put a mark on Cain, lest any who found him should attack him.<sup>16</sup>Then Cain went away from the presence of the LORD and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden.<sup>17</sup>Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch. When he built a city, he called the name of the city after the name of his son, Enoch.<sup>18</sup>To Enoch was born Irad, and Irad fathered Mehujael, and Mehujael fathered Methushael, and Methushael fathered Lamech.<sup>19</sup>And Lamech took two wives. The name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah.<sup>20</sup>Adah bore Jabal; he was the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock.<sup>21</sup>His brother's name was Jubal; he was the father of all those who play the lyre and pipe.<sup>22</sup>Zillah also bore Tubal-cain; he was the forger of all instruments of bronze and iron. The sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah.<sup>23</sup>Lamech said to his wives: "Adah and Zillah, hear my voice; you wives of Lamech, listen to what I say: I have killed a man for wounding me, a young man for striking me.<sup>24</sup>If Cain's revenge is sevenfold, then Lamech's is seventy-sevenfold."<sup>25</sup>And Adam knew his wife again, and she bore a son and called his name Seth, for she said, "God has appointed for me another offspring instead of Abel, for Cain killed him."<sup>26</sup>To Seth also a son was born, and he called his name Enosh. At that time people began to call upon the name of the LORD.
4.overview:
The fall of Genesis 3 moves immediately into fratricide in Genesis 4. The speed is deliberate: sin does not stay contained. Once the relationship with God is broken, the relationship between human beings fractures next, then the relationship with the ground (v.12). The spread of sin is not a trickle but a flood — and that flood is coming.

The contrast between Cain and Abel cuts deeper than jealousy. The LORD had "regard" for Abel and his offering, not for Cain's. Hebrews 11:4 says Abel offered his sacrifice "by faith," suggesting the issue was not the material offered but the orientation of the heart. Worship is always first a matter of the heart. God's gracious warning to Cain (v.7) is extraordinary: before the murder, God gives him the opportunity to see what is happening and choose differently. Cain refuses.

The chapter closes with hope in the darkness: "At that time people began to call upon the name of the LORD" (v.26). Even after murder, the human impulse toward the Creator is not extinguished. The line of Seth — those who call on the name of the LORD — will carry the seed of the woman through every catastrophe until the Promised One arrives.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Cain and Abel: The First Murder
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fall of Genesis 3 bears its first fruit in Genesis 4: fratricide. Cain and Abel are the first human brothers, and the first human murder is a brother's murder. The story moves from worship (offerings) to warning (God's counsel to Cain) to violence (the killing of Abel) to judgment (Cain cursed and exiled). The trajectory of sin — from one tree to one murder — accelerates rapidly, and the question of how fallen humanity will live east of Eden is posed in its starkest form.
verseByVerse.theology: The contrast between Cain and Abel is not occupational (farmer versus shepherd) but spiritual: God regards Abel's offering and not Cain's. The reason given implicitly relates to the condition of the offerer rather than the category of the gift (Heb. 11:4 says Abel offered 'by faith'). Cain's anger and downcast face reveal a heart that expected acceptance on his own terms. God's counsel to Cain — 'sin is crouching at the door; its desire is for you, but you must rule over it' — is among the most urgent pastoral words in Scripture: the battle with sin is real, personal, and winnable only by active resistance.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller on Genesis 4: the root of Cain's sin is the same as the root of the original fall — self-determination and the refusal to accept God's terms. Cain wants worship on his terms, brotherhood on his terms, and when denied, becomes the first murderer. The mark of Cain is both judgment (exile, wandering) and grace (protection): God does not abandon even the murderer but preserves his life. This pattern — judgment that contains mercy — runs through all of Genesis.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain, saying, "I have gotten a man with the help of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first baby in history is born outside the garden, and his mother says something remarkable over him: "I have gotten a man with the help of the LORD." The Hebrew is compressed and awkward, and some read it as a claim rather than a thanksgiving — I have produced a man, the LORD. Either way Eve is looking at this child through Genesis 3:15. God had promised an offspring who would crush the serpent, and here is an offspring, and she names him and hopes.

She is wrong about the child and right about the promise. That will happen again and again in this book: the mother who thinks the deliverer has arrived, and a long wait instead. Four thousand years later another woman would hold a firstborn son and be right (cf. Luke 2:6–7; Gal. 4:4).

verseByVerse.quote: And again, she bore his brother Abel. Now Abel was a keeper of sheep, and Cain a worker of the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two brothers, two trades. Abel keeps sheep; Cain works the ground — the same verb, abad, that was given to Adam in the garden (2:15). Both are honest callings, and Genesis takes no side between the shepherd and the farmer. Whatever goes wrong in this chapter, it is not that one of them chose the wrong job.

The name Abel is hebel — vapour, breath, the word Ecclesiastes uses seventy times for everything that does not last. His name is a warning label, and his life is short enough to earn it. Death has entered the world, exactly as God said it would, and the first person to die is not the guilty man who ate the fruit but a young man who did nothing wrong at all. That is how sin works; it rarely settles its bill with the person who ran it up.

verseByVerse.quote: In the course of time Cain brought to the LORD an offering of the fruit of the ground, and Abel also brought of the firstborn of his flock and of their fat portions. And the LORD had regard for Abel and his offering, but for Cain and his offering he had no regard. So Cain was very angry, and his face fell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Both brothers bring an offering, and God accepts one and not the other. This is the crux of the chapter and the reason many readers leave it feeling that God was arbitrary. He was not, and the text gives its clues in the wording.

Cain brought "an offering of the fruit of the ground." Abel brought "of the firstborn of his flock and of their fat portions." Cain brought some produce. Abel brought the first and the best — the firstborn, which in Israel's later law always belongs to God, and the fat, which was always his portion. One of them gave God something. The other gave God the top of the pile.

And notice the order in which God's regard is described: "the LORD had regard for Abel and his offering." The man first, the gift second. Hebrews puts it beyond guessing: "By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain" (Heb. 11:4). The difference was not the commodity — grain offerings are commanded in Leviticus 2 and are entirely acceptable — but the heart the gift came out of.

Which is a searching thing for anyone who gives God anything. It is possible to bring an offering that is real, and public, and costly enough to be noticed, and for God to be looking straight past it at the person holding it. Ask of your own giving, and your own Sunday: is this the firstborn and the fat, or is this what was left over after everything that actually mattered had been paid for?

"So Cain was very angry, and his face fell." He is not sorry. He is furious — and the anger goes sideways, at his brother, when the only person he has any business being angry with is himself.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Cain, "Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen? If you do well, will you not be accepted? And if you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is for you, and you must rule over it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God comes to Cain. That alone should stop the reader who thinks Cain was treated harshly. A man is standing there with a face like thunder over a rejected offering, and God walks up and asks him two gentle questions instead of leaving him to it.

"If you do well, will you not be accepted?" The door is not shut. Whatever was wrong with the first offering can be put right, and God says so before anything worse happens. This is a warning delivered in time, which is what warnings are for.

"And if you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is for you, and you must rule over it." The picture is of an animal flattened outside the entrance, waiting. Sin is not described here as a mistake or a weakness but as a predator with an appetite, and the appetite is for Cain personally. The two key words — desire and rule — are the same pair used of the ruined marriage four verses earlier (3:16): something straining to master you, and a struggle to hold it down.

Every believer knows the doorway. It is the moment when the resentment has been felt but not yet spoken, the browser not yet opened, the second drink not yet poured. Sin at the threshold can still be refused. Sin in the room does what it likes. And the command is not "manage it" but "rule over it" — which is precisely what Cain, in his own strength, is about to fail to do, and why the New Testament will offer not better resolve but a new master (cf. Rom. 6:12–14).

verseByVerse.quote: Cain spoke to Abel his brother. And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Cain spoke to Abel his brother." And the sentence stops. In Hebrew nothing follows — the words he said have been left out, as though the narrator turns his face away. Several ancient versions supply "Let us go out to the field," which may well be right, and if so the murder was premeditated and dressed up as an invitation.

"And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him." Four times in this short paragraph the text says brother. It will not let us call this a killing; it insists on calling it a fratricide. The second generation of the human race reduces itself by a quarter, and it takes one chapter to get from a stolen piece of fruit to a body in a field.

John draws the line straight from here to us: "We should love one another. We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one and murdered his brother" (1 John 3:11–12), and then adds that everyone who hates his brother is a murderer already. That is not rhetorical inflation. It is Genesis 4 read correctly. What came out in the field had been growing in the heart since the offering.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Cain, "Where is Abel your brother?" He said, "I do not know; am I my brother's keeper?" And the LORD said, "What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood is crying to me from the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Where is Abel your brother?" It is the same question God asked in the garden — "Where are you?" — put to the second generation, and again it is not a request for information but an opening for confession.

Cain slams it shut with a lie and a sneer. "I do not know" is false. "Am I my brother's keeper?" is worse, and it is one of the ugliest sentences in Scripture precisely because the word he chooses is shamar — to keep, to guard — the very word given to Adam about the garden (2:15). He picks up the vocabulary of God-given responsibility and uses it to deny that he has any.

The question has been asked ever since, usually without the sneer and always with the same intent: is this any of my business? The man on the road to Jericho was somebody's brother, and two religious men decided he was not theirs (Luke 10:31–32). The answer Scripture gives to Cain's question is yes, and it never wavers.

"The voice of your brother's blood is crying to me from the ground." Abel is dead and cannot speak, and God hears him anyway. That is the comfort buried in this grim chapter for anyone who has been wronged in a way no court will ever address: God does not need a witness statement. He hears blood. Hebrews sets one last comparison beside it — the sprinkled blood of Jesus, "that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel" (Heb. 12:24). Abel's blood cried for justice. Christ's cries for mercy, and it is louder.

verseByVerse.quote: And now you are cursed from the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand. When you work the ground, it shall no longer yield to you its strength. You shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sentence fits the crime with terrible precision. Cain is a farmer, and it is farming that is taken from him: "When you work the ground, it shall no longer yield to you its strength." The ground drank his brother's blood, and now it will not feed him. He must live somewhere else, doing something else.

"You shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth." His father was sent out of the garden but was still given ground to work (3:23). Cain is given no ground at all. Each generation of sin costs a little more than the last, and the exile gets longer.

Note what the curse does not say. God does not strike him down, and the law that will later require a murderer's life (9:6) is not applied here. Even in a sentence this severe, the man is left breathing.

verseByVerse.quote: Cain said to the LORD, "My punishment is greater than I can bear. Behold, you have driven me today away from the ground, and from your face I shall be hidden. I shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth, and whoever finds me will kill me." Then the LORD said to him, "Not so! If anyone kills Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold." And the LORD put a mark on Cain, lest any who found him should attack him. Then Cain went away from the presence of the LORD and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"My punishment is greater than I can bear." Read the speech that follows and count the times he mentions his brother: not once. He is sorry about the exile, the danger, the hiddenness of God's face, the loss of the ground. He is not sorry about Abel. This is remorse without repentance — grief over consequences, which can be very loud and change nothing (cf. 2 Cor. 7:10).

And then God does something nobody could have predicted. "Not so! If anyone kills Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold." God protects a self-pitying murderer who has not apologised. The mark is not a brand of shame; it is a guarantee of safety, put on him by the God he lied to twenty minutes earlier.

There it is, in the fourth chapter of the Bible: God restraining violence in a world that has just discovered it, and showing kindness to a man with no case to make. Grace in Scripture is never given because the recipient turned out to deserve it after all. Cain is the first proof.

"Then Cain went away from the presence of the LORD and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden." Nod means wandering; he settles down in a place called Restlessness. He is moving further east, away from the gate, and he takes his exile and makes a home of it. A man can build a whole life out of the far country and never once look back at the road he came down.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–26 — The Lines of Cain and Seth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 4 closes with two contrasting genealogical trajectories. The line of Cain produces the builders of cities and the inventors of culture — metalworking, music, husbandry — but also the escalating violence of Lamech, who boasts of killing for a mere wound and claims seventy-seven-fold vengeance. Over against this, Seth is born as the replacement for Abel, and with his son Enosh comes the first mention of calling upon the name of the LORD — the beginning of formal worship.
verseByVerse.theology: The Cainite line shows that human creativity and cultural achievement can develop independently of covenant relationship with God — civilization does not require worship. But the Cainite trajectory also shows the corruption of culture without God: the same iron-working that produced tools produced weapons, and Lamech's boast is the ultimate expression of the culture of violence. The Sethite line, by contrast, is marked by worship. The eschatological implication is that human culture — genuine and valuable as it is — cannot save; only the line that calls upon the name of the LORD carries the promise forward.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller observes that the cultural gifts of the Cainites — city-building, music, metalworking — are real goods that God allows to develop even outside the covenant community. He is not the God of only religious activities but the sustaining Creator of all human culture. The tragedy is that these gifts, divorced from worship, escalate violence. The Reformed tradition has always affirmed common grace: God allows fallen humanity to develop genuine goods, while reserving saving grace for the covenant line.

verseByVerse.quote: Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch. When he built a city, he called the name of the city after the name of his son, Enoch. To Enoch was born Irad, and Irad fathered Mehujael, and Mehujael fathered Methushael, and Methushael fathered Lamech. And Lamech took two wives. The name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah. Adah bore Jabal; he was the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock. His brother's name was Jubal; he was the father of all those who play the lyre and pipe. Zillah also bore Tubal-cain; he was the forger of all instruments of bronze and iron. The sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What follows is the strangest thing in the chapter: the line of Cain flourishes. The murderer's descendants build the first city, and out of them come the herdsmen who domesticate livestock, the musicians who invent the lyre and the pipe, and the metalworkers who forge bronze and iron. Civilisation — agriculture, art and technology — arrives through the family under judgment.

Which forbids two mistakes at once. It forbids the idea that culture is a worldly distraction fit only to be escaped; music and metallurgy are listed here without a word of criticism, and God had told humanity to fill the earth and subdue it long before Cain was born (1:28). And it forbids the assumption that prosperity is proof of God's approval. The city gets built. The songs get written. It settles nothing about the state of a man's soul.

Theologians call this common grace: God's gifts scattered across a fallen race without regard to whether the recipients love him. He "makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good" (Matt. 5:45). The surgeon who saves your child's life may not pray, and his skill is still a gift of God through him. Take the gift, thank the Giver, and do not confuse the two.

verseByVerse.quote: Lamech said to his wives: "Adah and Zillah, hear my voice; you wives of Lamech, listen to what I say: I have killed a man for wounding me, a young man for striking me. If Cain's revenge is sevenfold, then Lamech's is seventy-sevenfold."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lamech makes a poem. It is the second piece of poetry in the Bible; the first was Adam's song when he saw his wife (2:23). Adam's was a cry of delight at a person. Lamech's is a boast about a corpse.

"I have killed a man for wounding me, a young man for striking me." Cain killed out of jealousy and then hid. Lamech kills out of wounded pride and then sets it to music for his two wives — the first bigamist in Scripture, celebrating disproportionate revenge as an achievement. And he does his arithmetic on God's own words: "If Cain's revenge is sevenfold, then Lamech's is seventy-sevenfold." A promise of divine protection has been twisted into a licence for private vengeance.

Sin does not stay level. Five generations from Eden it has gone from a shameful murder to a bragging song, and the escalation is the whole point of the genealogy. The world is heading somewhere, and by chapter 6 the earth will be filled with violence.

Which is why one of the loveliest reversals in the Gospels is a number. Peter asks how often he must forgive — seven times? And Jesus answers, "not seven times, but seventy-seven times" (Matt. 18:21–22). He reaches back over four thousand years, takes Lamech's arithmetic of revenge, and turns it into the arithmetic of mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: And Adam knew his wife again, and she bore a son and called his name Seth, for she said, "God has appointed for me another offspring instead of Abel, for Cain killed him." To Seth also a son was born, and he called his name Enosh. At that time people began to call upon the name of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes by going back to the beginning. Another son is born, and Eve names him Seth — "God has appointed for me another offspring instead of Abel." She uses the same word God used in 3:15: offspring, seed. The line of promise looked as though it had been murdered in a field, and God has replaced it.

That is the pattern of the whole Bible in one verse. Every time the promise appears to have been extinguished — a barren womb, a famine, an exile, a cross — God appoints another, and the line runs on. Nothing that God has undertaken to do has ever been finally stopped by anyone's sin, including yours.

"At that time people began to call upon the name of the LORD." After a murder, a boast and a genealogy of exile, the last sentence of the chapter is about prayer. Public, corporate, unashamed calling on the covenant name. The line of Cain built a city; the line of Seth started worshipping.

Two ways of living in a fallen world are now on the page, and the whole of Scripture will keep them side by side to the end. One builds and names things after itself. The other has nothing to show and calls on the name of the LORD — and Paul, quoting Joel, says that this is exactly what saves: "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved" (Rom. 10:13).

4.theology:
Worship and the Heart. Genesis 4 establishes that acceptable worship is never merely formal. The issue with Cain was not his occupation or his offering's material but his heart. The entire sacrificial system of the Mosaic law, the prophets' critique of hollow ritual (Amos 5:21–24; Isa. 1:11–17), and Jesus's own teaching ("God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth," John 4:24) all flow from this foundational principle: you cannot separate the offering from the offerer.

The Spread of Sin. Genesis 4 traces what theologians call the total depravity of sin — not that fallen humanity is as bad as it could be, but that sin corrupts every dimension of human existence. The broken relationship with God (ch.3) produces broken relationships between humans (ch.4), and those broken relationships produce increasingly violent culture (Lamech's boast, vv.23–24). The flood of chapters 6–9 is not an overreaction; it is the logical consequence of a trajectory Genesis 4 has already mapped.
4.examples:
Then: The story of Cain and Abel addressed real questions for ancient Israel: why does faithful worship sometimes seem unrewarded? Why does the unjust prosper? The answers are theological, not pragmatic: God sees the heart, God protects even the guilty, and the line of faith persists through every catastrophe. For a people who had watched the righteous suffer in Egypt, these were not abstract questions.

Now: "Am I my brother's keeper?" remains the defining question of every era's social ethics. Individualism answers no; the gospel answers yes, at infinite cost. The mark of Cain speaks to criminal justice and mercy: even the guilty bear the image of God and cannot simply be discarded. And verse 26 — people calling on the name of the LORD in the midst of a violent world — is the posture of the church in every generation: not a triumphant majority but a remnant that calls on the name of the One who alone can heal what Cain began.

died.<sup>32</sup>After Noah was 500 years old, Noah fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is the first great genealogy of Genesis — ten generations from Adam to Noah, each entry following the same rhythm: he lived, he fathered, he had other sons and daughters, and he died. The drumbeat of death is relentless. Chapter 2 warned that disobedience would bring death; chapter 5 confirms it. The wages of sin is death (Rom. 6:23), and the genealogy is the receipt.

Yet the chapter is not merely a list of fatalities. Three interruptions crack the monotony. First, it opens by re-anchoring the genealogy in the imago Dei (v.1) — these are not merely mortal creatures but image-bearers whose death is therefore a tragedy, not a natural event. Second, Enoch “walked with God” (vv.22, 24) — the only character in the genealogy described by relationship rather than longevity — and was taken without dying: a luminous exception that proves the rule and anticipates resurrection. Third, Noah arrives with a name meaning “comfort” and a father’s hope that he will undo the curse.

The genealogy traces the line of the seed of the woman (3:15) through Seth, the replacement for Abel. Luke 3:38 traces Jesus’s genealogy to Adam, showing that the line of chapter 5 runs all the way to Bethlehem — the death-rhythm broken at last by the One who is the resurrection and the life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–32 — The Generations from Adam to Noah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The genealogy of Genesis 5 serves as a bridge between the primeval narratives of chapters 1–4 and the flood narrative of chapters 6–9. Its repetitive structure — birth, years of life, death — is deliberate: the refrain 'and he died' tolls like a funeral bell, confirming the judgment of Genesis 2:17 with grim regularity. Death is now the universal human experience. But within the repetition are two interruptions: Enoch, who walked with God and was taken; and Noah, named with a prophecy of rest and relief.
verseByVerse.theology: The genealogy is not merely demographic history but theological narrative. The decreasing lifespans (in some interpretations) and the universality of death confirm that sin has changed the human condition fundamentally. Enoch's translation without death (v.24) is the bright exception — a proleptic sign that death is not the final word for those who walk with God. The Epistle to the Hebrews lists Enoch among the heroes of faith (Heb. 11:5), and Jude quotes from 1 Enoch as background for his warnings about judgment. Noah's naming prophecy (v.29) introduces the theme of relief from the curse on the ground — anticipating both the flood and the new covenant.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes that the genealogy serves as a literary device to create distance between Eden and the flood, filling the narrative space with the weight of generations dying under the curse. The pattern 'he lived... he fathered... he lived... and he died' mirrors the creation pattern of 'and there was evening and there was morning' — but where creation's refrain marks the arrival of something new, chapter 5's refrain marks the departure of something precious. Calvin notes that the long lifespans of the antediluvian patriarchs served God's purposes for the development of early civilization.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the book of the generations of Adam. When God created man, he made him in the likeness of God. Male and female he created them, and he blessed them and named them Man when they were created.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new panel of the book opens: "This is the book of the generations of Adam." And before a single name is listed, the chapter goes back and repeats Genesis 1 — made in the likeness of God, male and female, blessed. The reader has just come through the fall, a murder and a boasting song, and the first thing he is told is that the image is still there.

That matters more than the arithmetic that follows. Sin has ruined the human race; it has not unmade it. The people in this list are fallen, and every one of them is an image-bearer, which is why God will still say after the flood that whoever sheds man's blood answers for it, "for God made man in his own image" (9:6).

verseByVerse.quote: When Adam had lived 130 years, he fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth. The days of Adam after he fathered Seth were 800 years; and he had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days that Adam lived were 930 years, and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"He fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image." The two words used of God and Adam in verse 1 are now used of Adam and Seth, deliberately and in the same order. The image is passed on. So is everything else. What Adam hands his son is a nature like his own — dignity and ruin together, in one child — and that is the plain sense of Paul's "sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men" (Rom. 5:12).

Then the sentence that will now toll through the whole chapter: "and he died." God had said that in the day they ate of it they would surely die (2:17). Nine hundred and thirty years is a long postponement and it is not a reprieve. The verdict lands.

verseByVerse.quote: When Seth had lived 105 years, he fathered Enosh. Seth lived after he fathered Enosh 807 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Seth were 912 years, and he died. When Enosh had lived 90 years, he fathered Kenan. Enosh lived after he fathered Kenan 815 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Enosh were 905 years, and he died. When Kenan had lived 70 years, he fathered Mahalalel. Kenan lived after he fathered Mahalalel 840 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Kenan were 910 years, and he died. When Mahalalel had lived 65 years, he fathered Jared. Mahalalel lived after he fathered Jared 830 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Mahalalel were 895 years, and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter settles into a formula and repeats it without variation: he lived, he fathered, he lived, he had other sons and daughters, all his days were, and he died. Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared. Read it aloud and it sounds like a bell being struck at intervals — and he died, and he died, and he died. The monotony is the message.

Here is the first Bible chapter given over almost entirely to the fact that people do not last, and it is placed immediately after the fall so that nobody can miss the connection. A long life is still a life with an end on it. The lifespans are extraordinary and they run out just the same, which is the one statistic the chapter cares about.

Readers reasonably ask about the ages, and honest Christians answer differently: some take the figures at face value in a world not long out of Eden; others note that ancient genealogies often skip generations and that round and symbolic numbers were used in the ancient Near East. The text itself does not argue the point and neither should we. What it does insist on is the drumbeat at the end of every line.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jared had lived 162 years, he fathered Enoch. Jared lived after he fathered Enoch 800 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Jared were 962 years, and he died. When Enoch had lived 65 years, he fathered Methuselah. Enoch walked with God after he fathered Methuselah 300 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Enoch were 365 years. Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the bell stops. "Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him." The formula that has run through six generations simply breaks. There is no "and he died."

Twice the text says he walked with God — a phrase that means not a mystical experience but a life lived in company, day after ordinary day, in step with someone else's pace. And notice when it starts: "Enoch walked with God after he fathered Methuselah." Whatever happened at the birth of his son, from then on this man lived differently, in the middle of a family, while the world of Lamech went on outside. Hebrews says he did it by faith and that "before he was taken he was commended as having pleased God" (Heb. 11:5).

His name means dedicated, and 365 years is the shortest life in the chapter — by three hundred years. He walked with God, and God took him early, and Genesis records it as the best thing that happened to anyone in the list.

Jude adds a detail found nowhere else: Enoch prophesied about the coming of the Lord with his holy ones to execute judgment (Jude 14–15). So the man in the seventh generation from Adam was preaching the second coming. And in a chapter whose entire subject is that everybody dies, God writes one exception into the record, thousands of years early, as if to say that the drumbeat is not the last word (cf. 1 Thess. 4:17).

verseByVerse.quote: When Methuselah had lived 187 years, he fathered Lamech. Methuselah lived after he fathered Lamech 782 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Methuselah were 969 years, and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Methuselah lives longer than any human being in Scripture — 969 years — and the only thing anyone remembers about him is the number. He fathered sons and daughters and he died, and there is nothing else on the record.

Add the figures and something surfaces. Methuselah dies in the very year the flood comes. The longest life in the Bible is lived out under a deferred judgment, and God holds it back until the old man is gone. The apostle Peter called that patience — God "waiting patiently in the days of Noah" (1 Pet. 3:20) — and the same slowness that looks like indifference is in fact mercy running the clock (2 Pet. 3:9).

verseByVerse.quote: When Lamech had lived 182 years, he fathered a son and called his name Noah, saying, "Out of the ground that the LORD has cursed, this one shall bring us relief from our work and from the painful toil of our hands." Lamech lived after he fathered Noah 595 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Lamech were 777 years, and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lamech — a different Lamech from the killer in chapter 4, and the contrast is deliberate — names his son Noah and says why: "Out of the ground that the LORD has cursed, this one shall bring us relief from our work and from the painful toil of our hands."

He is quoting Genesis 3:17. Ten generations later, out beyond the sealed gate, people are still living with a cursed ground and still remembering exactly what was said about it, and they are still hoping that someone will be born who can undo it. That hope is the pulse under the whole chapter of dying men.

Noah gave the world a reprieve, not relief; the thorns are still there. The one who finally answers Lamech's hope was born much later and did his work in another garden and on a hill, and he took the curse itself onto his own body (Gal. 3:13). One day the ground will be clear of it altogether (Rev. 22:3).

verseByVerse.quote: After Noah was 500 years old, Noah fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends without the formula. No total, no "and he died" — only Noah at five hundred years old and the names of his three sons. The bell that has tolled nine times falls silent, and the reader is left waiting.

Ten generations have taken us from the garden to a man whose father hoped he would be the relief of the world. Everything in the chapter has been running downhill towards death; the last line stops on a living man with a family and no ending given. God's line of promise has come through the fall, the murder and the long roll of graves, and it has not broken (cf. Luke 3:36–38).

5.theology:
Death as Theological Fact. The genealogy of chapter 5 is not primarily a historical record but a theological argument: death is real, universal, and unnatural. It is not the way things were supposed to be. This is the foundation of the Christian hope of resurrection — not merely that death is hard but that it is wrong, a catastrophe demanding reversal. The New Testament proclaims that reversal in the resurrection of Jesus: “the last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Cor. 15:26).

Walking with God. Enoch’s “walking with God” (vv.22, 24) is the most compressed definition of the life of faith in the Old Testament. It is not spectacular achievement but sustained orientation — a whole life turned toward God. The New Testament develops this as walking “by the Spirit” (Gal. 5:16), walking “in the light” (1 John 1:7), walking “worthy of the Lord” (Col. 1:10). Enoch’s translation is the sign that this kind of life has a destination beyond death — not because it earns immortality but because the God with whom one walks is the God of resurrection.
5.examples:
Then: Ancient Near Eastern king lists also recorded extraordinary lifespans for pre-flood monarchs (sometimes hundreds of thousands of years), presenting long life as divine favor. Genesis 5’s genealogy engages this cultural form while subverting it: the long-lived patriarchs all die, making the point that longevity does not conquer death. Enoch’s exception is therefore all the more striking in this context.

Now: The genealogy speaks to every culture obsessed with longevity and anti-aging — the biotech investment in immortality, the desperate attempt to outrun the death-rhythm. Genesis 5 says: you cannot. The only path past death runs through the One who walked into it and out the other side. And Enoch’s “walking with God” is the counter-cultural definition of a life well-lived: not accumulated experiences, achievements, or years, but a whole life in the direction of God.

6.title: Noah Found Favor in the Eyes of the LORD
6.text: <sup>1</sup>When man began to multiply on the face of the land and daughters were born to them,<sup>2</sup>the sons of God saw that the daughters of man were attractive. And they took as their wives any they chose.<sup>3</sup>Then the LORD said, "My Spirit shall not abide in man forever, for he is flesh: his days shall be 120 years."<sup>4</sup>The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also afterward, when the sons of God came in to the daughters of man and they bore children to them. These were the mighty men who were of old, the men of renown.<sup>5</sup>The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.<sup>6</sup>And the LORD regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart.<sup>7</sup>So the LORD said, "I will blot out man whom I have created from the face of the land, man and animals and creeping things and birds of the heavens, for I am sorry that I have made them."<sup>8</sup>But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.<sup>9</sup>These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation.
