Behold, I will destroy them with the earth.<sup>14</sup>Make yourself an ark of gopher wood. Make rooms in the ark, and cover it inside and out with pitch.<sup>15</sup>This is how you are to make it: the length of the ark 300 cubits, its breadth 50 cubits, and its height 30 cubits.<sup>16</sup>Make a roof for the ark, and finish it to a cubit above, and set the door of the ark in its side. Make it with lower, second, and third decks.<sup>17</sup>For behold, I will bring a flood of waters upon the earth to destroy all flesh in which is the breath of life under heaven. Everything that is on the earth shall die.<sup>18</sup>But I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall come into the ark, you, your sons, your wife, and your sons' wives with you.<sup>19</sup>And of every living thing of all flesh, you shall bring two of every sort into the ark to keep them alive with you. They shall be male and female.<sup>20</sup>Of the birds according to their kinds, and of the animals according to their kinds, of every creeping thing of the ground, according to its kind, two of every sort shall come in to you to keep them alive.<sup>21</sup>Also take with you every sort of food that is eaten, and store it up. It shall serve as food for you and for them."<sup>22</sup>Noah did this; he did all that God commanded him.
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is one of the most theologically dense chapters in Genesis, containing the divine assessment of human corruption (“every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually,” v.5), the grief of God (v.6), the announcement of the flood (vv.7, 13), and the extraordinary counter-declaration: “But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD” (v.8). That “but” is one of the most important conjunctions in Scripture — a pivot from universal condemnation to particular grace.

The grief of God (v.6) is one of the most striking anthropomorphic statements in the Old Testament. The God who cannot be surprised or defeated is described as grieved, as regretting. This is not a divine mistake but a genuine expression of the pain that human rebellion causes to the God who made humanity for fellowship with himself. Keller notes that this verse shows the cross was not a plan B — the suffering of God over human sin is woven into the fabric of the divine-human relationship from the beginning.

Noah’s ark is one of the Bible’s most developed types of Christ. Just as Noah and his family were saved through the ark while judgment fell on the world outside, so those who are “in Christ” are safe from the judgment that falls on sin. 1 Peter 3:20–21 makes this explicit, calling the ark a type of baptism — the waters of judgment becoming the waters of salvation for those inside the vessel God provided.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Corruption of the Earth and the Call of Noah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 6 opens with one of the most debated passages in Scripture — the sons of God and the daughters of man — and moves to the shattering announcement of divine judgment: God will blot out the human race he has made. The corruption of the earth is so pervasive that God regrets making man. Yet within this overwhelming judgment stands one man: Noah, who found favor in the eyes of the LORD. The chapter ends with God's call to Noah and the commission to build the ark.
verseByVerse.theology: The theological weight of Genesis 6 is enormous. The 'grieving' of God's heart (v.6) reveals that God is not a detached deity unmoved by human rebellion; he is a personal God who experiences the moral catastrophe of the fall with something like sorrow. The flood is not capricious destruction but the response of holy love to pervasive evil. Yet God's judgment always contains mercy: the ark is simultaneously an instrument of judgment (it escapes the flood by riding above it) and of salvation (it preserves the remnant through whom the promise will continue). Noah's obedience — building the ark without having seen rain — is the paradigm of faith that Hebrews 11:7 will celebrate.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller on Genesis 6: the sons of God/daughters of man passage most likely describes the intermarriage of the covenant line (Sethites) with the surrounding culture, resulting in the dilution of covenant faithfulness. The 'Nephilim' and the great wickedness that follows describe the cultural corruption that results when the people of God are assimilated into the world rather than remaining distinct. Wenham argues that the flood narrative, whatever its precise historical form, functions theologically as the reversal of creation: the waters of chaos return, and only the ark — a floating garden — preserves the seed of new creation.

verseByVerse.quote: When man began to multiply on the face of the land and daughters were born to them, the sons of God saw that the daughters of man were attractive. And they took as their wives any they chose. Then the LORD said, "My Spirit shall not abide in man forever, for he is flesh: his days shall be 120 years." The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also afterward, when the sons of God came in to the daughters of man and they bore children to them. These were the mighty men who were of old, the men of renown.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These four verses are the hardest in the chapter, and it is better to lay out the options than to pretend there is only one. Who are "the sons of God" who took "the daughters of man"?

Three readings have serious defenders. The first is that the sons of God are the godly line of Seth and the daughters of man the line of Cain, so that the sin is the collapse of the boundary between the worshipping line and the world — an old and widely held view, and it fits the two family lines chapters 4 and 5 have just laid out. The second is that they are angelic beings; everywhere else in the Old Testament "sons of God" means heavenly beings (Job 1:6; 38:7), and Jude and 2 Peter both speak of angels who "did not stay within their own position of authority," setting them beside Sodom's sexual sin (Jude 6–7; 2 Pet. 2:4). The third is that they are royal despots — ancient kings claimed divine sonship — and the offence is tyrants building harems, which fits "they took as their wives any they chose."

What all three agree on is the offence, and Moses is more interested in that than in the identification. Some boundary God set has been trampled by the powerful, and the language is the language of Eden: they saw that they were good, and they took (compare 3:6). Whatever else has changed, the grammar of sin has not.

God's answer is a limit: "his days shall be 120 years." Read it as a shortening of the human lifespan, or as a deadline before the flood — either way it is a mercy with a fence round it. And the Nephilim, whoever they were, are described as "the mighty men who were of old, the men of renown." That is not praise. It is the world's word for greatness — celebrity, reputation, the name everybody knows — put into a paragraph that ends with the whole earth destroyed. Renown is not the same thing as being right with God, and God is about to prove it.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually. And the LORD regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 5 is the bleakest verdict on the human race in Scripture, and every word of it is doing work. The wickedness was great. It was in the intention of the thoughts of his heart — not merely the behaviour, but the workshop behind it, the place where actions are designed before anyone sees them. It was only evil, and it was evil continually. There is no gap, no exception, no better half.

This is the passage Reformed theology is pointing at when it speaks of total depravity, and the phrase is often misheard. It does not mean everyone is as bad as they could possibly be; the men of renown were building a civilisation. It means there is no part of a person left untouched — mind, will, desire, heart — and therefore nothing in us that could serve as the clean corner from which we might repair ourselves.

"And the LORD regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart." Does God change his mind? Elsewhere Scripture says he does not (Num. 23:19; 1 Sam. 15:29). The word here, nacham, is emotional as much as it is decisional — the same word will describe the comfort Noah's name was supposed to bring (5:29). God has not been taken by surprise and is not revising a plan. He is showing us what human sin does to him.

Hold onto that clause, because a great deal of bad theology dies on it. The God of the Bible is not the impassive philosopher's deity who observes the world without feeling. Sin grieves him to the heart. And it will grieve him again, one day, in a garden, in a man kneeling among olive trees with sweat like drops of blood.

verseByVerse.quote: So the LORD said, "I will blot out man whom I have created from the face of the land, man and animals and creeping things and birds of the heavens, for I am sorry that I have made them." But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I will blot out man whom I have created from the face of the land." The verb is the one used for wiping a dish. This is not a temper; it is the Creator reversing his own work, and the animals go with the people, because the sin of the image-bearer wrecks the world he was given to keep.

And then five words that change everything: "But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD." Favor is chen — the Old Testament's word for grace, and this is the first time it appears in the Bible. It appears in a sentence about the end of the world.

Get the order right, because the chapter is careful about it. Verse 8 comes before verse 9. Noah found favour first; only then are we told he was righteous and blameless and walked with God. He was not saved because he was good. He was good because God had already looked at him with favour. If the sentence ran the other way round, this would be the story of one man's achievement. As it stands it is the story of grace choosing a man, and everything in Noah's life afterwards is the fruit of verse 8, not the cause of it (cf. Eph. 2:8–9).

Eight people out of a world. Grace is not measured by how many receive it, and it never comes because the recipient had made himself worth rescuing.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation. Noah walked with God. And Noah had three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Now the earth was corrupt in God's sight, and the earth was filled with violence. And God saw the earth, and behold, it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted their way on the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation. Noah walked with God." Blameless does not mean sinless — chapter 9 will make that painfully clear. It means whole, of a piece, without the double life; and "in his generation" is the key phrase. He was upright in a world where nobody else was, which is by far the harder version.

The description given him is the one given to Enoch: he walked with God (5:24). In a chapter where every intention of every heart is only evil continually, there is one man taking a daily walk with the LORD. Faith is not usually heroic; it is usually just persistent, and persistent in the wrong company.

Then the diagnosis is repeated with a new word. Twice the earth is "corrupt" and once it is "filled with violence" — hamas, the word for brutality, oppression, blood in the streets. What broke the world was not private irreligion. It was people hurting people, and God noticed the bruises.

And there is an awful symmetry in the language. God looked at his finished creation and saw that it was very good (1:31); now "God saw the earth, and behold, it was corrupt." The same verb, the same posture of looking, and the opposite verdict.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said to Noah, "I have determined to make an end of all flesh, for the earth is filled with violence through them. Behold, I will destroy them with the earth. Make yourself an ark of gopher wood. Make rooms in the ark, and cover it inside and out with pitch. This is how you are to make it: the length of the ark 300 cubits, its breadth 50 cubits, and its height 30 cubits. Make a roof for the ark, and finish it to a cubit above, and set the door of the ark in its side. Make it with lower, second, and third decks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Noah exactly what is coming and exactly what to build. The reason given is the one from verse 11: "the earth is filled with violence through them." Judgment in the Bible is never arbitrary, and God states his grounds.

Then the specification, and look at what kind of vessel this is. Three hundred cubits by fifty by thirty is roughly 450 feet long — a barge, not a ship. It has no rudder, no sail, no mast and no prow. It is a floating box built to survive, not to be steered. Noah is not being made a sailor; he is being put in a container and given nowhere to go but wherever God takes him.

"Set the door of the ark in its side." One door, put there by God, in a structure with no other way in. It is not fanciful to see what the whole flood account is a picture of, since Peter says it plainly: the eight who were brought safely through the water correspond to baptism, "which now saves you... through the resurrection of Jesus Christ" (1 Pet. 3:20–21). Judgment fell, and it fell on the outside of the ark, and everyone inside came out into a washed world.

And the wood is sealed with pitch, inside and out. The Hebrew word for pitch, kopher, is from the same root as the word for atonement — a covering applied so the water of judgment cannot get in.

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, I will bring a flood of waters upon the earth to destroy all flesh in which is the breath of life under heaven. Everything that is on the earth shall die. But I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall come into the ark, you, your sons, your wife, and your sons' wives with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For behold, I will bring a flood of waters upon the earth... Everything that is on the earth shall die." God says it twice over so that Noah is under no illusion about what he is building for.

"But I will establish my covenant with you." That word turns the verse and the chapter. Covenant appears here for the first time in Scripture — a sworn, binding arrangement in which God attaches himself to people by promise. In the middle of a sentence about the death of everything, God commits himself to somebody.

Notice who is included: "you, your sons, your wife, and your sons' wives with you." One man found favour, and his household came in on his account. God has a habit of dealing with families, and it runs the length of Scripture — Abraham and his house, Rahab and hers, the jailer at Philippi and all his (Acts 16:31). If you are the only believer in your family, this verse is not a promise you can cash, but it is a pattern you may pray along.

verseByVerse.quote: And of every living thing of all flesh, you shall bring two of every sort into the ark to keep them alive with you. They shall be male and female. Of the birds according to their kinds, and of the animals according to their kinds, of every creeping thing of the ground, according to its kind, two of every sort shall come in to you to keep them alive. Also take with you every sort of food that is eaten, and store it up. It shall serve as food for you and for them." Noah did this; he did all that God commanded him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The animals come. And note the direction of travel in verse 20: "two of every sort shall come in to you." Noah does not have to trap them or hunt them down; he has to have the doors open. The God who made every kind can manage the logistics of getting them aboard.

Noah's part is the food. "Take with you every sort of food that is eaten, and store it up." It is the least dramatic instruction in the chapter and it took years. Most obedience looks like that: not a moment of heroism but a long, unglamorous stockpiling of provisions for a rain nobody else believes in. Peter calls him "a herald of righteousness" (2 Pet. 2:5), and Hebrews says that by his faith "he condemned the world" (Heb. 11:7) — meaning simply that his hammering was a sermon.

"Noah did this; he did all that God commanded him." The chapter that began with the whole earth doing what it liked ends with one man doing what he was told. It is the only sentence of pure obedience in Genesis 6, and God builds the rescue of the world on it.

6.theology:
The Grief of God. Verse 6 reveals that God is not a detached First Cause but a personal God whose relationship with humanity involves genuine pain when that relationship is violated. The theological tradition has rightly distinguished between divine impassibility (God is not controlled by passions as we are) and divine feeling (God genuinely responds to his creation). The cross is the definitive statement: God’s response to human sin was not detached judgment but the grief of the Father and the suffering of the Son.

The Ark as Type of Christ. Peter explicitly calls the ark a type (1 Pet. 3:20–21): as Noah and his family were saved through water while the world outside perished, so baptism — the sign of union with Christ — saves through the death and resurrection of the One who bore judgment for us. The ark is not an escape from judgment but a vessel that goes through judgment while bearing its passengers safely. Christ does not remove his people from the presence of death; he goes through death with them and out the other side.
6.examples:
Then: The flood narrative has parallels in ancient Near Eastern literature (especially the Gilgamesh epic), confirming that memory of a great flood was widespread in the ancient world. Genesis engages these traditions while transforming them: the flood is not the whim of competing gods disturbed by human noise but the just response of the one holy God to universal corruption, tempered by grace for one man and his family. The theological difference is total.

Now: Verse 5’s diagnosis of the human heart (“only evil continually”) sounds extreme to ears formed by Enlightenment optimism about human nature. But the twentieth century — with its genocides, gulags, and weapons of mass destruction — has provided empirical support for the biblical diagnosis. The culture that denies total depravity has no adequate account of Auschwitz. And verse 8 — “But Noah found favor” — is the grace that every generation needs: not a better moral strategy but a God who intervenes.

7.title: The Flood

They were blotted out from the earth. Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ark.<sup>24</sup>And the waters prevailed on the earth 150 days.
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is the flood itself — de-creation and judgment on the grandest scale the Old Testament records. The waters of chaos that God separated on day two of creation (1:6–8) now return: the “fountains of the great deep” burst open and the “windows of the heavens” open, and creation is undone. The carefully ordered world of Genesis 1 is overwhelmed. This is not merely weather; it is cosmic judgment, a reversal of creation by the Creator himself.

In the midst of the catastrophe, one of the most tender verses in Genesis: “And the LORD shut him in” (v.16). God himself closes the door of the ark. Noah does not secure his own salvation; the God who commanded him to build the ark is the same God who seals him inside it. This small detail carries enormous theological weight: salvation from first to last is the work of God, not the achievement of the saved.

Jesus uses the flood as a picture of the suddenness of eschatological judgment: “As were the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matt. 24:37). The world goes about its business, eating and drinking, until the judgment arrives. The flood is not merely a past event but a type of the final judgment — and the ark is not merely a boat but a picture of the only safety that judgment day will leave standing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–24 — The Flood: Judgment and Preservation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 7 narrates the flood itself: the entry into the ark, the coming of the waters, and the comprehensive destruction of all life outside the ark. The precision of the dates and the systematic enumeration of those who entered and those who died serve the text's theological purposes: this is real history, not mythology, and its reality is the basis for its typological significance throughout Scripture.
verseByVerse.theology: The flood is simultaneously the most comprehensive judgment in biblical history before the final judgment and the most dramatic rescue. The same waters that destroy the wicked preserve the righteous — judgment and salvation accomplished by the same act. This pattern recurs at the Red Sea (drowning the Egyptians, saving Israel), at Calvary (God's wrath poured out on the Son saves those who shelter in him), and at the last day (the destruction of the ungodly and the salvation of the elect). Peter explicitly draws the parallel: Noah's family saved through water prefigures baptism (1 Pet. 3:20–21).
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes the flood narrative is composed with careful literary artistry — the numbers of days form a chiastic pattern, the waters rise and fall symmetrically, the divine speech frames the entire narrative. This is not primitive mythology but sophisticated theological history. Keller observes that the ark is the clearest type of Christ in the Old Testament: the only safety from the judgment of God is to be inside the one vessel God himself has provided.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Noah, "Go into the ark, you and all your household, for I have seen that you are righteous before me in this generation. Take with you seven pairs of all clean animals, the male and his mate, and a pair of the animals that are not clean, the male and his mate, and seven pairs of the birds of the heavens also, male and female, to keep their offspring alive on the face of all the earth. For in seven days I will send rain on the earth forty days and forty nights, and every living thing that I have made I will blot out from the face of the ground." And Noah did all that the LORD had commanded him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Go into the ark." Not send your family in — go, you first. God does not invite Noah to supervise a rescue; he calls him into the box he has spent years building, and Noah has to trust his own obedience with his life.

"For I have seen that you are righteous before me in this generation." Chapter 6 established the ground of that: Noah found favour first (6:8), and the righteousness followed. God is not now discovering a merit he had overlooked; he is stating the standing his own grace produced.

The clean animals come in sevens rather than pairs, and the reader may wonder how Noah knows which are clean when Leviticus is nine hundred years away. The distinction plainly predates the written law, and the reason for the extra numbers appears at the end of the next chapter: some of these will be sacrificed on an altar (8:20). God provides the offering before the worshipper knows he will need it.

"For in seven days I will send rain." Seven more days of the world going about its business — Jesus said they were eating and drinking and marrying, right up to the day Noah entered the ark (Matt. 24:38–39). Seven days is not much of a warning, but a hundred and twenty years of hammering had gone before it. God does not announce judgment without notice, and the notice is rarely as short as it looks.

"And Noah did all that the LORD had commanded him." The refrain of the whole account, and the only human achievement in it.

verseByVerse.quote: Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters came upon the earth. And Noah and his sons and his wife and his sons' wives with him went into the ark to escape the waters of the flood. Of clean animals, and of animals that are not clean, and of birds, and of everything that creeps on the ground, two and two, male and female, went into the ark with Noah, as God had commanded Noah. And after seven days the waters of the flood came upon the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The passenger list is read out with a strange, deliberate calm — sons, wife, sons' wives, then the animals, two and two, clean and unclean together. Genesis lingers over the loading the way a man lingers over a photograph, because in a week this will be everyone alive.

Twice in five verses the narrator says it was "as God had commanded Noah." There is no improvisation, no last-minute addition, nobody smuggled aboard out of pity. Salvation here runs entirely on the terms God set, which is not cruelty but clarity: the door was open for a century and the specification was published.

A reader comparing verse 9 with verse 2 may think the numbers have slipped — "two and two" here, seven pairs of clean animals there. They agree. Verse 2 gives the detail, verse 9 the summary: everything came male and female, in pairs, and of the clean kinds there were seven such pairs rather than one. The extra clean animals are for the altar that is coming (8:20).

"And after seven days the waters of the flood came upon the earth." Seven days of silence. Everyone aboard, the sky unchanged, the neighbours presumably still laughing. Faith is very often a week of nothing happening after you have already committed yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on that day all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the windows of the heavens were opened. And rain fell upon the earth forty days and forty nights. On the very same day Noah and his sons, Shem and Ham and Japheth, and Noah's wife and the three wives of his sons with them entered the ark, they and every beast, according to its kind, and all the livestock according to their kinds, and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth, according to its kind, and every bird, according to its kind, every winged creature. They went into the ark with Noah, two and two of all flesh in which there was the breath of life. And those that entered, male and female of all flesh, went in as God had commanded him. And the LORD shut him in.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The date is given to the day — the six hundredth year, second month, seventeenth day. Genesis is not telling a fable; it is filing a record.

And then the mechanism, which is the point. "All the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the windows of the heavens were opened." This is not heavy rain. It is the two great separations of creation week coming undone at once: the waters below and the waters above (1:6–7), released back over the dry land that had been lifted out of them (1:9). The flood is de-creation, the world running backwards, God withdrawing the order he imposed and letting the deep have it again.

Which is what makes the next chapter's wind over the waters so striking, and why judgment in Scripture is never merely destructive. God unmakes in order to make again.

"And the LORD shut him in." Five words, and they are among the most tender in the book. Noah built the ark and Noah could have closed the door, and God does not let him. The safety of the eight does not depend on how well the man fastened the latch. God shuts it, from the outside, and no one aboard has to spend the next hundred and fifty days wondering whether the seal will hold. Everyone who has ever lain awake asking whether his grip on God is strong enough is being answered here: the hand on the door is not yours (cf. John 10:28–29).

verseByVerse.quote: The flood continued forty days on the earth. The waters increased and bore up the ark, and it rose high above the earth. The waters prevailed and increased greatly on the earth, and the ark floated on the face of the waters. And the waters prevailed so mightily on the earth that all the high mountains under the whole heaven were covered. The waters prevailed above the mountains, covering them fifteen cubits deep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the verbs. The waters increased, the waters prevailed, the waters prevailed greatly, the waters prevailed so mightily. Four times in four verses, climbing. It is the sound of something rising past every place a person might have run to.

"And the waters increased and bore up the ark, and it rose high above the earth." The same water that drowned the world lifted the ark. That is the whole doctrine of judgment and salvation in one sentence: not two different events, but one event met in two different places. The flood did not go round the eight who were saved. It went under them.

Which is why the cross can be described the same way. The judgment that fell did not miss anyone; it fell on the ark. Those inside were carried by the very thing that destroyed everything outside.

Was the flood worldwide or regional? Bible-believing Christians divide here, and it should be named rather than hurried past. The language is sweeping — all the high mountains under the whole heaven, covered — and the straightforward reading is global. Others point out that Hebrew often uses "all the earth" of a known region (as in 41:57, where all the earth comes to Egypt to buy grain), and read a vast inundation of the inhabited world. What neither reading can soften is the thing the chapter is actually saying: God judged the world of that day completely, and the only survivors were the ones he put inside a boat.

verseByVerse.quote: And all flesh died that moved on the earth, birds, livestock, beasts, all swarming creatures that swarm on the earth, and all mankind. Everything on the dry land in whose nostrils was the breath of life died. He blotted out every living thing that was on the face of the ground, man and animals and creeping things and birds of the heavens. They were blotted out from the earth. Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ark. And the waters prevailed on the earth 150 days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The account does not hurry past the dying. "All flesh died... Everything on the dry land in whose nostrils was the breath of life died." That last phrase is taken straight from the making of Adam (2:7). What God breathed in, he has taken back, and Genesis will not let the reader treat it as a statistic.

This is the passage people most often bring against the character of God, and it should not be dodged. The answer Scripture gives is not that the flood was small or that the dead were monsters, but that the earth was "filled with violence" (6:11) and that the Judge of all the earth does what is right (18:25). God is not obliged to leave a rebellion running forever. And the same chapter that records the drowning records a door standing open for a hundred and twenty years while a preacher hammered.

"Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ark." One family. The Lord Jesus used exactly this scene to describe his own return, and the sting in his telling is not the water but the ordinariness: they knew nothing until the flood came and swept them all away (Matt. 24:37–39). Nobody in that generation thought they were living in the last week.

"And the waters prevailed on the earth 150 days." Five months of grey water in every direction, and a floating box with no window to see out of. The rescue was certain from the first day and it still took the best part of a year. God's deliverances are rarely quick, and their slowness is not evidence that they have failed.

And in the end the chapter is not about the water; it is about a place to be. Noah was no safer than anyone else in himself — chapter 9 will show what he was made of — and what stood between him and the flood was not his character but a structure God designed, with one door, which God shut. There is only ever one question about a day of judgment, and it is not how bad the storm will be. It is where a person is standing. "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Rom. 8:1) — in him, the way eight people were in a boat while the world went under.

7.theology:
Judgment and Grace. The flood holds together two truths that the contemporary mind tends to separate: God’s holiness demands judgment on sin, and God’s love provides a way of salvation within judgment. These are not in tension; the cross is their resolution. At Calvary, the judgment that the flood pre-figured falls on the Son of God, and those who are in him are shut into the safety he provides. The flood without the ark is law without gospel; the ark without the flood is cheap grace. Genesis 7 holds both.

De-creation and New Creation. The flood’s reversal of creation (the return of the deep, the dissolution of the dry land) establishes a pattern: judgment is de-creation, and salvation is new creation. This pattern recurs in the exodus (the Red Sea as de-creation for Egypt, new creation for Israel), in the exile (the return to formlessness), and supremely in the death and resurrection of Christ. The resurrection is the new creation that the flood dimly foreshadowed: the old creation undone, the new creation breaking through.
7.examples:
Then: The forty days and forty nights of rain (v.4) became a symbolic number in Israel’s imagination: Moses was on the mountain forty days (Exod. 24:18), the spies searched Canaan forty days (Num. 13:25), Israel wandered forty years, and Jesus fasted forty days (Matt. 4:2). The number carries the weight of trial, purification, and preparation for what comes next. Ancient Israel knew the flood story as the paradigm for all subsequent tests of faithfulness.

Now: Jesus’s use of the flood in Matthew 24:37–39 is a standing warning against spiritual complacency: the world before the flood did not see it coming because it was too busy with ordinary life to read the signs. The application is not that Christians should be anxious about the end but that they should be alert — “watching” in the posture of faith that characterized Noah. And the remnant theology of verse 23 speaks to every minority church in a hostile culture: you are not a failed majority but a preserved remnant, held by the same God who shut Noah in.

8.title: God Remembered Noah
8.text: <sup>1</sup>But God remembered Noah and all the beasts and all the livestock that were with him in the ark. And God made a wind blow over the earth, and the waters subsided.<sup>2</sup>The fountains of the deep and the windows of the heavens were closed, the rain from the heavens was restrained,<sup>3</sup>and the waters receded from the earth continually. At the end of 150 days the waters had abated,<sup>4</sup>and in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat.<sup>5</sup>And the waters continued to abate until the tenth month; in the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains were seen.<sup>6</sup>At the end of forty days Noah opened the window of the ark that he had made<sup>7</sup>and sent forth a raven. It went to and fro until the waters were dried up from the earth.<sup>8</sup>Then he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters had subsided from the face of the ground.<sup>9</sup>But the dove found no place to set her foot, and she returned to him to the ark, for the waters were still on the face of the whole earth. So he put out his hand and took her and brought her into the ark with him.<sup>10</sup>He waited another seven days, and again he sent forth the dove out of the ark.<sup>11</sup>And the dove came back to him in the evening, and behold, in her mouth was a freshly plucked olive leaf. So Noah knew that the waters had subsided from the earth.<sup>12</sup>Then he waited another seven days and sent forth the dove, and she did not return to him anymore.<sup>13</sup>In the six hundred and first year, in the first month, the first day of the month, the waters were dried from off the earth. And Noah removed the covering of the ark and looked, and behold, the face of the ground was dry.<sup>14</sup>In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth had dried out.<sup>15</sup>Then God said to Noah,<sup>16</sup>"Go out from the ark, you and your wife, and your sons and your sons' wives with you.<sup>17</sup>Bring out with you every living thing that is with you of all flesh—birds and animals and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth—that they may swarm on the earth, and be fruitful and multiply on the earth."<sup>18</sup>So Noah went out, and his sons and his wife and his sons' wives with him.<sup>19</sup>Every beast, every creeping thing, and every bird, everything that moves on the earth, went out by families from the ark.<sup>20</sup>Then Noah built an altar to the LORD and took some of every clean animal and some of every clean bird and offered burnt offerings on the altar.<sup>21</sup>And when the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma, the LORD said in his heart, "I will never again curse the ground because of man, for the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth. Neither will I ever again strike down every living creature as I have done.<sup>22</sup>While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, shall not cease."
8.overview:
The flood ends the way it began — with a divine act and a divine word. “But God remembered Noah” (v.1) does not mean God had forgotten; in biblical idiom, to “remember” someone is to act on their behalf in covenant faithfulness. God’s memory is always active. The wind that drives back the waters deliberately echoes the Spirit hovering over the deep at creation (1:2) — the flood’s judgment giving way to new creation.

Noah’s first act upon leaving the ark is worship: he builds an altar and offers burnt offerings (v.20). Before planting, before settling — he worships. This is the proper ordering of a restored life: the first response to salvation is doxology. The LORD’s response — “I will never again curse the ground because of man” (v.21) — is not a declaration that humanity has improved but a unilateral commitment of grace. God acknowledges that “the intention of man’s heart is evil from his youth” (v.21) and commits to patience anyway.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Recession of the Flood and Noah's Worship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 8 narrates the recession of the flood and Noah's emergence from the ark with the same careful precision that marked its onset. The pivot of the chapter — and of the entire flood narrative — is verse 1: 'But God remembered Noah.' This divine remembrance is not the recovery of forgotten information but the decisive, saving action of a God who acts on his covenant commitments. The flood recedes; the earth dries; Noah exits; and his first act on dry ground is to build an altar and offer burnt offerings.
verseByVerse.theology: Noah's worship on dry ground establishes the pattern for all subsequent covenant worship: the first act after salvation is sacrifice, gratitude expressed in the costliest form available. The LORD's response — smelling the pleasing aroma and resolving never again to curse the ground because of man — is the establishment of common grace, the post-flood ordering of the world that makes human civilization possible. The promise embedded in 8:21–22 is the foundation of what Kuyper called the 'common grace' that sustains all of human culture and civilization.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham on Genesis 8: the chapter is structured as the mirror image of chapter 7 — the waters rise for the same number of days they take to recede, Noah opens what God closed, the birds are sent in reverse order from their entry. The literary symmetry signals theological completeness: what God undid by judgment he remakes by mercy. Calvin notes that God's 'remembrance' of Noah is one of the most comforting phrases in Scripture for believers in distress — it means the God who made the covenant is acting upon it, and no circumstance can make him forget those he has covenanted to save.

verseByVerse.quote: But God remembered Noah and all the beasts and all the livestock that were with him in the ark. And God made a wind blow over the earth, and the waters subsided. The fountains of the deep and the windows of the heavens were closed, the rain from the heavens was restrained, and the waters receded from the earth continually. At the end of 150 days the waters had abated, and in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. And the waters continued to abate until the tenth month; in the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains were seen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But God remembered Noah." In Hebrew, to remember is never merely to recall something that had slipped the mind; it is to act on a commitment. God remembers his covenant and rescues Israel (Exod. 2:24). God remembers Hannah and she conceives (1 Sam. 1:19). A dying criminal asks to be remembered and is told, today you will be with me in Paradise (Luke 23:42–43). The word marks the moment God moves.

And it is the hinge of the entire flood account. Everything before it goes up; everything after it goes down. This is the sentence a reader needs who is five months into grey water with no window — not that God has noticed, but that God has begun to act.

Then: "God made a wind blow over the earth, and the waters subsided." The word for wind is ruach, the same word translated Spirit in Genesis 1:2, where the Spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters. The flood undid creation; now the same Spirit moves over the same waters, and the world is made again. Judgment is not God's last word even in the chapter where he executes it.

The fountains are closed and the windows shut, and the recession is dated as carefully as the rising was. God is as precise in mercy as he was in judgment.

"The ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat" — the highlands of eastern Turkey and Armenia, a range rather than the single peak of popular imagination; the text says mountains, plural, and never names a summit. The verb is quiet and exact. After a year of being carried, the box that could not be steered comes to rest, and it comes to rest where God brought it.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of forty days Noah opened the window of the ark that he had made and sent forth a raven. It went to and fro until the waters were dried up from the earth. Then he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters had subsided from the face of the ground. But the dove found no place to set her foot, and she returned to him to the ark, for the waters were still on the face of the whole earth. So he put out his hand and took her and brought her into the ark with him. He waited another seven days, and again he sent forth the dove out of the ark. And the dove came back to him in the evening, and behold, in her mouth was a freshly plucked olive leaf. So Noah knew that the waters had subsided from the earth. Then he waited another seven days and sent forth the dove, and she did not return to him anymore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Noah opens a window and sends out a raven, and it goes to and fro. A raven is a scavenger and can settle on anything, so it tells him nothing. Then he sends a dove — a clean bird that will not perch on carrion — and she comes back, because "the dove found no place to set her foot."

"So he put out his hand and took her and brought her into the ark with him." It is a small, warm gesture in a large grim story: a man reaching out of a window over a drowned world to bring one exhausted bird back inside. The world had no rest to offer her. It has none to offer anyone, which is why the invitation of Christ is phrased as it is — come to me, and I will give you rest (Matt. 11:28).

Seven days later she comes back with a freshly plucked olive leaf. Not driftwood; something green and growing. Life has restarted under the water while Noah has been sitting in the dark. The olive branch has been the world's sign for peace ever since, and it began as evidence that God had finished being angry.

Then he waits another seven days and she does not come back. Notice the waiting. Twice he waits seven days, and the whole passage is a study in a man learning the pace of God — sending, waiting, sending again, and not once opening the door until he is told.

Scripture does not forget this bird. When the waters of judgment had been faced again — this time by a man standing in the Jordan on behalf of sinners who belonged there and he did not — the heavens opened and the Spirit descended on him like a dove (Matt. 3:16). The sign that the judgment is over and a new world has begun comes down out of the sky in the same shape both times.

verseByVerse.quote: In the six hundred and first year, in the first month, the first day of the month, the waters were dried from off the earth. And Noah removed the covering of the ark and looked, and behold, the face of the ground was dry. In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth had dried out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Noah removed the covering of the ark and looked, and behold, the face of the ground was dry." He can see it with his own eyes. The water is gone. And he does not move.

Look at the dates. The ground is dry on the first day of the first month; he leaves on the twenty-seventh day of the second month. Nearly two months with the roof off, the sun on his face, the evidence plain, and he stays inside — because God said go in (7:1), and God has not yet said come out.

That is a rarer kind of obedience than the building of the ark, and a harder one. Most Christians can be persuaded to act. Far fewer can wait in a place they are free to leave, on nothing but the word of God, when every visible circumstance says the wait is over.

verseByVerse.quote: Then God said to Noah, "Go out from the ark, you and your wife, and your sons and your sons' wives with you. Bring out with you every living thing that is with you of all flesh—birds and animals and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth—that they may swarm on the earth, and be fruitful and multiply on the earth." So Noah went out, and his sons and his wife and his sons' wives with him. Every beast, every creeping thing, and every bird, everything that moves on the earth, went out by families from the ark.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then God said to Noah, 'Go out from the ark.'" The word comes, and the family walks out into a world with nobody else in it.

And listen to the commission: "that they may swarm on the earth, and be fruitful and multiply on the earth." It is Genesis 1:22 spoken again, word for word, over the same kinds of creature. God is starting his creation project over with the same blessing he began it with. He has not changed his mind about what he wants the world to be.

"Every beast, every creeping thing, and every bird... went out by families from the ark." They went in two by two and they come out in families. A year in the dark, and the ark is fuller leaving than it was arriving. God's rescues do not merely preserve; they increase.

Do not romanticise the scene they stepped into. It was a clean world and it was also a graveyard — every place they had known, everyone they had known, gone. Survival is not the same as recovery, and the man who walked down that ramp had buried a civilisation. Anyone who has come through a catastrophe and found the sunshine strangely unbearable is standing where Noah stood, and Scripture does not pretend the ground under him was easy.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Noah built an altar to the LORD and took some of every clean animal and some of every clean bird and offered burnt offerings on the altar. And when the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma, the LORD said in his heart, "I will never again curse the ground because of man, for the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth. Neither will I ever again strike down every living creature as I have done. While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, shall not cease."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first thing Noah does on dry ground is build an altar. Not a house, not a fence, not a store — an altar. And it costs him: he takes "some of every clean animal and some of every clean bird," out of the only breeding stock in the world. This is the reason for the sevens in 7:2, and it is why the extra animals were loaded before Noah knew what he would need them for.

"And when the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma..." The picture is homely and deliberate: the smell of a meal that pleases the one it is offered to. Paul takes the phrase and puts it where it was always heading — Christ "gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God" (Eph. 5:2).

And then God speaks, not to Noah but "in his heart," and the reason he gives is astonishing. "I will never again curse the ground because of man, for the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth." That is the same diagnosis that justified the flood in 6:5 — and here it is used as the reason for restraint. God will not drown the world again, and the reason is not that people have improved. It is that he has decided to deal with the problem another way. If human sin were the trigger, the flood would be an annual event.

"While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, shall not cease." Every planted field and every ordinary sunrise since has been the keeping of that promise. The stability of the world is not physics; it is a vow. And the God who swore it is the one who says that heaven and earth will pass away before his words do (Matt. 24:35).

8.theology:
New Creation. Genesis 8 deliberately echoes Genesis 1: the wind (Spirit) moves over the waters, the dry land appears, the living creatures come out. The flood was de-creation; the recession of the waters is new creation. This typological pattern runs through Scripture — exodus, return from exile, and the resurrection of Christ (the new creation breaking into the old). Every act of divine redemption is a new creation, and the final new creation is the new heavens and earth of Revelation 21.

The Patience of God. Verse 21 is one of the Bible’s most profound statements about grace: God commits to patience with a race whose “heart is evil from youth.” Peter calls it “the patience of our Lord” (2 Pet. 3:15) and connects it to salvation: God waits so that more might be saved. The cross is what made it possible for God to commit to this patience without compromising his justice.
8.examples:
Then: Noah’s immediate act of worship (v.20) would have been instructive to Israelite readers familiar with burnt offerings: the great patriarch of the renewed creation was, above all, a worshiper. The olive leaf (v.11) became a universal symbol of peace precisely because of this story’s cultural reach across ancient civilization.

Now: “God remembered Noah” (v.1) is the pastoral anchor of the chapter. In the long silences — the unanswered prayer, the protracted suffering, the season in which God seems absent — the covenant promise is: he has not forgotten. His remembering is always the turn of the tide. And verse 21’s honest anthropology — evil from youth, yet God commits to patience — is the realistic foundation of Christian mission: we do not expect the gospel to improve human nature but to create new creatures within fallen nature.

9.title: The Covenant with Noah
9.text: <sup>1</sup>And God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth.<sup>2</sup>The fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every beast of the earth and upon every bird of the heavens, upon everything that creeps on the ground and all the fish of the sea. Into your hand they are delivered.<sup>3</sup>Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you. And as I gave you the green plants, I give you everything.<sup>4</sup>But you shall not eat flesh with its life, that is, its blood.<sup>5</sup>And for your lifeblood I will require a reckoning: from every beast I will require it and from man. From his fellow man I will require a reckoning for the life of man.<sup>6</sup>"Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image.<sup>7</sup>And you, be fruitful and multiply, increase greatly on the earth and multiply in it."<sup>8</sup>Then God said to Noah and to his sons with him,<sup>9</sup>"Behold, I establish my covenant with you and your offspring after you,<sup>10</sup>and with every living creature that is with you, the birds, the livestock, and every beast of the earth with you, as many as came out of the ark; it is for every beast of the earth.<sup>11</sup>I establish my covenant with you, that never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood, and never again shall there be a flood to destroy the earth."<sup>12</sup>And God said, "This is the sign of the covenant that I make between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for all future generations:<sup>13</sup>I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth.<sup>14</sup>When I bring clouds over the earth and the bow is seen in the clouds,<sup>15</sup>I will remember my covenant that is between me and you and every living creature of all flesh. And the waters shall never again become a flood to destroy all flesh.<sup>16</sup>When the bow is in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is on the earth."<sup>17</sup>God said to Noah, "This is the sign of the covenant that I have established between me and all flesh that is on the earth."<sup>18</sup>The sons of Noah who went forth from the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. (Ham was the father of Canaan.)<sup>19</sup>These three were the sons of Noah, and from these the people of the whole earth were dispersed.<sup>20</sup>Noah began to be a man of the soil, and he planted a vineyard.<sup>21</sup>He drank of the wine and became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent.<sup>22</sup>And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father and told his two brothers outside.<sup>23</sup>Then Shem and Japheth took a garment, laid it on both their shoulders, and walked backward and covered the nakedness of their father. Their faces were turned backward, and they did not see their father's nakedness.<sup>24</sup>When Noah awoke from his wine and knew what his youngest son had done to him,<sup>25</sup>he said, "Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be to his brothers."<sup>26</sup>He also said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem; and let Canaan be his servant.<sup>27</sup>May God enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant."<sup>28</sup>After the flood Noah lived 350 years.<sup>29</sup>All the days of Noah were 950 years, and he died.
9.overview:
Chapter 9 establishes the Noahic covenant — the first of the great biblical covenants to be formally ratified with a sign. God re-issues the cultural mandate (v.1, echoing 1:28), establishes the sanctity of human life rooted in the imago Dei (v.6), and seals his promise with a rainbow. The covenant is explicitly universal: not just with Noah and his family but with “every living creature” (v.10) and “all future generations” (v.12). It is the framework within which all subsequent history, and all subsequent covenants, operate.

The rainbow is one of Scripture’s most theologically rich signs. God hangs his weapon of war in the sky — a bow pointed upward, toward heaven — as a pledge that he will not destroy the earth by flood again. The sign is primarily for God, not humanity: “when I bring clouds over the earth and the bow is seen in the clouds, I will remember my covenant” (vv.14–15). The chapter closes honestly: Noah’s drunkenness and shame (vv.20–21) remind us that the flood did not change human nature. The new creation still needs a new Adam.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 9 establishes the first formally named covenant in Scripture. God blesses Noah with the creation mandate renewed, grants permission to eat meat, institutes capital punishment as the sanction for murder (grounding it in the image of God), and seals the covenant with the sign of the rainbow. The covenant is unconditional, universal, and everlasting — encompassing all humanity and all living creatures, not just Israel.
verseByVerse.theology: The Noahic covenant establishes the conditions for human civilization: the preservation of human life, the restraint of violence through the principle of accountability for murder, the stability of the natural order. These are not merely social arrangements but theological ordinances grounded in creation theology: human life has dignity because humans bear God's image; taking human life without authorization is an offense against God himself. The rainbow covenant sign transforms what was a natural phenomenon into a divine memorial — God binds his own memory to a meteorological occurrence, promising to see the bow and remember his covenant.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes that the Noahic covenant is the foundation of all subsequent covenants: it establishes the world in which the Abrahamic, Mosaic, and Davidic covenants will operate. Without the Noahic promise of creation's stability, none of the subsequent redemptive covenants have a theater in which to unfold. Keller observes that the covenant with Noah includes 'every living creature' — the most comprehensive covenant in Scripture, establishing God's commitment to his entire creation, not just to human beneficiaries.

verseByVerse.quote: And God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth. The fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every beast of the earth and upon every bird of the heavens, upon everything that creeps on the ground and all the fish of the sea. Into your hand they are delivered. Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you. And as I gave you the green plants, I give you everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them, 'Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth.'" It is Genesis 1:28 again, spoken over a new first family in a washed world. God is not starting a different project; he is restarting the same one.

But two things have changed, and the differences tell you what the flood did not fix. The word dominion has gone, and in its place comes "the fear of you and the dread of you." The relationship between humanity and the animals is no longer the peaceable rule of Eden; it is wariness on one side and power on the other. Anything wild runs from a man now, and that is a loss, not a promotion.

And the diet changes. "Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you." Before the flood the grant was vegetation (1:29); now meat is permitted explicitly. Take this seriously against any Christian teaching that treats eating meat as sin — God gives it in so many words, and Jesus later "declared all foods clean" (Mark 7:19). It is a concession to a harder world, not a rescinding of Eden's gentleness, and one day the wolf will lie down with the lamb again (Isa. 11:6–9).

verseByVerse.quote: But you shall not eat flesh with its life, that is, its blood. And for your lifeblood I will require a reckoning: from every beast I will require it and from man. From his fellow man I will require a reckoning for the life of man. "Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image. And you, be fruitful and multiply, increase greatly on the earth and multiply in it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
One restriction comes with the new permission: "you shall not eat flesh with its life, that is, its blood." Blood in the Bible stands for life, and life belongs to God. The rule taught the human race, at every meal, that the taking of life is a serious thing and that the life poured out is God's to receive. The whole sacrificial system will be built on the same principle: "the life of the flesh is in the blood... it is the blood that makes atonement" (Lev. 17:11).

Then God moves from animal life to human life, and the tone hardens. "Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed." This is the first delegation of judicial authority to human society in Scripture — the seed of every court and every police force. God had personally protected Cain from private vengeance (4:15); he now places the restraint of violence into human hands, under his authority, so that a Lamech cannot simply set his revenge to music. Paul says the governing authority "does not bear the sword in vain" (Rom. 13:4), and this verse is where the sword is first handed over.

And notice the reason given: "for God made man in his own image." Not because society needs order, not because murder is inconvenient, but because a human being is the image of God and to destroy one is to strike at him. That reason has not expired — Genesis 1:27 is quoted here, after the fall and after the flood, of people God has just described as evil from their youth. The image is defaced in all of us and cancelled in none of us, which is the ground of every claim about human rights that anyone has ever made stick.

verseByVerse.quote: Then God said to Noah and to his sons with him, "Behold, I establish my covenant with you and your offspring after you, and with every living creature that is with you, the birds, the livestock, and every beast of the earth with you, as many as came out of the ark; it is for every beast of the earth. I establish my covenant with you, that never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood, and never again shall there be a flood to destroy the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, I establish my covenant with you and your offspring after you." Watch who does the talking. God says "I establish" three times in four verses, and Noah is not asked to agree to anything, promise anything or perform anything. There are no conditions in this covenant at all. It is not a contract between two parties; it is a bond God ties to himself.

And look at the range of it: "with every living creature that is with you, the birds, the livestock, and every beast of the earth." The first covenant in Scripture includes the animals. God's commitment is to the world, not merely to the religious part of it, which is why Paul can say the whole creation waits on tiptoe for the revealing of the sons of God (Rom. 8:19–21).

"Never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood." A guarantee of the world's continuance, given to a race whose hearts God has just described as evil from youth. Every human being who has ever lived since has done so under the protection of a promise made to people who did not deserve it and were not asked to earn it.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "This is the sign of the covenant that I make between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for all future generations: I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth. When I bring clouds over the earth and the bow is seen in the clouds, I will remember my covenant that is between me and you and every living creature of all flesh. And the waters shall never again become a flood to destroy all flesh. When the bow is in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is on the earth." God said to Noah, "This is the sign of the covenant that I have established between me and all flesh that is on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives a sign, and the sign is a rainbow. The Hebrew word is simply qeshet, bow — the weapon. God hangs his war-bow in the clouds, pointed away from the earth and up towards heaven, and says: this is the sign. The instrument of judgment has been unstrung and put up on the wall.

Then the astonishing part, and it is easy to read past. Whose memory is the sign for? "When the bow is in the clouds, I will see it and remember." Not so that we remember. So that God does. He does not need reminding, of course; this is God binding himself in language a child could follow, promising to look at the sky and act on what he sees. The sign is put where he can see it.

Which is exactly how the other signs work. At the Passover, the blood on the doorposts was not so the family would remember but so that "when I see the blood, I will pass over you" (Exod. 12:13). And at the table where the Lord's people break bread, the pledge is not primarily to their memory but to God's covenant in his Son's blood. Assurance never rests on how well you remember. It rests on what God has undertaken to see.

Readers sometimes ask whether this means there had never been a rainbow before. The text does not say so. God takes a thing and assigns it a meaning — which is what he does with water in baptism and with bread on a table. The physics were presumably always there; what is new is the covenant now attached to them.

So the next time the rain stops and the light comes through it, the arc over the fields is a promise God made about not drowning the world, hung where he looks. He has kept it for every one of the days since.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–29 — The Sin of Ham and the Prophecy over the Sons of Noah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of Genesis 9 introduces the first post-flood failure: Noah's drunkenness and the sin of Ham. The episode is brief and difficult — its precise nature debated — but its consequences are long-lasting: the curse of Canaan and the blessing of Shem, anticipating the entire subsequent history of Israel's relationship to the Canaanites. The chapter ends with Noah's death at 950 years.
verseByVerse.theology: The sin of Ham — seeing his father's nakedness and reporting it to his brothers rather than covering it — represents a failure of honor, a refusal of the duty to protect family dignity. His brothers' response — walking backward, covering their father without looking — is the right behavior that exposes Ham's failure by contrast. The curse falls not on Ham but on Canaan, Ham's son, anticipating Israel's conquest of Canaan and the theological framework within which it should be understood: Canaan's subjugation is the consequence of an ancestral moral failure, not an arbitrary judgment.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes that the episode is deliberately placed immediately after the Noahic covenant to show that the flood did not solve the problem of human sin — the same moral failures that characterized the pre-flood world reappear immediately in the new world. Kidner observes that Noah's failure (drunkenness) and Ham's failure (dishonor of a parent) together show the persistence of the two great categories of sin: sins against God (failing to govern oneself) and sins against neighbor (failing to honor and protect others).

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Noah who went forth from the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. (Ham was the father of Canaan.) These three were the sons of Noah, and from these the people of the whole earth were dispersed. Noah began to be a man of the soil, and he planted a vineyard. He drank of the wine and became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent. And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father and told his two brothers outside. Then Shem and Japheth took a garment, laid it on both their shoulders, and walked backward and covered the nakedness of their father. Their faces were turned backward, and they did not see their father's nakedness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter turns, and it turns downwards. "Noah began to be a man of the soil, and he planted a vineyard. He drank of the wine and became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent." The righteous man, blameless in his generation, the only survivor of the judgment of the world, is lying naked and insensible in a tent before the chapter is out.

Genesis does not flinch at this and neither should the reader. The flood washed the earth and it did not wash the human heart; God said as much in 8:21 while Noah's altar was still smoking. The problem was never only out there. Take away every wicked person on the planet and leave one good family, and within a generation you have this. No change of environment has ever produced a change of nature, which is precisely why the gospel offers a new birth and not a fresh start.

And since the failure begins with a vineyard, the question deserves a straight answer: is drinking wine a sin? Scripture does not say so. It calls wine a gift that gladdens the heart of man (Ps. 104:15), the Lord Jesus made a great deal of it at a wedding, and Paul told Timothy to take a little for his stomach (1 Tim. 5:23). What Scripture condemns without exception is drunkenness (Eph. 5:18; Prov. 23:29–35), and Genesis 9 shows why: a man loses his judgment, loses his covering, and the damage lands on his children. If you cannot take it or leave it, that is the verse for you rather than the freedom.

"And Ham... saw the nakedness of his father and told his two brothers outside." The text is restrained about what happened, and speculation about worse crimes goes beyond the evidence. What is clear is the telling. He looked, and then he went out and made his father's shame into something to be shared — the oldest and most respectable form of cruelty there is.

His brothers do the opposite, and the description is almost comic in its care: a garment over both their shoulders, walking backwards, faces turned away. They would not even look. Peter must have had scenes like this in mind when he wrote that love covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet. 4:8) — and the covering here is literal cloth, carried backwards, so that a man's dignity survived his worst night.

verseByVerse.quote: When Noah awoke from his wine and knew what his youngest son had done to him, he said, "Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be to his brothers." He also said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem; and let Canaan be his servant. May God enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant." After the flood Noah lived 350 years. All the days of Noah were 950 years, and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Noah wakes and speaks, and the first question is why the curse falls on Canaan when the offender was Ham. Scripture does not explain it, and honest readers have suggested several things: that Canaan was somehow involved, that the son of the offender is named to make the point that sin runs in families, or that Moses is telling Israel, on the edge of the land, exactly where the Canaanite nations came from. The last is almost certainly part of it. Chapter 10 will list Canaan's descendants, and chapter 19 will show what Sodom had become.

What must be said plainly is what this passage does not say. It is not about skin colour, it names no race, and it pronounces nothing over Africa or over anyone alive today. For centuries it was quoted to justify the enslavement of black people, and that reading is a lie built on a text that says nothing of the kind. The curse is on one man's line, it concerns the Canaanites of Palestine, and it was worked out in the conquest of a land under judgment for its own sins (Lev. 18:24–25).

The blessing, meanwhile, is aimed somewhere. "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem" — Noah does not bless Shem; he blesses Shem's God, which is a way of saying that the line of promise runs here. Out of Shem come the Semitic peoples, and out of them Abraham, and out of Abraham the Christ. And "may God enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem" is a sentence with a very long fuse: the outsider brought in to live in the household of the covenant. Every Gentile reader of this commentary is standing in that tent (cf. Eph. 2:12–13).

"All the days of Noah were 950 years, and he died." The formula of chapter 5 returns, and the drumbeat picks up where it left off. The man who survived the end of the world still goes into the ground. Whatever else the flood accomplished, it did not deal with death, and the world is still waiting for the offspring promised in 3:15.

9.theology:
Common Grace. The Noahic covenant introduces what Reformed theology calls “common grace” — God’s non-saving grace extended to all people, preserving the created order and enabling human civilization. The regularity of seasons (8:22), the restraint of evil, the capacity for beauty and justice even among the unredeemed — all flow from this covenant. Common grace does not save, but it makes human life possible and valuable, and it is the framework within which saving grace operates.

The Rainbow and the Cross. The rainbow as God’s sign — a weapon pointed upward — prefigures the cross. At Calvary, the judgment that the flood represented fell on the Son of God, satisfying divine justice and making it possible for God to commit to patience with a fallen world. The rainbow promises the flood will not return; the cross explains how God can keep that promise without ignoring sin.
9.examples:
Then: The Noahic covenant established the framework for all human civilization and law. Verse 6 (blood for blood) is the basis for proportional justice underlying all legal systems. The rainbow was a visible covenant sign in an era before written documents — God’s public promise inscribed in the sky for every generation.

Now: The misuse of verses 24–27 to justify slavery demands explicit correction: the “curse of Ham” has no biblical basis and is one of the most destructive exegetical errors in history. The chapter’s actual message is the Noahic covenant’s universal scope: every morning that dawns, every harvest that succeeds, every civilization that sustains human life — these are gifts of covenant faithfulness to a world that does not deserve them. Creation care is therefore not merely a secular concern but a theological one.

10.title: The Table of Nations
10.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the generations of the sons of Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Sons were born to them after the flood.<sup>2</sup>The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras.<sup>3</sup>The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah.<sup>4</sup>The sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim.<sup>5</sup>From these the coastland peoples spread in their lands, each with his own language, by their clans, in their nations.<sup>6</sup>The sons of Ham: Cush, Egypt, Put, and Canaan.<sup>7</sup>The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.<sup>8</sup>Cush fathered Nimrod; he was the first on earth to be a mighty man.<sup>9</sup>He was a mighty hunter before the LORD. Therefore it is said, "Like Nimrod a mighty hunter before the LORD."<sup>10</sup>The beginning of his kingdom was Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.<sup>11</sup>From that land he went into Assyria and built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah, and<sup>12</sup>Resen between Nineveh and Calah; that is the great city.<sup>13</sup>Egypt fathered Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim,<sup>14</sup>Pathrusim, Casluhim (from whom the Philistines came), and Caphtorim.<sup>15</sup>Canaan fathered Sidon his firstborn and Heth,<sup>16</sup>and the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites,<sup>17</sup>the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites,<sup>18</sup>the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites. Afterward the clans of the Canaanites dispersed.<sup>19</sup>And the territory of the Canaanites extended from Sidon in the direction of Gerar as far as Gaza, and in the direction of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha.<sup>20</sup>These are the sons of Ham, by their clans, their languages, their lands, and their nations.<sup>21</sup>To Shem also, the father of all the children of Eber, the elder brother of Japheth, children were born.<sup>22</sup>The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram.<sup>23</sup>The sons of Aram: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash.<sup>24</sup>Arpachshad fathered Shelah; and Shelah fathered Eber.<sup>25</sup>To Eber were born two sons: the name of the one was Peleg, for in his days the earth was divided, and his brother's name was Joktan.<sup>26</sup>Joktan fathered Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah,<sup>27</sup>Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah,<sup>28</sup>Obal, Abimael, Sheba,<sup>29</sup>Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab; all these were the sons of Joktan.<sup>30</sup>The territory in which they lived extended from Mesha in the direction of Sephar to the hill country of the east.<sup>31</sup>These are the sons of Shem, by their clans, their languages, their lands, and their nations.<sup>32</sup>These are the clans of the sons of Noah, according to their genealogies, in their nations, and from these the nations spread abroad on the earth after the flood.
10.overview:
The Table of Nations in Genesis 10 is one of the most remarkable documents in the ancient world — a comprehensive map of human ethnicity covering seventy nations descended from Noah’s three sons. It is theology presented as geography: every people group on earth is connected to the one family preserved in the ark, and therefore to the one God who preserved them.

The chapter sits between the Noahic covenant (ch.9) and the Tower of Babel (ch.11), showing that God’s covenant has produced a fruitful humanity while laying the groundwork for the Babel narrative. The seventy nations will become a recurring number in Israel’s theology — the seventy elders of Exodus 24, the seventy sent by Jesus in Luke 10 — signaling the scope of God’s concern for all peoples. The genealogy traces through Shem to Eber (the ancestor of the Hebrews), narrowing toward Abraham: from seventy nations, God will call one man, through whom he intends to bless all the others.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 10, the table of nations, is one of the most remarkable chapters in the ancient world's literature — a comprehensive genealogical map of the known world's peoples derived from Noah's three sons. Seventy nations are listed, organized by geography and kinship, establishing the unity of the human race in its diversity: all humanity descends from Noah, and through him from Adam. The table answers the question raised by the flood: what happened to the nations that came from Noah's sons?
verseByVerse.theology: The theological function of the table of nations is to establish the context for the call of Abraham (ch.12): God does not call Abraham in a vacuum but in a world of diverse nations, and his promise to Abraham — 'in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed' (12:3) — is intelligible only against the backdrop of these seventy families. The nations that seem merely to be geographical and genealogical data are the object of God's redemptive purpose, the 'panta ta ethne' of the Great Commission (Matt. 28:19). Every nation in chapter 10 is a nation that God intends to bless through the seed of Abraham.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes that the table of nations is unique in ancient literature — no other ancient document attempts such a comprehensive ethnographic survey. It reflects a theological worldview in which all nations are known to God, derive from a common ancestor, and stand under a single Creator's governance.
