Four eastern kings led by Chedorlaomer of Elam have held the five cities of the Jordan plain as tributary vassals for twelve years; in the thirteenth the five rebel; in the fourteenth the army comes back.

The detail is not decoration. Genesis has just spent two chapters on one man and his tents, and now it puts him inside real international politics — coalitions, tribute, rebellion, reprisal. The family we are following does not live in a religious bubble; it lives in a world of armies, and the God who called Abram is the God of that world too.

And there is a quiet point in the arrangement. Chapter 13 ended with Lot settling near Sodom because the valley was well watered. He chose on the strength of rainfall and grass, and the one factor he did not weigh was that the place was a rebellious vassal state of an eastern empire. Nobody assessing a decision by what he can see ever has the whole board in front of him.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him came and defeated the Rephaim in Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzim in Ham, the Emim in Shaveh-kiriathaim, and the Horites in their hill country of Seir as far as El-paran on the border of the wilderness. Then they turned back and came to En-mishpat (that is, Kadesh) and defeated all the country of the Amalekites, and also the Amorites who were dwelling in Hazazon-tamar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The campaign route in these verses is a long sweep — down the eastern side of the Dead Sea, round the southern end, and back up through the Negeb. Rephaim, Zuzim, Emim, Horites, Amalekites, Amorites: six peoples flattened on the way.

This is not a raid. It is an empire putting down a rebellion and taking the scenic route through everybody else's territory to make sure the point is understood. By the time it reaches the Valley of Siddim, Chedorlaomer's army has beaten six nations in a single season.

Hold that number, because Genesis is establishing a scale on purpose. What one man with 318 household servants is about to do only registers if you know what he is going after.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king of Sodom, the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar) went out, and they joined battle in the Valley of Siddim with Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of Goiim, Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar, four kings against five. Now the Valley of Siddim was full of bitumen pits, and as the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, some fell into them, and the rest fled to the hill country. So the enemy took all the possessions of Sodom and Gomorrah, and all their provisions, and went their way. They also took Lot, the son of Abram's brother, who was dwelling in Sodom, and his possessions, and went their way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The five kings of the plain go out and lose badly. "Now the Valley of Siddim was full of bitumen pits, and as the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, some fell into them." There is a grim irony in it: the tar that made the region wealthy swallows the men running away from the consequences of its wealth.

"So the enemy took all the possessions of Sodom and Gomorrah, and all their provisions, and went their way." A whole city's goods loaded onto carts and taken east. Everything Lot had chosen the valley for goes over the horizon in an afternoon.

Then the sentence the chapter has been building towards, and it is almost thrown away in a subordinate clause: "They also took Lot, the son of Abram's brother, who was dwelling in Sodom, and his possessions."

In chapter 13 he moved his tent as far as Sodom. Now he is dwelling in it, and when the city goes under he goes with it. He has committed no crime here; he simply lives at the address, and when the soldiers came they did not stop to check his personal file. A man who pitches his life among people who do not fear God will share their weather, and it will not feel fair when it happens.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one who had escaped came and told Abram the Hebrew, who was living by the oaks of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and of Aner. These were allies of Abram. When Abram heard that his kinsman had been taken captive, he led forth his trained men, born in his house, 318 of them, and went in pursuit as far as Dan. And he divided his forces against them by night, he and his servants, and defeated them and pursued them to Hobah, north of Damascus. Then he brought back all the possessions, and also brought back his kinsman Lot with his possessions, and the women and the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Abram the Hebrew" — the first time anyone in the Bible is given that name. The word probably means one from the other side: the man from across the river, the immigrant, the outsider. It is what other people called him, not what he called himself, and Genesis uses it at precisely the moment he risks his life for the country that regards him as a foreigner.

Note too that he has allies — Mamre, Eshcol and Aner, three Amorite brothers. The man who lives in tents and worships the true God has working relationships with his Canaanite neighbours, and they will fight alongside him. Separation from the world in Scripture has never meant having nothing to do with anyone in it.

"He led forth his trained men, born in his house, 318 of them, and went in pursuit as far as Dan." A hundred and twenty miles north, against an army that has just destroyed six nations. He divides his forces and attacks at night, which is the tactic of a man who knows he cannot win in daylight, and he chases the survivors past Damascus. It works completely.

Now consider who he is doing this for. Lot took the best land, drifted towards Sodom, settled in it, and is not recorded as having said a word to his uncle since the day they parted. Abram is under no obligation of any kind, legal or moral. He hears the news and goes.

Set that beside the man of two chapters earlier who handed his wife to Pharaoh to save his own skin. Grace does not remake a person overnight, but it does remake him, and the evidence turns up in what he does when somebody else is in trouble and there is nothing in it for him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Melchizedek and the King of Sodom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The return from battle brings Abram into encounters with two kings that function as a theological test: Melchizedek of Salem blesses Abram in the name of God Most High and receives tithes; the king of Sodom offers Abram the plunder. Abram's response to each encounter reveals his theological convictions: he honors Melchizedek as a priest of the true God and refuses the king of Sodom's gift so that his prosperity will be attributed to God alone and not to any earthly king.
verseByVerse.theology: Melchizedek appears without genealogy, without predecessor, without successor — which is exactly what the author of Hebrews will use to argue for his typological significance as a figure of the eternal priesthood of Christ. The tithe Abram pays to Melchizedek acknowledges a priestly authority higher than Abram's own covenant standing. This pre-Levitical priesthood — Gentile, royal, based in Jerusalem — is the priestly order that Psalm 110 will assign to the Messiah, and that Hebrews 7 will develop as the eternal priesthood that supersedes Aaron's.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham on Genesis 14:17–24: the juxtaposition of the two encounters is deliberate. The king of Sodom's offer — 'give me the people and keep the goods for yourself' — is superficially generous but actually places Abram in his debt. Abram's refusal protects his independence and his testimony: he will not allow any earthly benefactor to claim credit for the covenant blessing. The principle is permanent: the blessing of God's covenant people must never be attributed to the generosity of those who oppose God's purposes, however attractive the offer appears.

verseByVerse.quote: After his return from the defeat of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, the king of Sodom went out to meet him at the Valley of Shaveh (that is, the King's Valley). And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. (He was priest of God Most High.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two kings come out to meet Abram, and the chapter is deliberately arranged so that the second one interrupts the first. The king of Sodom sets out in verse 17 — and then has to wait until verse 21, because somebody far stranger arrives first.

"And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. (He was priest of God Most High.)"

Everything about him is unexpected. He appears from nowhere, with no genealogy, no father named, no successor, and after this chapter he vanishes from Genesis entirely. His name means king of righteousness. Salem means peace, and is almost certainly the old name of Jerusalem (cf. Ps. 76:2) — so he is king of righteousness and king of peace, in that order, which is the order Hebrews notices (Heb. 7:2).

And he is a priest of El Elyon, God Most High. Abram does not correct his theology, does not evangelise him, and in a moment will adopt his title for God as his own. There was a man in Canaan, outside the covenant family, who knew and served the true God before Israel existed. God has never been without a witness anywhere.

verseByVerse.quote: And he blessed him and said, "Blessed be Abram by God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth; and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand!" And Abram gave him a tenth of everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And he blessed him... And Abram gave him a tenth of everything." Two actions, and both put Melchizedek above Abram. In Scripture the greater blesses the lesser, and the lesser pays the tithe. The man who has just defeated four kings, who carries the promise that all the families of the earth will be blessed in him, takes the junior place without a moment's hesitation.

Then Melchizedek disappears for a thousand years — until a psalm says of Israel's coming king, "You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek" (Ps. 110:4). That is a startling line, because Israel's kings came from Judah and her priests from Levi, and no man was permitted to be both; King Uzziah was struck with leprosy for trying (2 Chron. 26:16–21). The psalm is promising somebody who will hold both offices legitimately, on a warrant older than Aaron's.

A thousand years after the psalm, Hebrews takes these two verses and builds a chapter on them (Heb. 7). Jesus is a priest of a different and older order than Aaron's — appointed not by descent but "by the power of an indestructible life" (Heb. 7:16), king and priest at once, with no predecessor and no successor. And Hebrews presses the tithe: Levi, whose sons would one day receive tithes from Israel, was still in the body of his ancestor Abraham when Abraham paid this one — so the whole Levitical priesthood, in its founder, bowed to this priest (Heb. 7:9–10).

Two fair questions arise. Who was Melchizedek? Some rabbis identified him with Shem, who by the reckoning of chapter 11 was still alive; some Christians have taken him for an appearance of the pre-incarnate Christ. The second is ruled out by Hebrews itself, which says he was "resembling the Son of God" (Heb. 7:3) — you do not say that a man resembles himself. The straightforward reading is that he was a real Canaanite priest-king who worshipped the true God, and that God arranged his one recorded appearance so that the pattern would be on the page when it was needed.

And what does Hebrews mean by "without father or mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life"? Not that he had no parents. The argument is from the silence of the record: in a book obsessed with genealogies, where a priest's right to serve depended entirely on proving his descent, this priest arrives with no lineage, no birth, no death and no successor. Scripture leaves him standing there permanently, and that is what makes him a picture of a priest whose office never ends.

Then the tithe, which is the first in the Bible and raises a fair question: are Christians bound to give a tenth? The New Testament never restates it as a law. What it asks for is giving that is regular, planned, proportionate to income, generous and cheerful (1 Cor. 16:2; 2 Cor. 9:6–7). But notice where the tenth turns up here — not under law, four centuries before Sinai, given spontaneously by a man overwhelmed at having met a priest of God Most High. It is not a tax. It is what worship did with a wallet, and the believer hunting for the minimum has already misread the chapter.

And the priest of Salem brought out bread and wine. Genesis offers no explanation and none should be manufactured. But a priest-king coming out to meet a weary man returning from battle, with bread and wine in his hands, is not a scene the church has ever managed to read without thinking of another table.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king of Sodom said to Abram, "Give me the persons, but take the goods for yourself." But Abram said to the king of Sodom, "I have lifted my hand to the LORD, God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth, that I would not take a thread or a sandal strap or anything that is yours, lest you should say, 'I have made Abram rich.' I will take nothing but what the young men have eaten, and the share of the men who went with me. Let Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre take their share."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the king of Sodom finally gets his sentence, and it is an offer: "Give me the persons, but take the goods for yourself." By every custom of the ancient world the spoil belongs to the victor. This is generous, it is legal, and Abram has earned it.

He refuses it flat. "I have lifted my hand to the LORD, God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth, that I would not take a thread or a sandal strap or anything that is yours."

Two things in that. He has already sworn it — the oath was made before the offer came, which is the only way anyone ever refuses a windfall. Decisions of this kind are not made in the moment; they are made beforehand and merely executed in the moment. And he uses Melchizedek's own title for God, Possessor of heaven and earth, which he heard perhaps ten minutes earlier. The blessing has gone in and come straight out again as conviction.

His stated reason is reputation: "lest you should say, 'I have made Abram rich.'" He has been made rich once already by a pagan king, in Egypt, on the strength of a lie about his wife (12:16), and it went badly. He will not leave the source of his prosperity open to question a second time.

Run that as a test on your own accounts. Is there anything you would find awkward to explain the origin of — any gain that would let somebody else plausibly claim the credit for what you would rather attribute to God? Abram walked away from a king's fortune to keep the answer to that question clean, and he did it on the same afternoon he had been offered it legally.

And the last line matters as much as the refusal. "I will take nothing but what the young men have eaten, and the share of the men who went with me. Let Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre take their share." His vow binds him and he does not impose it on his allies. They fought; they are paid.

That is a distinction a great many earnest Christians never learn to draw. A private conviction, however right, is not a rule for everyone in the room, and a man of real principle does not make his neighbours live inside his vow. Abram draws the line in a single sentence, and Paul spends most of Romans 14 saying the same thing.

14.theology:
The Order of Melchizedek. Melchizedek is the Bible’s most developed Christological type before the New Testament. The four elements of his description — king and priest simultaneously, king of peace (Salem), priest of God Most High, bringer of bread and wine — each find their fulfillment in Jesus: the king who is also high priest (Heb. 4:14), whose kingdom is peace (Eph. 2:14–15), who is the Son of God Most High (Mark 5:7), and who at the Last Supper institutes the bread and wine of the new covenant. To read Genesis 14 in canonical context is to see Christ present in the shadows of Abram’s world.

The Superiority of Christ’s Priesthood. Hebrews’ use of Melchizedek establishes the theological argument for the new covenant: the Levitical priesthood, however divinely ordained, was never the final word. It was itself subordinate to an older, greater order — a priesthood without genealogical succession and without repeated sacrifice. Jesus fulfils this order perfectly: he is priest by divine oath (“the LORD has sworn and will not change his mind,” Ps. 110:4), his priesthood is permanent (“forever”), and his sacrifice is once for all (Heb. 7:27).
14.examples:
Then: The coalition of kings in chapter 14 reflects the political realities of the ancient Near East, where city-states formed and broke alliances constantly and where regional hegemony shifted with military campaigns. That Abram — a single clan patriarch with 318 trained men — defeated a coalition of kings is presented as a miracle of divine enabling (v.20: “God Most High... has delivered your enemies into your hand”), not military strategy. Salem (Jerusalem) appears here for the first time — the city that will eventually house the temple and the throne of David, where the Son of David will be crucified and rise.

Now: The Melchizedek encounter speaks directly to the contemporary temptation to allow worldly sources — employers, governments, markets, benefactors — to become the perceived source of our prosperity, such that their claims on us feel as strong as God’s. Abram’s refusal of Sodom’s king’s goods (“lest you should say I have made Abram rich”) is the posture of the person who knows where their life comes from and cannot afford to let that clarity be muddied. And the bread and wine of Melchizedek are the standing invitation: the eternal priest-king still brings the table, and every eucharist is a meeting with the one who is greater than Abraham.

15.title: The LORD Your Shield and Reward
15.text: <sup>1</sup>After these things the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision: "Fear not, Abram, I am your shield; your reward shall be very great."<sup>2</sup>But Abram said, "O Lord GOD, what will you give me, for I continue childless, and the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?"<sup>3</sup>And Abram said, "Behold, you have given me no offspring, and a member of my household will be my heir."<sup>4</sup>And behold, the word of the LORD came to him: "This man shall not be your heir; your very own son shall be your heir."<sup>5</sup>And he brought him outside and said, "Look toward heaven, and number the stars, if you are able to number them." Then he said to him, "So shall your offspring be."<sup>6</sup>And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness.<sup>7</sup>And he said to him, "I am the LORD who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land to possess."<sup>8</sup>But he said, "O Lord GOD, how am I to know that I shall possess it?"<sup>9</sup>He said to him, "Bring me a heifer three years old, a female goat three years old, a ram three years old, a turtledove, and a young pigeon."<sup>10</sup>And he brought him all these, cut them in half, and laid each half over against the other. But he did not cut the birds in half.<sup>11</sup>And when birds of prey came down on the carcasses, Abram drove them away.<sup>12</sup>As the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell on Abram. And behold, dreadful and great darkness fell upon him.<sup>13</sup>Then the LORD said to Abram, "Know for certain that your offspring will be sojourners in a land that is not theirs and will be servants there, and they will be afflicted for four hundred years.<sup>14</sup>But I will bring judgment on the nation that they serve, and afterward they shall come out with great possessions.<sup>15</sup>As for you, you shall go to your fathers in peace; you shall be buried in a good old age.<sup>16</sup>And they shall come back here in the fourth generation, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete."<sup>17</sup>When the sun had gone down and it was dark, behold, a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces.<sup>18</sup>On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, "To your offspring I give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates,<sup>19</sup>the land of the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites,<sup>20</sup>the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim,<sup>21</sup>the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites and the Jebusites."
15.overview:
Genesis 15 contains two of the most theologically significant moments in the entire Bible. The first is verse 6: “And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness.” Paul quotes this verse in Romans 4:3 and Galatians 3:6 as the definitive Old Testament statement of justification by faith — the declaration that right standing before God comes not through works but through trust in God’s promise. This verse is the theological center of gravity of the entire patriarchal narrative and, ultimately, of the doctrine of salvation.

The second is the covenant-cutting ceremony of verses 9–17. Abram prepares the animals, splits them in two, and lays the halves opposite each other — the standard form of an ancient Near Eastern covenant ceremony, in which both parties would walk between the pieces, invoking the self-curse: “may what happened to these animals happen to me if I break this covenant.” Then Abram falls into a deep sleep, and God alone — represented by the smoking fire pot and flaming torch — passes between the pieces. Abram does not walk. The covenant is unilateral: God swears by himself (Heb. 6:13), taking the full obligation of the covenant on himself. If the covenant breaks, it will cost God, not Abram.

This is the theological shape of grace: God takes the curse of covenant-breaking upon himself. The cross is where that self-curse was fulfilled: God the Son bore the judgment that the broken covenant demanded, walking through the pieces so that his people would not have to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Covenant Confirmed: Abram's Faith and God's Oath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 15 is one of the most theologically significant chapters in the Old Testament. It contains the first direct divine statement that faith is credited as righteousness (v.6), the formal ratification of the covenant by divine oath (vv.9–21), and the first explicit prophecy of Israel's Egyptian bondage and the Exodus (vv.13–16). The chapter is in two movements: a dialogue about the promise of offspring (vv.1–6), and a covenant ratification ceremony about the promise of land (vv.7–21).
verseByVerse.theology: Genesis 15:6 is the theological summit of the Abraham narrative and the center of Paul's argument in Romans 4 and Galatians 3: 'And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness.' Righteousness before God is not achieved by human moral accomplishment but received through faith — trust in the God who makes and keeps promises. Abram's faith is described in a moment of particular darkness: he is an old man with no heir, the promise of offspring seems impossible, and God is asking him to believe it anyway. The faith credited as righteousness is not easy confidence but trust maintained against appearances.
verseByVerse.examples: The covenant ratification ceremony of vv.9–21 is the most remarkable ceremony in Genesis. God instructs Abram to cut animals in half and arrange them in two rows — the standard ancient Near Eastern covenant ratification ceremony in which both parties would walk between the pieces, invoking upon themselves the fate of the animals if they broke the covenant. But Abram does not walk between the pieces; only God does — represented by the smoking fire pot and the flaming torch. God swears the covenant with himself, making the covenant's fulfillment dependent entirely on God's own faithfulness. This is the most unconditional covenant in Scripture: its guarantee is not human obedience but divine self-oath.

verseByVerse.quote: After these things the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision: "Fear not, Abram, I am your shield; your reward shall be very great." But Abram said, "O Lord GOD, what will you give me, for I continue childless, and the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?" And Abram said, "Behold, you have given me no offspring, and a member of my household will be my heir."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"After these things" — after the rescue, after Melchizedek, after refusing a king's fortune. And the first thing God says is "Fear not." A man does not need that said to him unless he is afraid, and Abram has just made enemies of four kings and turned down the protection of a fifth. The great acts of faith are usually followed by a bad night.

"I am your shield; your reward shall be very great." Both halves answer what he has just done. He has no army worth the name, so God is his shield. He has just refused a thread and a sandal strap, so God is his reward. Notice that God does not promise to give him a great reward; some translations catch it better — I am your very great reward. The gift is the Giver.

And then Abram answers, and it is the most honest speech in the book so far. "O Lord GOD, what will you give me, for I continue childless?" He is not worshipping. He is arguing, and the argument is: everything you have promised runs through a son, and there is no son. My heir is a servant from Damascus.

God does not rebuke him for it. That should be said plainly to anyone who has been taught that questions are the opposite of faith. Abram takes his complaint to God rather than about him, and the whole chapter is God's reply. There is a world of difference between the doubt that walks away and the doubt that stands in front of God and says, I do not understand this.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, the word of the LORD came to him: "This man shall not be your heir; your very own son shall be your heir." And he brought him outside and said, "Look toward heaven, and number the stars, if you are able to number them." Then he said to him, "So shall your offspring be."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"This man shall not be your heir; your very own son shall be your heir." God answers the actual question, without softening it and without delay.

"And he brought him outside." It is night. The old man is taken out of the tent and made to stand under the desert sky, where the stars are not the faint handful visible from a lit street but a blazing spill from horizon to horizon. "Look toward heaven, and number the stars, if you are able to number them." Then he said to him, "So shall your offspring be."

God could have said it inside. He takes him out and shows him something, because faith is strengthened by being given a picture rather than a proposition. Every clear night for the rest of his life, Abram would walk out of his tent and see the promise over his head, uncountable.

Which is a mercy God still deals in. He gives his people signs they can look at — a bow in the cloud, water, bread broken, a cup — because he knows what we are made of, and that a man standing in the dark needs something to see.

verseByVerse.quote: And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness."

Fifteen English words, and the New Testament will build the doctrine of justification on them. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 4 and again in Galatians 3; James quotes it too. It is the hinge on which the Reformation turned, and it is sitting in Genesis, four hundred years before the law was given.

Take the three words one at a time. He believed — the Hebrew is from the root that gives us amen; it means to lean one's weight on something reliable. Abram did not achieve anything, promise anything or perform anything. He rested on what God said. Counted is an accounting word — reckoned, credited, entered in the ledger. And righteousness is the standing of a man who is right with God.

Now put it together, and notice what is not there. There is no altar in this verse, no sacrifice, no circumcision — Paul makes a great deal of the fact that this happened before chapter 17, so that Abraham was justified as an uncircumcised man and is therefore the father of believing Gentiles too (Rom. 4:9–12). There is no obedience being rewarded. A man believed a promise about a son he did not have, and God credited righteousness to his account.

So the ledger is the thing to see. Righteousness is not manufactured in Abram and then noticed by God; it is reckoned to him, put to his account from outside, on the basis of faith. That is exactly how it still works. "To the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness" (Rom. 4:5). Justifies the ungodly — Paul's word, not a softer one.

And the faith itself is not the achievement. Abram's believing did not earn anything; it laid hold of something. A drowning man who takes a rope has not performed a feat of strength. What saved him was the rope and the arm on the other end of it.

James, who quotes this same verse to say that faith without works is dead (James 2:23), is not contradicting Paul. He is watching the same man from further down the road, at Genesis 22, and asking what a real faith does over forty years. Abram was justified in chapter 15 and proved in chapter 22, and both writers quote the same sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "I am the LORD who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land to possess." But he said, "O Lord GOD, how am I to know that I shall possess it?" He said to him, "Bring me a heifer three years old, a female goat three years old, a ram three years old, a turtledove, and a young pigeon." And he brought him all these, cut them in half, and laid each half over against the other. But he did not cut the birds in half. And when birds of prey came down on the carcasses, Abram drove them away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"How am I to know that I shall possess it?" He has just been credited with righteousness for believing, and now he asks for proof. Faith and the desire for assurance are not enemies; the same man does both in the space of two verses.

God's answer is not a lecture but an instruction: bring a heifer, a goat, a ram, a dove and a pigeon. Abram knows exactly what to do with them, because this is how covenants were made in his world. The animals are cut in half and the halves laid facing each other with a path between, and the parties to the agreement walk down that aisle of blood, saying in effect: may I be as these animals if I break my word. A covenant was not signed; it was cut, and the Hebrew idiom says so.

"And when birds of prey came down on the carcasses, Abram drove them away." Hours of it, in the heat, waving off vultures over the pieces of a covenant that has not yet been ratified. Sometimes the work of faith is nothing more dignified than keeping the scavengers off a promise while you wait for God to move.

verseByVerse.quote: As the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell on Abram. And behold, dreadful and great darkness fell upon him. Then the LORD said to Abram, "Know for certain that your offspring will be sojourners in a land that is not theirs and will be servants there, and they will be afflicted for four hundred years. But I will bring judgment on the nation that they serve, and afterward they shall come out with great possessions. As for you, you shall go to your fathers in peace; you shall be buried in a good old age. And they shall come back here in the fourth generation, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"As the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell on Abram." It is the same word used of Adam when God built the woman from his side (2:21), and both times it marks the point where the man is taken out of the action so that God can work alone.

"And behold, dreadful and great darkness fell upon him." Not merely night — terror. Coming into the presence of the living God is not a warm experience in Scripture, and the man who is about to receive the most extravagant promise in the book receives it flat on the ground in the dark and afraid.

And what God says into that darkness is not reassurance. It is four hundred years of slavery. "Know for certain that your offspring will be sojourners in a land that is not theirs and will be servants there, and they will be afflicted." God tells him the truth about the future of his family before he confirms the covenant, and the truth includes Egypt.

Read that carefully if you have been told that God's plan for his people is a smooth road. Between the promise and the possession lies four centuries of affliction, and God says so in advance, in the same speech in which he swears the land to them. The suffering was not a failure of the plan. It was inside the plan, and God's people were told.

The figures raise two fair questions. Four hundred years here, and 430 in Exodus 12:40 — the one is a round number for the same span, as Stephen also reckons it (Acts 7:6). And "the fourth generation" beside four centuries: a generation in this passage is plainly a long unit, and Exodus supplies the arithmetic — Levi, Kohath, Amram, Moses is exactly four (Exod. 6:16–20).

Then two mercies. "As for you, you shall go to your fathers in peace" — Abram himself will die before any of it. And "they shall come back here in the fourth generation, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete."

That last clause is one of the most important sentences in the Old Testament, and it answers a question that troubles many readers of Joshua. Why did God give this land to Israel by conquest? Because four hundred years later its inhabitants would be ripe for judgment — and note the corollary, which is startling: God delays his own promise to Abram for four centuries because the Amorites are not yet guilty enough to be evicted. He will not judge a people before their time. The patience the world reads as absence is God giving generations to nations that never asked for the delay (cf. 2 Pet. 3:9).

verseByVerse.quote: When the sun had gone down and it was dark, behold, a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces. On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, "To your offspring I give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates, the land of the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites and the Jebusites."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When the sun had gone down and it was dark, behold, a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces."

Everything in the chapter has been leading here, and the whole gospel is in what happens next — or rather, in what does not happen. Abram is asleep. He never walks the path. Only God passes between the pieces, in the fire and smoke that signal his presence throughout Scripture, and he goes down that aisle alone.

Take the measure of that. In a normal covenant both parties walk, and both take on the curse if they fail. Here God binds himself to keep both sides. He is saying, in the language Abram understood perfectly: if I fail to keep this, may I be torn in pieces — and if you fail to keep it, may I be torn in pieces.

Which is exactly what happened. Centuries later the sky went dark over a hill outside Jerusalem in the middle of the afternoon, and God kept the terms of a covenant that his people had broken in every generation, and he kept them in his own body. "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us" (Gal. 3:13).

"On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram" — literally, cut a covenant. And the boundaries are given, and the ten nations named, land that Israel would not hold for the best part of five hundred years.

Readers rightly ask whether that land grant was ever fulfilled, and Christians answer it differently. Solomon's kingdom is said to have reached from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt (1 Kings 4:21), and Joshua says that not one word of all the LORD's good promises failed (Josh. 21:43–45) — so one reading is that it was fulfilled in the history of Israel and finds its lasting substance in Christ, in whom all God's promises are Yes (2 Cor. 1:20), and in the new earth that Paul calls Abraham's inheritance of "the world" (Rom. 4:13). Others, holding that God's promises to Israel as a nation stand unrepealed, expect a future literal possession of these boundaries. Both readings are held by people who love this book and take it at its word, and the disagreement is about the shape of the fulfilment, never about whether God keeps his oath. What Genesis 15 settles is the second question, and it settles it absolutely: God has sworn, alone, on himself.

The man who received it was asleep in the dark and afraid, and had done nothing but believe and drive off some birds. That is how God's people have always come into anything. He does the walking, he takes the curse, and he keeps the promise on both our behalf and his own.

15.theology:
Justification by Faith. Genesis 15:6 is the Old Testament’s clearest statement of what the Reformation recovered: righteousness before God comes through faith, not works. Paul’s argument in Romans 4 is that this has always been the case — Abraham was justified before circumcision, before the law, before any ritual or moral achievement. The God who credited faith as righteousness to Abram “also will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification” (Rom. 4:24–25). The path to God has never changed: not by works but by trust in the promise.

The Unilateral Covenant. The covenant-cutting ceremony of Genesis 15 establishes the unconditional character of God’s commitment to Abraham. God swears by himself (there is no greater oath, Heb. 6:13–14) and takes the full burden of covenant obligation on himself. This does not mean Abram’s obedience is irrelevant — it means that the security of the promise does not rest on Abram’s faithfulness but on God’s. The cross is the climactic fulfillment of this self-imposed obligation: God the Son bore the curse his own covenant required, guaranteeing the blessing by absorbing the judgment.
15.examples:
Then: The covenant ceremony of Genesis 15 would have been immediately recognizable to ancient Near Eastern readers: the splitting of animals and walking between the pieces was a documented treaty form (Jer. 34:18–20 uses the same imagery as a warning). What was radical was that only one party walked. The stars as the symbol of the promise (v.5) would have carried enormous weight in the ancient world, where stars were associated with divine power and destiny. God is saying: what you associate with divine power and destiny — I am using to promise you a family.

Now: The honesty of Abram’s complaint (vv.2–3) is a standing permission for lament in Christian prayer. The prosperity-gospel version of faith — perpetual positivity, suppressed doubt, cheerful acceptance of unanswered prayer — has no biblical precedent. Abram brought his pain directly to God, and God met him there. The church that creates space for honest lament is more biblically faithful than the church that expects its members to perform contentment. And verse 6 remains the theological foundation of every sinner’s only hope: not what I have done, but what I have trusted.

16.title: Hagar and Ishmael
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Sarai, Abram's wife, had borne him no children. She had a female Egyptian servant whose name was Hagar.<sup>2</sup>And Sarai said to Abram, "Behold now, the LORD has prevented me from bearing children. Go in to my servant; it may be that I shall obtain children by her." And Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.<sup>3</sup>So, after Abram had lived ten years in the land of Canaan, Sarai, Abram's wife, took Hagar the Egyptian, her servant, and gave her to Abram her husband as a wife.<sup>4</sup>And he went in to Hagar, and she conceived. And when she saw that she had conceived, she looked with contempt on her mistress.<sup>5</sup>And Sarai said to Abram, "May the wrong done to me be on you! I gave my servant to your embrace, and when she saw that she had conceived, she looked on me with contempt. May the LORD judge between you and me!"<sup>6</sup>But Abram said to Sarai, "Behold, your servant is in your power; do to her as you please." Then Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her.<sup>7</sup>The angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness, the spring on the way to Shur.<sup>8</sup>And he said, "Hagar, servant of Sarai, where have you come from and where are you going?" She said, "I am fleeing from my mistress Sarai."<sup>9</sup>The angel of the LORD said to her, "Return to your mistress and submit to her."<sup>10</sup>The angel of the LORD also said to her, "I will surely multiply your offspring so that they cannot be numbered for multitude."<sup>11</sup>And the angel of the LORD said to her, "Behold, you are pregnant and shall bear a son. You shall call his name Ishmael, because the LORD has listened to your affliction.<sup>12</sup>He shall be a wild donkey of a man, his hand against everyone and everyone's hand against him, and he shall dwell over against all his kinsmen."<sup>13</sup>So she called the name of the LORD who spoke to her, "You are a God of seeing," for she said, "Truly here I have seen him who looks after me."<sup>14</sup>Therefore the well was called Beer-lahai-roi; it lies between Kadesh and Bered.<sup>15</sup>And Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram called the name of his son, whom Hagar bore, Ishmael.<sup>16</sup>Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to Abram.
16.overview:
Genesis 16 is a story of faith’s impatience — of what happens when the people of God try to help God keep his promises. Ten years have passed since the covenant of chapter 15, and Sarai is still childless. Her solution is practical and culturally sanctioned: give her servant Hagar to Abram as a surrogate, and build a family through her. It was standard practice in the ancient Near East. It was also a failure of faith — an attempt to achieve through human strategy what God had promised to accomplish by his own means.

Paul reads the Hagar-Ishmael / Sarah-Isaac narrative as an allegory of law and gospel (Gal. 4:21–31): Hagar represents the Sinai covenant (works-based approach to God, producing slaves), and Sarah represents the covenant of promise (grace-based, producing free children). The child born of the flesh (Ishmael) and the child born of the Spirit (Isaac) represent the two fundamentally different ways of relating to God — by human effort or by divine promise. Ishmael is not evil, but he is not the promised son.

The chapter contains one of the most beautiful divine encounters in Genesis: the angel of the LORD meets Hagar in the wilderness, sees her affliction, and speaks to her personally. Hagar — a slave woman, an Egyptian, a social nobody — gives God a name: “El Roi,” the God who sees (v.13). She is the first person in Scripture to name God. The God who chose Abraham is also the God who sees the overlooked and forgotten.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Hagar and Ishmael: Faith's Impatience
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 16 narrates the first recorded human attempt to help God fulfill his promise — and its tragic consequences. Ten years have passed since the covenant promise of offspring (ch.12), and Sarai is still barren. The solution proposed — Abram taking Hagar as a surrogate wife — was legally common in the ancient Near East, but it represents faith's capitulation to worldly wisdom over divine patience. The result is relational catastrophe: contempt, affliction, flight, and the birth of a son who will be 'a wild donkey of a man, his hand against everyone.' The first child of the promise period is not the covenant child but the child of impatience.
verseByVerse.theology: The theological problem of chapter 16 is the problem of all impatient faith: when God's promise seems delayed, the temptation is to take matters into our own hands, to provide by human strategy what God has promised by divine gift. Sarai's plan is not wicked in intent — she wants the promised heir — but wrong in method: she substitutes human engineering for divine faithfulness. The result is that two women and two sons will contest the covenant blessing for generations. Paul will use the Hagar-Sarah typology in Galatians 4:21–31 to describe the difference between law-righteousness (the Hagar covenant, producing slaves) and grace-righteousness (the Sarah covenant, producing free children of the promise).
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham on Genesis 16: the episode shows how human attempts to fulfill divine promises on our own timeline produce results that cannot be undone. Ishmael is real — a real child, a real person, loved by God (v.11, 'the LORD has listened to your affliction'). The consequences of Sarai and Abram's impatience will run through the biblical narrative and into the present day. Keller observes that the Hagar narrative also contains one of the most moving encounters with God in Genesis: the angel of the LORD who finds Hagar in the wilderness and speaks to her by name establishes that God sees the afflicted, even the ones who have been wronged by the people of the covenant.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Sarai, Abram's wife, had borne him no children. She had a female Egyptian servant whose name was Hagar. And Sarai said to Abram, "Behold now, the LORD has prevented me from bearing children. Go in to my servant; it may be that I shall obtain children by her." And Abram listened to the voice of Sarai. So, after Abram had lived ten years in the land of Canaan, Sarai, Abram's wife, took Hagar the Egyptian, her servant, and gave her to Abram her husband as a wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Now Sarai, Abram's wife, had borne him no children." Ten years have passed since the promise in chapter 12, and the count is given deliberately: "after Abram had lived ten years in the land of Canaan." A decade of nothing.

Sarai's proposal was legal and normal in that world; contracts from the period provide for exactly this, a barren wife supplying a servant so the household has an heir. It was also, in her own words, an attempt to help God: "Behold now, the LORD has prevented me from bearing children." She has the theology right — she knows her barrenness is from God's hand — and she draws the wrong conclusion from it. If God has closed the door, we shall have to find a window.

"And Abram listened to the voice of Sarai." That phrasing is not neutral. The same construction was used of Adam — "because you have listened to the voice of your wife" (3:17) — and Moses is holding up the two scenes side by side: a man who had heard God speak, taking his instructions from someone else, in a matter God had already settled.

What makes this dangerous is that it is not a rebellion. It is impatience dressed as practicality, by two people who genuinely believed the promise and could not see how it would work. Faith rarely fails by denying that God will act. It fails by deciding he needs help with the timetable, and the arrangements we make in the meantime tend to outlive us.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went in to Hagar, and she conceived. And when she saw that she had conceived, she looked with contempt on her mistress. And Sarai said to Abram, "May the wrong done to me be on you! I gave my servant to your embrace, and when she saw that she had conceived, she looked on me with contempt. May the LORD judge between you and me!" But Abram said to Sarai, "Behold, your servant is in your power; do to her as you please." Then Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The plan works and the household falls apart. Hagar conceives, and having conceived "she looked with contempt on her mistress" — the servant who can do the one thing the mistress cannot. Sarai turns on Abram: "May the wrong done to me be on you!" It was her idea, and she blames her husband. Then she invokes God as her judge, which is bold for a woman standing in the wreckage of her own scheme.

And Abram, who could have taken responsibility for a child that was his, steps aside entirely: "Behold, your servant is in your power; do to her as you please." It is the same passivity as the garden — the man present, silent, and letting it happen — and the result is that a pregnant foreign slave is treated so harshly she runs into the desert alone.

Nobody in this paragraph is innocent, and Genesis names all three. Contempt from the servant, cruelty from the mistress, cowardice from the husband. This is what the shortcut cost, and it kept costing: the descendants of these two sons are still not at peace.

verseByVerse.quote: The angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness, the spring on the way to Shur. And he said, "Hagar, servant of Sarai, where have you come from and where are you going?" She said, "I am fleeing from my mistress Sarai." The angel of the LORD said to her, "Return to your mistress and submit to her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The angel of the LORD found her." First appearance of that figure in Scripture, and he speaks in the next verses as God himself in the first person — "I will surely multiply your offspring." Genesis will keep doing this: an appearance of God in a form that can be met, spoken to, and looked at.

Now consider who is being looked for. Not the patriarch. A pregnant Egyptian slave girl, running away, with no standing, no rights, no claim on the covenant and no name in anyone's genealogy — and the first person in the Bible the angel of the LORD comes to find is her. He also uses her name: "Hagar, servant of Sarai." The woman whom Sarai called only "my servant" and Abram called only "your servant" is addressed by God by name.

"Where have you come from and where are you going?" She can answer the first half and not the second. She is fleeing from, with no idea what she is fleeing to, which is the honest position of most people in flight.

"Return to your mistress and submit to her." That is a hard word, and it should not be softened into something it is not. God is not endorsing Sarai's cruelty; he is sending Hagar back with a promise in her hands that she did not have when she left, and he is protecting her child, who would not have survived the desert. Scripture does not tell every mistreated person to go back — and in chapter 21 God will send Hagar away permanently and provide for her there. But it does say that God's care for a person is often exercised inside a hard situation before it is exercised by removing them from it.

verseByVerse.quote: The angel of the LORD also said to her, "I will surely multiply your offspring so that they cannot be numbered for multitude." And the angel of the LORD said to her, "Behold, you are pregnant and shall bear a son. You shall call his name Ishmael, because the LORD has listened to your affliction. He shall be a wild donkey of a man, his hand against everyone and everyone's hand against him, and he shall dwell over against all his kinsmen."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the promise, and it is remarkable for who receives it. "I will surely multiply your offspring so that they cannot be numbered for multitude" — almost the words spoken to Abram himself (15:5). God makes a covenant-shaped promise to a runaway slave.

"You shall call his name Ishmael, because the LORD has listened to your affliction." Ishmael means God hears. She had told nobody. There is no record of her praying. Nobody in the camp asked how she was, and Abram let her be driven out — and God says, I heard it. Every time she said her son's name for the rest of her life she was saying that sentence out loud.

"He shall be a wild donkey of a man." It sounds like an insult and is not quite one. The wild donkey in Scripture is the untameable free creature of the desert (Job 39:5–8), and the description is of a fiercely independent people who will not be domesticated by anyone. It is realism, not a curse — and it is accurate.

verseByVerse.quote: So she called the name of the LORD who spoke to her, "You are a God of seeing," for she said, "Truly here I have seen him who looks after me." Therefore the well was called Beer-lahai-roi; it lies between Kadesh and Bered. And Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram called the name of his son, whom Hagar bore, Ishmael. Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to Abram.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"So she called the name of the LORD who spoke to her, 'You are a God of seeing.'" A pregnant Egyptian slave becomes the only person in the entire Bible to give God a name, and the name she gives him is El Roi — the God who sees me.

Sit with who is speaking. Not Abraham, not Moses, not David. A foreign domestic servant, used by her mistress, abandoned by her master, sitting by a spring in the desert with nowhere to go. What she discovered out there was not that God would fix her circumstances — he sends her straight back into them — but that he had seen her, and that he had come out to where she was.

"Truly here I have seen him who looks after me." The well was named for it: Beer-lahai-roi, the well of the Living One who sees me. A place on the map, in the middle of nowhere, called after the fact that God noticed somebody nobody else did.

If you have ever been the person in the room whose situation nobody asked about — the one carrying something at home that no one at church has any idea of — this chapter was put in the Bible with you in view. The God of Abraham is also the God of the servant girl Abraham failed, and he went to find her first.

"Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael." And then the narrative goes silent for thirteen years. God says nothing more to Abram until chapter 17, when he is ninety-nine. The shortcut did not produce the promised son; it produced a boy Abraham loved, a household divided, and thirteen years of silence.

16.theology:
The Two Sons as Allegory. Paul’s allegory in Galatians 4:21–31 is the New Testament’s definitive reading of the Hagar-Sarah narrative. Hagar/Ishmael represents the Sinai covenant, the attempt to achieve righteousness through law-keeping, the slavery of works-based religion. Sarah/Isaac represents the covenant of promise, the freedom of those who are children of grace. The application is pointed: those who seek to be justified by law are, in the deepest sense, children of Hagar — slaves, not sons. Those who trust the promise of the gospel are children of Sarah — free, heirs, sons of God.

The God Who Sees the Overlooked. The divine encounter with Hagar establishes a principle that the entire Bible will develop: the God of Israel is also the God of the outsider, the slave, the forgotten. The Psalms celebrate him as the one who “lifts the needy from the ash heap” (Ps. 113:7). The prophets condemn Israel for forgetting the widow, the orphan, and the foreigner — those whom God specially sees. Jesus embodies this perfectly: his ministry is persistently oriented toward those who have no social claim on grace.
16.examples:
Then: Surrogacy through a female slave was legally recognized in the ancient Near East (documented in the Code of Hammurabi and the Nuzi tablets). Sarai’s proposal was therefore not scandalous to her contemporaries but entirely normal. What Genesis presents as a failure of faith, the ancient world would have seen as reasonable problem-solving. The narrative is an implicit critique of the “reasonable” human solution that bypasses trust in divine promise.

Now: The Hagar episode speaks to every Christian who has grown impatient with God’s timing and implemented their own solution — the marriage that seemed close enough to God’s will, the career decision that got ahead of his leading, the ministry strategy that substituted human cleverness for divine direction. The “Ishmael solutions” of our lives produce their own conflicts and do not become the promised child simply because we name them after God’s promise. And the El Roi encounter speaks to everyone who feels invisible: the God who found Hagar in the wilderness is still the God who sees what no one else notices.

17.title: Walk Before Me and Be Blameless
17.text: <sup>1</sup>When Abram was ninety-nine years old the LORD appeared to Abram and said to him, "I am God Almighty; walk before me, and be blameless,<sup>2</sup>that I may make my covenant between me and you, and may multiply you greatly."<sup>3</sup>Then Abram fell on his face. And God said to him,<sup>4</sup>"Behold, my covenant is with you, and you shall be the father of a multitude of nations.<sup>5</sup>No longer shall your name be called Abram, but your name shall be Abraham, for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations.<sup>6</sup>I will make you exceedingly fruitful, and I will make you into nations, and kings shall come from you.<sup>7</sup>And I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your offspring after you.<sup>8</sup>And I will give to you and to your offspring after you the land of your sojournings, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession, and I will be their God."<sup>9</sup>And God said to Abraham, "As for you, you shall keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you throughout their generations.<sup>10</sup>This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your offspring after you: Every male among you shall be circumcised.<sup>11</sup>You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskins, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you.<sup>12</sup>He who is eight days old among you shall be circumcised. Every male throughout your generations, whether born in your house or bought with your money from any foreigner who is not of your offspring,<sup>13</sup>both he who is born in your house and he who is bought with your money, shall surely be circumcised. So shall my covenant be in your flesh an everlasting covenant.<sup>14</sup>Any uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin shall be cut off from his people; he has broken my covenant."<sup>15</sup>And God said to Abraham, "As for Sarai your wife, you shall not call her name Sarai, but Sarah shall be her name.<sup>16</sup>I will bless her, and moreover, I will give you a son by her. I will bless her, and she shall become nations; kings of peoples shall come from her."<sup>17</sup>Then Abraham fell on his face and laughed and said to himself, "Shall a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old? Shall Sarah, who is ninety years old, bear a child?"<sup>18</sup>And Abraham said to God, "Oh that Ishmael might live before you!"<sup>19</sup>God said, "No, but Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac. I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant for his offspring after him.<sup>20</sup>As for Ishmael, I have heard you; behold, I have blessed him and will make him fruitful and multiply him greatly. He shall father twelve princes, and I will make him into a great nation.<sup>21</sup>But I will establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you at this time next year."<sup>22</sup>When he had finished talking with him, God went up from Abraham.<sup>23</sup>Then Abraham took Ishmael his son and all those born in his house or bought with his money, every male among the men of Abraham's house, and he circumcised the flesh of their foreskins that very day, as God had said to him.<sup>24</sup>Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.<sup>25</sup>And Ishmael his son was thirteen years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.<sup>26</sup>That very day Abraham and his son Ishmael were circumcised.<sup>27</sup>And all the men of his house, those born in the house and those bought with money from a foreigner, were circumcised with him.
17.overview:
Chapter 17 marks a new stage in the Abrahamic covenant: after thirteen years of silence (Ishmael is now thirteen, v.25), God appears again with a new divine name, a new human name for Abram, a new covenant sign, and the most specific promise yet — Sarah herself will bear the son of promise (v.16). The silence of those thirteen years was not divine absence but divine patience, and its end is a renewal and deepening of everything promised in chapters 12 and 15.

God introduces himself as “God Almighty” (El Shaddai) — a name that appears at key moments of covenant-making and is associated with the power to do what is humanly impossible. He is not merely the God of Abraham’s tribe but the God of impossible things. The command that follows — “walk before me, and be blameless” — is not a condition of the covenant but its ethical shape. The covenant creates a people; “walk before me and be blameless” describes what that people looks like in motion.

Circumcision is established as the sign of the covenant — a permanent, embodied mark that distinguishes the covenant community and, importantly, is applied to every male, including slaves and foreigners (vv.12–13). The sign is inclusive beyond bloodline, yet specific in its requirement. Paul’s interpretation in Romans 4:11 is key: circumcision was a sign of the righteousness that Abram already had by faith (15:6) before circumcision was instituted. The sign follows the faith; it does not create it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 17 records a fresh divine appearance to Abram when he is 99 years old — thirteen years after Ishmael's birth. God comes with a new name (El Shaddai, God Almighty), a new command (walk before me and be blameless), a new covenant sign (circumcision), and new names for both Abram and Sarai. The covenant is formally established with every male in Abram's household. The chapter is the most covenant-dense passage in the Abraham narrative: the word 'covenant' appears thirteen times, forming the backbone of the chapter.
verseByVerse.theology: Circumcision as the covenant sign is theologically rich. It marks the body permanently, making the covenant commitment visible and physical — covenant membership is not an abstract spiritual state but an embodied reality. It is applied to the organ of generation, connecting the sign to the promise of offspring: every act of generation within the covenant household is marked with the covenant sign. And it involves the shedding of blood, anticipating the atonement logic of the sacrificial system: covenant membership costs something, involves pain, and is sealed with blood. The New Testament will reinterpret circumcision as pointing to the circumcision of the heart (Col. 2:11) and to baptism (Col. 2:12) — the new covenant sign that replaces the old.
verseByVerse.examples: Waltke on Genesis 17: the new names — Abram ('exalted father') to Abraham ('father of a multitude of nations') and Sarai to Sarah (both meaning 'princess') — are not merely name changes but identity transformations. God renames the people through whom his purposes will run, claiming them as his own in the most personal way possible. The name-change anticipates the new creation: when God transforms what someone is, he gives them a new name (cf. Rev. 2:17). Abraham's laughter at the impossibility of Sarah's bearing a son at 90 is met not with rebuke but with patient reaffirmation: 'Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac.'

verseByVerse.quote: When Abram was ninety-nine years old the LORD appeared to Abram and said to him, "I am God Almighty; walk before me, and be blameless, that I may make my covenant between me and you, and may multiply you greatly." Then Abram fell on his face. And God said to him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thirteen years of silence end with a name. "I am God Almighty" — El Shaddai, and this is its first appearance in Scripture. The exact sense of Shaddai is debated, but the force is not: the God of overwhelming sufficiency, the God for whom the physical impossibility of a ninety-year-old womb is not a consideration. He gives Abram that name at the moment the promise has become absurd.

"Walk before me, and be blameless." Two things, in that order. To walk before God is to live your whole life in his sight, with nothing arranged for the times he is not looking. Blameless is the word used of Noah (6:9) — not sinless, but whole, undivided, all of a piece. And the command comes after thirteen years in which Abram has demonstrably not managed it. God does not lower the standard; he states it, and then keeps his covenant with the man anyway.

"Then Abram fell on his face." Not a gesture of politeness. In the presence of El Shaddai a ninety-nine-year-old man goes down flat on the ground, and stays there through most of the chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, my covenant is with you, and you shall be the father of a multitude of nations. No longer shall your name be called Abram, but your name shall be Abraham, for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations. I will make you exceedingly fruitful, and I will make you into nations, and kings shall come from you. And I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your offspring after you. And I will give to you and to your offspring after you the land of your sojournings, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession, and I will be their God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God restates the covenant, and this time he changes the man's name. Abram means exalted father, which had been an awkward name for a childless man for twenty-four years. Abraham means father of a multitude — and it is given to him while he has exactly one son, by the wrong mother.

Consider what that meant socially. Every time he introduced himself for the next year, to servants, to traders, to neighbouring chiefs, a man of ninety-nine with one teenage boy had to say: I am the father of a multitude. God gave him a name that would be a standing embarrassment until it came true. Faith is often obliged to keep saying out loud what is not yet visible.

And notice the tense: "for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations." Past tense, before the child exists. That is how God talks — he "calls into existence the things that do not exist" (Rom. 4:17), and Paul quotes this very verse to prove it.

Three things are promised, and the third is the greatest. Nations and kings will come from him. The land of his sojournings will be an everlasting possession. And, at the centre of it: "to be God to you and to your offspring after you... and I will be their God." That short clause is the heartbeat of every covenant in Scripture, repeated to Moses, to David, through the prophets, and at the very end: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man... and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God" (Rev. 21:3). Land and descendants are the packaging. God himself is the gift.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said to Abraham, "As for you, you shall keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you throughout their generations. This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your offspring after you: Every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskins, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you. He who is eight days old among you shall be circumcised. Every male throughout your generations, whether born in your house or bought with your money from any foreigner who is not of your offspring, both he who is born in your house and he who is bought with your money, shall surely be circumcised. So shall my covenant be in your flesh an everlasting covenant. Any uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin shall be cut off from his people; he has broken my covenant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Abraham is given something to do, and it is a sign cut into the body. Every male in the household is to be circumcised — sons, servants, foreigners bought with money, every one.

Why this sign? Several things converge. It is permanent and cannot be taken off or forgotten. It is private, so it is not a badge to be displayed. It is marked on the organ of generation, in a covenant that is all about offspring — the promise of a seed is signed in the flesh that produces one. And it says something severe: that what human nature produces needs to be cut, that the line of promise does not run on natural vigour, and that flesh must be dealt with before it can bear fruit.

"He who is eight days old among you shall be circumcised." The sign is put on infants who understand nothing, believe nothing and have done nothing. The covenant comes to them before they can respond to it, which is why Christians who baptise their children point to this chapter, and why Paul can call circumcision "a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith" (Rom. 4:11) — a seal on a promise, not a receipt for a performance.

Christians who love this chapter divide over what follows from it. Those who baptise infants argue that the covenant sign has always been given to the children of believers and that Colossians 2:11–12 sets circumcision and baptism side by side. Those who baptise only professing believers argue that the new covenant sign belongs to those who have actually believed, and that the New Testament never records an infant being baptised. Both sides are reading this chapter seriously; the disagreement is real and it is not a disagreement about the gospel.

Two other phrases need a plain answer. "An everlasting covenant" and "an everlasting possession" — the Hebrew olam means for the long duration, lasting to the far horizon; it can mean unending, and here it means at minimum that this is not a temporary arrangement God will get tired of. And to be "cut off from his people" is the standard penalty language of the law: excluded from the covenant community, and in the severest cases the loss of one's line altogether. The man who refused the sign was declaring that he did not belong, and God took him at his word.

And the sign never saved anyone. Moses will tell Israel to circumcise their hearts (Deut. 10:16); Jeremiah accuses a nation full of circumcised men of being uncircumcised in heart (Jer. 9:26); Paul says plainly that a real Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is "a matter of the heart, by the Spirit" (Rom. 2:28–29). The mark on the body was always pointing at something that had to happen underneath it. A person can be baptised, confirmed, church-membered and entirely outside the covenant, and this chapter has said so from the beginning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–27 — Sarah's New Name and the Promise of Isaac
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of Genesis 17 brings the covenant promise to its sharpest and most personal focus: Sarah will bear a son, and his name will be Isaac. The promise has been moving from the general (offspring like the stars, ch.15) to the specific (a son from your own body, 15:4) and now to the most specific of all: a named son, born within one year, from a wife who is 90 years old and long past menopause. Abraham's laughter at this announcement is the most humanly understandable response in the chapter — and God's patient response to it is among the most grace-filled moments in the patriarchal narrative.
verseByVerse.theology: The naming of Isaac before his conception is the ultimate assertion of divine sovereignty over the covenant promise. God does not wait for the child to be born and then name him; he names the child who does not yet exist, whose mother cannot by any natural means bear him. The name 'Isaac' (Yitzhaq, 'he laughs') commemorates Abraham's laughter of incredulity, transforming it into a covenant name — a permanent reminder that the covenant child was born against all human expectation, from God's laughter-inducing power. Every time Isaac is called by name, the story of impossible grace is told again.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes that the chapter's concern with circumcision (vv.1–14) and with the specific promise of Isaac (vv.15–27) together make the same point: the covenant is God's free gift, but it is received through specific means (the covenant sign, the covenant son) — not through any alternative human provision. Ishmael is not the covenant child despite Abraham's plea (v.18); the covenant will run through the impossible son, not the possible one. This is the pattern of grace: it works through what is humanly impossible so that the glory belongs entirely to God.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said to Abraham, "As for Sarai your wife, you shall not call her name Sarai, but Sarah shall be her name. I will bless her, and moreover, I will give you a son by her. I will bless her, and she shall become nations; kings of peoples shall come from her." Then Abraham fell on his face and laughed and said to himself, "Shall a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old? Shall Sarah, who is ninety years old, bear a child?" And Abraham said to God, "Oh that Ishmael might live before you!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sarai is renamed too — Sarah, princess — and the promise is finally, explicitly attached to her: "I will give you a son by her." For twenty-four years God had said offspring and never said whose womb. Now he says it, and closes every remaining door.

"Then Abraham fell on his face and laughed." The father of the faithful, prone on the ground before God, laughing. He does the arithmetic out loud — a hundred years old, and Sarah ninety — and the sum is ridiculous.

Scripture does not condemn him for it. There is no rebuke here at all, and Paul, looking back, says he did not weaken in faith even though he considered his own body as good as dead (Rom. 4:19–20). Which means a man can be genuinely staggered by a promise and still be trusting the one who made it. Faith is not the absence of astonishment.

"Oh that Ishmael might live before you!" And there is the ache. He has loved this boy for thirteen years, and what he is really saying is: could this not just be him? Could you not use what I have already got? God is offering the impossible, and Abraham asks him to settle for the achievable — which is the most understandable prayer in the chapter and the one God says no to.

verseByVerse.quote: God said, "No, but Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac. I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant for his offspring after him. As for Ishmael, I have heard you; behold, I have blessed him and will make him fruitful and multiply him greatly. He shall father twelve princes, and I will make him into a great nation. But I will establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you at this time next year." When he had finished talking with him, God went up from Abraham.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"No, but Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac." God refuses the request, names the child, and fixes the date. Isaac means he laughs. Abraham laughed at the promise; the promise will be called Laughter for the rest of his life, and it will be an entirely different kind of laugh (21:6).

Then, in the same breath: "As for Ishmael, I have heard you." God says no to Abraham's prayer and yes to his love. Ishmael is blessed, made fruitful, multiplied, given twelve princes and a great nation. What Abraham asked for was that Ishmael be the covenant child; what he receives is that Ishmael will be cared for.

Carry that distinction into your own praying. God's no is very rarely a no to the person you are praying for. It is often a no to the particular shape you had drawn for the answer, and the thing he does instead is better than the thing you asked for and does not look like it at the time.

"But I will establish my covenant with Isaac." The line runs through the child of promise, not the child of the shortcut — which is exactly the point Paul builds his argument on in Galatians 4: one son born according to the flesh, one born through promise, and the children of promise are the true heirs (Gal. 4:22–28). God's people are never produced by human capability.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abraham took Ishmael his son and all those born in his house or bought with his money, every male among the men of Abraham's house, and he circumcised the flesh of their foreskins that very day, as God had said to him. Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin. And Ishmael his son was thirteen years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin. That very day Abraham and his son Ishmael were circumcised. And all the men of his house, those born in the house and those bought with money from a foreigner, were circumcised with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then Abraham took Ishmael his son and all those born in his house... and he circumcised the flesh of their foreskins that very day."

Count what that obedience cost. He is ninety-nine years old, performing on himself a painful operation with no anaesthetic and no antibiotics, and then on his thirteen-year-old son, and then on every male in a household large enough to field 318 fighting men. It cannot have been done quietly and it cannot have been popular. The camp would have been immobilised for days — as Genesis 34 will show, painfully.

And there is no interval. God finished speaking and went up from Abraham, and that same day the knife came out. No consultation, no waiting for a better season, no asking whether the household would take it well. The man who spent thirteen years living with the consequences of not waiting has learned something about not delaying either.

The chapter began with a man on his face before God Almighty and ends with him carrying out the most personally costly instruction he has yet been given, on the day he was given it. Between them lies the whole of what it means to walk before God and be blameless.

17.theology:
Covenant Sign and Seal. Circumcision is the Old Testament’s primary covenant sign — an embodied, permanent, given-before-performance mark of belonging to the covenant community. Paul’s point in Romans 4 is that it is a sign (pointing to something, namely the righteousness of faith) and a seal (confirming what faith has received), not the thing itself. The Reformers used this distinction to explain baptism: as circumcision was the sign and seal of the old covenant, baptism is the sign and seal of the new. The sign does not create faith; it marks the community of those who receive the promise by faith.

The God Who Renames. The renaming of Abram and Sarai is a pattern of divine sovereignty over identity. God renames Jacob (Israel), Simon (Peter), and Saul (Paul). In each case, the new name is not a description of present character but a declaration of covenantal destiny — a new identity spoken into existence before it is lived out. The resurrection is the ultimate renaming: “I will give him a white stone, with a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it” (Rev. 2:17). Our truest identity is always the one God speaks, not the one we construct.
17.examples:
