Then: Thirteen years of silence between chapters 16 and 17 are compressed into a single verse (16:16 to 17:1). For the original audience, familiar with the frustration of waiting on covenant promises in the wilderness, this long silence would have resonated painfully. The reappearance of God after silence — with more specific and more expansive promises — was the narrative pattern of Israel’s own experience: silence in Egypt, then the burning bush; silence during the exile, then the return. God’s silence is not absence.

Now: The command “walk before me, and be blameless” (v.1) is the Old Testament’s summary of the Christian life: not occasional acts of obedience but a life lived in the continuous awareness of divine presence. Keller describes this as the “coram Deo” life — before the face of God. The person who lives this way does not need an audience for their virtue, does not perform goodness when watched and relax it when unobserved, because they are always in the presence of the one who sees everything. And Abraham’s laughter (v.17) gives permission for the honest emotional response to grace: the promise is so good it seems laughable, and God is not offended by the laughter.

18.title: Is Anything Too Hard for the LORD?

When he saw them, he ran from the tent door to meet them and bowed himself to the earth<sup>3</sup>and said, "O Lord, if I have found favor in your sight, do not pass by your servant.<sup>4</sup>Let a little water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree,<sup>5</sup>while I bring a morsel of bread, that you may refresh yourselves, and after that you may pass on— since you have come to your servant." So they said, "Do as you have said."<sup>6</sup>And Abraham went quickly into the tent to Sarah and said, "Quick! Three seahs of fine flour! Knead it, and make cakes."<sup>7</sup>And Abraham ran to the herd and took a calf, tender and good, and gave it to a young man, who prepared it quickly.<sup>8</sup>Then he took curds and milk and the calf that he had prepared, and set it before them. And he stood by them under the tree while they ate.<sup>9</sup>They said to him, "Where is Sarah your wife?" And he said, "She is in the tent."<sup>10</sup>The LORD said, "I will surely return to you about this time next year, and Sarah your wife shall have a son." And Sarah was listening at the tent door behind him.<sup>11</sup>Now Abraham and Sarah were old, advanced in years. The way of women had ceased to be with Sarah.<sup>12</sup>So Sarah laughed to herself, saying, "After I am worn out, and my lord is old, shall I have pleasure?"<sup>13</sup>The LORD said to Abraham, "Why did Sarah laugh and say, 'Shall I indeed bear a child, now that I am old?'<sup>14</sup>Is anything too hard for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you, about this time next year, and Sarah shall have a son."<sup>15</sup>But Sarah denied it, saying, "I did not laugh," for she was afraid. He said, "No, but you did laugh."<sup>16</sup>Then the men set out from there, and they looked down toward Sodom. And Abraham went with them to set them on their way.<sup>17</sup>The LORD said, "Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do,<sup>18</sup>seeing that Abraham shall surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him?<sup>19</sup>For I have chosen him, that he may command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD by doing righteousness and justice, so that the LORD may bring to Abraham what he has promised him."<sup>20</sup>Then the LORD said, "Because the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great and their sin is very grave,<sup>21</sup>I will go down to see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry that has come to me. And if not, I will know."<sup>22</sup>So the men turned from there and went toward Sodom, but Abraham still stood before the LORD.<sup>23</sup>Then Abraham drew near and said, "Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?<sup>24</sup>Suppose there are fifty righteous within the city. Will you then sweep away the place and not spare it for the fifty righteous who are in it?<sup>25</sup>Far be it from you to do such a thing, to put the righteous to death with the wicked, so that the righteous fare as the wicked! Far be that from you! Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?"<sup>26</sup>And the LORD said, "If I find at Sodom fifty righteous in the city, I will spare the whole place for their sake."<sup>27</sup>Abraham answered and said, "Behold, I have undertaken to speak to the Lord, I who am but dust and ashes.<sup>28</sup>Suppose five of the fifty righteous are lacking. Will you destroy the whole city for lack of five?" And he said, "I will not destroy it if I find forty-five there."<sup>29</sup>Again he spoke to him and said, "Suppose forty are found there." He answered, "For the sake of forty I will not do it."<sup>30</sup>Then he said, "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak. Suppose thirty are found there." He answered, "I will not do it, if I find thirty there."<sup>31</sup>He said, "Behold, I have undertaken to speak to the Lord. Suppose twenty are found there." He answered, "For the sake of twenty I will not destroy it."<sup>32</sup>Then he said, "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak again but this once. Suppose ten are found there." He answered, "For the sake of ten I will not destroy it."<sup>33</sup>And the LORD went his way, when he had finished speaking to Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place.
18.overview:
Genesis 18 is one of the most intimate chapters in all of Scripture. Three visitors appear at the heat of the day, and Abraham runs to meet them, providing lavish hospitality. Only gradually does the narrative reveal who these visitors are: the LORD himself, accompanied by two angels (cf. 19:1). The New Testament reflects on this encounter with the observation: “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Heb. 13:2). The divine condescension to appear in human form, to receive food and rest in a human tent, anticipates the incarnation — God choosing to enter the creaturely world in the most particular and embodied way.

The chapter centers on two dramatic moments: the promise of a son within the year (vv.9–15), met with Sarah’s incredulous laughter and the divine challenge “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” (v.14); and Abraham’s intercessory prayer for Sodom (vv.22–33), in which he boldly negotiates with God on behalf of the righteous. The two moments are linked: the same God who can give a child to a ninety-year-old woman can hear the prayer of one man on behalf of a city. Nothing is too hard for the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Three Visitors and the Promise to Sarah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 18 opens with one of the most intimate theophanies in Scripture: three men appear to Abraham at the oaks of Mamre, and in the course of a meal, the covenant promise of Isaac is renewed directly to Sarah — who hears it for the first time and laughs. The scene is domestic, warm, and theologically profound. Abraham's hospitality is exemplary; the meal is prepared with care; and the divine visitors eat, recline, and speak in the most ordinary human setting. The God who made heaven and earth sits under a terebinth tree at midday and eats with a nomadic patriarch.
verseByVerse.theology: The identification of the three visitors with the LORD and two angels (and with the pre-incarnate Christ in some theological traditions) has occupied commentators throughout history. The text moves fluidly between the three visitors as a group and the LORD speaking in the first person — a literary phenomenon that points to the mystery of divine presence in human form. What is theologically clear is that the visit is a genuine theophany: these visitors know things no human could know (Sarah's laugh), and their promises carry divine authority.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham on Genesis 18:1–15: Sarah's laughter (v.12) is compared by God to Abraham's earlier laughter (17:17), but with a different response — God addresses Sarah's laughter directly ('Why did Sarah laugh?') while he addressed Abraham's more gently. The difference may reflect that Sarah's laughter was more skeptical ('After I am worn out, and my lord is old...') than Abraham's. Both laughters, however, are met not with judgment but with the question that ends all human impossibility: 'Is anything too hard for the LORD?'

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat at the door of his tent in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, three men were standing in front of him. When he saw them, he ran from the tent door to meet them and bowed himself to the earth and said, "O Lord, if I have found favor in your sight, do not pass by your servant. Let a little water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree, while I bring a morsel of bread, that you may refresh yourselves, and after that you may pass on— since you have come to your servant." So they said, "Do as you have said."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And the LORD appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat at the door of his tent in the heat of the day." An ordinary afternoon, the hottest part of it, a man sitting in the shade doing nothing in particular. God turns up in the middle of a nap.

"Three men were standing in front of him." No announcement, no glory, no trumpet — three travellers on the road who look like anybody else. One of them is addressed throughout as the LORD; the other two turn out to be angels who go on to Sodom (19:1). Whether Abraham knows at first is not stated, and Hebrews takes this as the classic case: "Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares" (Heb. 13:2).

Readers ask whether the three are the Trinity. Almost certainly not, and the text itself rules it out: two of them walk on to Sodom as angels while the LORD stays with Abraham (18:22; 19:1). What we have is one appearance of God in human form, attended by two created messengers. Genesis is not embarrassed by this — God has already walked in a garden in the cool of the day, and one day he will eat fish on a beach with his friends.

"He ran from the tent door to meet them and bowed himself to the earth." A man of ninety-nine, running. And then he undersells what he intends to give: "Let a little water be brought... while I bring a morsel of bread." In that culture you always promised less than you meant to provide. He is about to serve a banquet.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abraham went quickly into the tent to Sarah and said, "Quick! Three seahs of fine flour! Knead it, and make cakes." And Abraham ran to the herd and took a calf, tender and good, and gave it to a young man, who prepared it quickly. Then he took curds and milk and the calf that he had prepared, and set it before them. And he stood by them under the tree while they ate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now count the work. "Quick! Three seahs of fine flour!" — something like twenty litres, enough bread for a small village, from a household of three. He runs to the herd and picks out a calf, "tender and good," which means a whole animal killed for three men who have not said how long they are staying. Curds and milk are set out alongside.

The morsel of bread has become a feast, prepared at speed, in the heat, by an old man sprinting round his own camp for strangers whose names he does not know and who have offered him nothing.

"And he stood by them under the tree while they ate." He does not sit down with them. The richest man in the district waits on his guests standing, like a servant, and that detail is the point of the whole scene. Hospitality in Scripture is not entertaining; it is putting yourself at someone's disposal at your own expense. It is costly, it is hurried, and it does not stop to work out whether the guest deserves it.

Which is not an incidental virtue. The New Testament makes it a requirement for elders (1 Tim. 3:2) and a command for everyone (Rom. 12:13; 1 Pet. 4:9), and the Lord Jesus made a whole parable turn on it: "I was a stranger and you welcomed me" (Matt. 25:35). Abraham does not know who is at his tent door. That is exactly the situation the command is written for.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Where is Sarah your wife?" And he said, "She is in the tent." The LORD said, "I will surely return to you about this time next year, and Sarah your wife shall have a son." And Sarah was listening at the tent door behind him. Now Abraham and Sarah were old, advanced in years. The way of women had ceased to be with Sarah. So Sarah laughed to herself, saying, "After I am worn out, and my lord is old, shall I have pleasure?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Where is Sarah your wife?" They know her name. That is the first hint to Abraham that these are no ordinary travellers, and the question is asked out loud so that she will hear what follows.

"I will surely return to you about this time next year, and Sarah your wife shall have a son." The promise now has a date on it, and it is said within earshot of the woman it concerns.

"And Sarah was listening at the tent door behind him. Now Abraham and Sarah were old, advanced in years. The way of women had ceased to be with Sarah." The narrator puts the medical facts in plainly, because the promise is about to be measured against them.

"So Sarah laughed to herself, saying, 'After I am worn out, and my lord is old, shall I have pleasure?'" It is not a giggle. It is the bitter, private laugh of a woman who gave up hoping a long time ago and has taught herself not to want it any more — and the phrase "after I am worn out" is the sound of someone who has stopped expecting anything good to happen to her body again.

Anyone who has quietly buried a hope will recognise it. The laugh is not rebellion; it is self-protection. She had been disappointed for so long that believing had become the more painful option.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Abraham, "Why did Sarah laugh and say, 'Shall I indeed bear a child, now that I am old?' Is anything too hard for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you, about this time next year, and Sarah shall have a son." But Sarah denied it, saying, "I did not laugh," for she was afraid. He said, "No, but you did laugh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The LORD said to Abraham, 'Why did Sarah laugh...?'" She laughed to herself, in silence, inside her own head, behind a tent flap, with her back to the company — and God answers it out loud, to her husband, across the camp.

Nothing is hidden from him. Not the sarcastic thought, not the resignation that nobody else notices, not the prayer given up on years ago and never mentioned to anyone. "Even before a word is on my tongue, behold, O LORD, you know it altogether" (Ps. 139:4).

Then the question that stands over the whole book: "Is anything too hard for the LORD?" The Hebrew word means too wonderful, too extraordinary, beyond anyone's reach. It is what Genesis has been asking since chapter 12, and the answer will arrive as a baby. Gabriel put the same sentence to another astonished woman about another impossible pregnancy: "For nothing will be impossible with God" (Luke 1:37).

"But Sarah denied it, saying, 'I did not laugh,' for she was afraid. He said, 'No, but you did laugh.'" God will not let the lie stand — and he does not retaliate either. He corrects her, quietly, in five words, and then keeps the promise anyway. When the boy is born it is Sarah who says, "God has made laughter for me" (21:6). The woman who laughed in unbelief gets to laugh for joy, and he never once holds the first laugh against her.

How, then, does Hebrews say that "by faith Sarah herself received power to conceive" (Heb. 11:11)? The two are not in conflict. Hebrews is not describing the afternoon; it is describing the year. What God credits to her is not the laugh at the tent door but the fact that, having laughed, she went on to trust "him faithful who had promised." A faith that begins badly and holds on is still faith, and God writes up the outcome rather than the first reaction.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second movement of Genesis 18 is the most remarkable intercession in the Old Testament before Moses. God discloses to Abraham that he is going to investigate Sodom's wickedness and determine whether it merits destruction. Abraham then engages God in a negotiation that begins at fifty righteous people and descends to ten — and God agrees to spare the city for the sake of ten. The passage establishes the principle of intercession as a covenant privilege and reveals the character of God as a judge who desires justice but is willing to be moved by prayer.
verseByVerse.theology: The theological heart of the intercession is Abraham's appeal: 'Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?' (v.25). This is one of the most important theological statements in Genesis: God's justice is the foundation of Abraham's prayer, not a threat to it. Abraham does not bargain with an unjust God; he appeals to the justice of the righteous Judge. The intercession works because it is aligned with God's own character. The failure to find ten righteous people in Sodom is the narrative's indictment of Sodom's wickedness: even ten — a minyan, the minimum for Jewish communal worship — could not be found.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller on Genesis 18:16–33: Abraham's intercession is the model for all covenant prayer. He approaches God boldly but humbly ('I who am but dust and ashes,' v.27), he appeals to God's character rather than his own merit ('shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?'), and he persists through multiple rounds of negotiation without losing reverence. The intercession does not save Sodom — because Sodom's wickedness is total — but it saves Lot (19:29: 'God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow'). Intercession does not always change outcomes, but it is always heard, always remembered, always effective in ways the intercessor may not anticipate.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men set out from there, and they looked down toward Sodom. And Abraham went with them to set them on their way. The LORD said, "Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do, seeing that Abraham shall surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him? For I have chosen him, that he may command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD by doing righteousness and justice, so that the LORD may bring to Abraham what he has promised him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?" God says it aloud, as though deliberating in the man's hearing, and the effect is startling: he is about to tell a human being what he intends to do with two cities, before he does it.

That is what it means to be a friend of God, and Scripture uses exactly that word for Abraham three times (2 Chron. 20:7; Isa. 41:8; James 2:23). The Lord Jesus drew the same line for his disciples: "No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you" (John 15:15).

"For I have chosen him, that he may command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD by doing righteousness and justice, so that the LORD may bring to Abraham what he has promised him."

Take that sentence apart, because it is the plainest statement in Genesis of what God chooses people for. Election here is not a private ticket with no consequences attached; it is a commission that runs through a household. God chose him so that he would raise his family in the way of the LORD — and the content of that way is specified: righteousness and justice, right living and fair dealing.

Whatever else a Christian parent has to do, this verse says that teaching the children is not an optional extra bolted onto the faith of the household. It is one of the reasons God stated for calling the man in the first place. And notice the last clause: it is the means by which "the LORD may bring to Abraham what he has promised him." God's sovereign promise and a father's daily instruction are not two competing explanations. They are the same plan.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said, "Because the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great and their sin is very grave, I will go down to see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry that has come to me. And if not, I will know."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Because the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great and their sin is very grave." The word for outcry is the word used of the cry of the oppressed — of Israel groaning under Egypt (Exod. 3:7), of the widow and the orphan (Exod. 22:22–23), of the wages of a defrauded labourer crying out against the man who kept them (James 5:4).

So there are people in those cities being hurt, and the sound of it has reached heaven. Whatever else Sodom was, it was a place where somebody was screaming. Ezekiel fills in the picture: "she and her daughters had pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy" (Ezek. 16:49).

"I will go down to see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry that has come to me. And if not, I will know." God does not need to go and look, and the language is deliberately judicial. He is showing us a Judge who investigates before he sentences — as he did at Babel, where he "came down to see" the tower (11:5), and in Eden, where he asked questions he knew the answers to. No case in God's court is ever decided on hearsay, and no one will stand before him and say that his file was never read.

verseByVerse.quote: So the men turned from there and went toward Sodom, but Abraham still stood before the LORD. Then Abraham drew near and said, "Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked? Suppose there are fifty righteous within the city. Will you then sweep away the place and not spare it for the fifty righteous who are in it? Far be it from you to do such a thing, to put the righteous to death with the wicked, so that the righteous fare as the wicked! Far be that from you! Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?" And the LORD said, "If I find at Sodom fifty righteous in the city, I will spare the whole place for their sake."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But Abraham still stood before the LORD." The angels walk on towards Sodom and Abraham does not move. He has just been told that a city is going to be destroyed and his nephew is in it, and what follows is the first extended intercession in the Bible.

"Then Abraham drew near." He does not shout after God as he leaves; he comes closer. The whole conversation is conducted at close quarters by a man who knows exactly whom he is talking to.

Now look at the ground he argues on, because it is not the obvious one. He never mentions Lot. Not once, in eleven verses about a city his nephew lives in. He does not appeal to family, or to his own service, or even to mercy. He appeals to God's character: "Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?... Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?"

It is one of the boldest sentences ever addressed to God, and it is not impertinent, because it is asking God to be what he has revealed himself to be. That is the strongest thing any believer ever brings into prayer — not the urgency of the need, but the revealed character of the one being asked.

"If I find at Sodom fifty righteous in the city, I will spare the whole place for their sake." Read that carefully, because it inverts the assumption everybody brings to it. Abraham proposes that fifty good men might be saved out of a doomed city. God replies that fifty good men would save the city.

A handful of the righteous are enough to hold back judgment on a whole population. That is what Jesus meant by calling his people the salt of the earth (Matt. 5:13) — salt was what kept meat from rotting — and it is a reason to take far more seriously than we do the presence of a few faithful people in a street, a workplace or a nation. Their neighbours have no idea what they are being spared on account of.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham answered and said, "Behold, I have undertaken to speak to the Lord, I who am but dust and ashes. Suppose five of the fifty righteous are lacking. Will you destroy the whole city for lack of five?" And he said, "I will not destroy it if I find forty-five there." Again he spoke to him and said, "Suppose forty are found there." He answered, "For the sake of forty I will not do it." Then he said, "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak. Suppose thirty are found there." He answered, "I will not do it, if I find thirty there." He said, "Behold, I have undertaken to speak to the Lord. Suppose twenty are found there." He answered, "For the sake of twenty I will not destroy it." Then he said, "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak again but this once. Suppose ten are found there." He answered, "For the sake of ten I will not destroy it." And the LORD went his way, when he had finished speaking to Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The bargaining that follows is one of the strangest and warmest passages in Scripture. Forty-five. Forty. Thirty. Twenty. Ten. Six times he asks, and six times God agrees without a moment's hesitation and without once telling him to stop.

And listen to how he speaks while he does it. "Behold, I have undertaken to speak to the Lord, I who am but dust and ashes." "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak." "Let me speak again but this once."

Here is the balance the Bible asks for and that almost nobody manages: enormous boldness and complete humility in the same breath. He knows he is dust, and he asks anyway; he asks anyway, and he never forgets he is dust. Reverence in Scripture is not the opposite of confidence in prayer — the same letter that calls God a consuming fire tells us to draw near to the throne of grace with confidence (Heb. 4:16; 12:29).

He stops at ten. Nobody knows quite why. Perhaps ten was the smallest number that could count as a community; perhaps Lot's household came to about that, and he could not bring himself to go lower and hear the answer. What is certain is that God does not end the conversation. God agrees to ten, and then goes his way, and Abraham returns to his place.

What did it accomplish? The city was destroyed; there were not ten. But the next chapter opens with angels seizing Lot by the hand and dragging him out "the LORD being merciful to him" (19:16), and the narrator says plainly that "God remembered Abraham" when he did it (19:29). The prayer was not answered in the form it was prayed and it was not wasted. Ask for the city, and you may be given the man.

And there is a longer answer still. Abraham asked whether a whole place could be spared for the sake of a few righteous within it, and God said yes, and kept saying yes as the number fell. The arithmetic was eventually pressed past anything Abraham dared: not fifty, not ten, but one — one righteous man, and a world spared for his sake. There were not ten in Sodom. There was one at Calvary, and he was enough.

18.theology:
Divine Condescension. The appearance of the LORD in human form at Mamre — eating food, receiving hospitality, sitting in a tent in the heat of the day — is one of the Old Testament’s most striking anticipations of the incarnation. The God who fills the heavens condescends to the particular, the creaturely, the embodied. John’s Prologue is the full statement: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). The incarnation is not alien to the character of the God revealed in Genesis; it is its fullest expression.

Intercessory Prayer. Abraham’s intercession for Sodom establishes the pattern and the permission for bold intercessory prayer. He argues from divine justice, not human sentimentality. He persists without presuming — “let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak” (v.30). He does not give up prematurely. The New Testament develops this into the image of the persistent widow (Luke 18:1–8) and Jesus’s own perpetual intercession (Heb. 7:25: “he always lives to make intercession for them”). We pray within the intercession of the one who is both the Abraham who pleads and the LORD who hears.
18.examples:
Then: Hospitality to strangers was a sacred duty in the ancient Near East — refusal was a serious social transgression. Sodom’s violation of Lot’s guests in chapter 19 is therefore not only a sexual sin but a profound violation of the hospitality code that structured ancient society. Abraham’s extravagant welcome to the three visitors is the counter-portrait: the covenant community defined by generous welcome, not hostile rejection.

Now: “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” (v.14) is the question every prayer should begin with — not as a formula but as a genuine theological orientation. When we are tempted to edit our prayers to fit what seems possible, this verse calls us back: the God to whom we pray is the God of the impossible. And Abraham’s bold intercession gives permission for passionate, specific, persistent prayer for those who are perishing. To stand before the LORD and plead for the lost city is not presumption; it is the highest form of friendship with God available to the creature.

19.title: The Destruction of Sodom
19.text: <sup>1</sup>The two angels came to Sodom in the evening, and Lot was sitting in the gate of Sodom. When Lot saw them, he rose to meet them and bowed himself with his face to the earth<sup>2</sup>and said, "My lords, please turn aside to your servant's house and spend the night and wash your feet. Then you may rise up early and go on your way." They said, "No; we will spend the night in the town square."<sup>3</sup>But he pressed them strongly; so they turned aside to him and entered his house. And he made them a feast and baked unleavened bread, and they ate.<sup>4</sup>But before they lay down, the men of the city, the men of Sodom, both young and old, all the people to the last man, surrounded the house.<sup>5</sup>And they called to Lot, "Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us, that we may know them."<sup>6</sup>Lot went out to the men at the entrance, shut the door after him,<sup>7</sup>and said, "I beg you, my brothers, do not act so wickedly.<sup>8</sup>Behold, I have two daughters who have not known any man. Let me bring them out to you, and do to them as you please. Only do nothing to these men, for they have come under the shelter of my roof."<sup>9</sup>But they said, "Stand back!" And they said, "This fellow came to sojourn, and he has become the judge! Now we will deal worse with you than with them." Then they pressed hard against the man Lot, and drew near to break the door down.<sup>10</sup>But the men reached out their hands and brought Lot into the house with them and shut the door.<sup>11</sup>And they struck with blindness the men who were at the entrance of the house, both small and great, so that they wore themselves out groping for the door.<sup>12</sup>Then the men said to Lot, "Have you anyone else here? Sons-in-law, sons, daughters, or anyone you have in the city, bring them out of the place.<sup>13</sup>For we are about to destroy this place, because the outcry against its people has become great before the LORD, and the LORD has sent us to destroy it."<sup>14</sup>So Lot went out and said to his sons-in-law, who were to marry his daughters, "Up! Get out of this place, for the LORD is about to destroy the city." But he seemed to his sons-in-law to be jesting.<sup>15</sup>As morning dawned, the angels urged Lot, saying, "Up! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, lest you be swept away in the punishment of the city."<sup>16</sup>But he lingered. So the men seized him and his wife and his two daughters by the hand, the LORD being merciful to him, and they brought him out and set him outside the city.<sup>17</sup>And as they brought them out, one said, "Escape for your life. Do not look back or stop anywhere in the valley. Escape to the hills, lest you be swept away."<sup>18</sup>And Lot said to them, "Oh, no, my lords.<sup>19</sup>Behold, your servant has found favor in your sight, and you have shown me great kindness in saving my life. But I cannot escape to the hills, lest the disaster overtake me and I die.<sup>20</sup>Behold, this city is near enough to flee to, and it is a little one. Let me escape there—is it not a little one?—and my life will be saved!"<sup>21</sup>He said to him, "Behold, I grant you this favor also, that I will not overthrow the city of which you have spoken.<sup>22</sup>Escape there quickly, for I can do nothing till you arrive there." Therefore the name of the city was called Zoar.<sup>23</sup>The sun had risen on the earth when Lot came to Zoar.<sup>24</sup>Then the LORD rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the LORD out of heaven.<sup>25</sup>And he overthrew those cities, and all the valley, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and what grew on the ground.<sup>26</sup>But Lot's wife, behind him, looked back, and she became a pillar of salt.<sup>27</sup>And Abraham went early in the morning to the place where he had stood before the LORD.<sup>28</sup>And he looked down toward Sodom and Gomorrah and toward all the land of the valley, and he looked and, behold, the smoke of the land went up like the smoke of a furnace.<sup>29</sup>So it was that, when God destroyed the cities of the valley, God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow when he overthrew the cities in which Lot had lived.<sup>30</sup>Now Lot went up out of Zoar and lived in the hills with his two daughters, for he was afraid to live in Zoar. So he lived in a cave with his two daughters.<sup>31</sup>And the firstborn said to the younger, "Our father is old, and there is not a man on earth to come in to us after the manner of all the earth.<sup>32</sup>Come, let us make our father drink wine, and we will lie with him, that we may preserve offspring from our father."<sup>33</sup>So they made their father drink wine that night. And the firstborn went in and lay with her father. He did not know when she lay down or when she arose.<sup>34</sup>The next day, the firstborn said to the younger, "Behold, I lay last night with my father. Let us make him drink wine tonight also. Then you go in and lie with him, that we may preserve offspring from our father."<sup>35</sup>So they made their father drink wine that night also. And the younger arose and lay with him, and he did not know when she lay down or when she arose.<sup>36</sup>Thus both the daughters of Lot became pregnant by their father.<sup>37</sup>The firstborn bore a son and called his name Moab. He is the father of the Moabites to this day.<sup>38</sup>The younger also bore a son and called his name Ben-ammi. He is the father of the Ammonites to this day.
19.overview:
Genesis 19 is one of the most difficult chapters in the Bible — difficult morally (Lot’s offer of his daughters, vv.8; his daughters’ later actions, vv.30–38), difficult theologically (the total destruction of the cities), and difficult pastorally (it has been used and misused in every generation). The chapter must be read carefully and canonically.

The wickedness of Sodom, often reduced in popular discussion to a single sin, is described in the Old Testament more broadly: “Behold, this was the guilt of your sister Sodom: she and her daughters had pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy” (Ezek. 16:49). The violation of Lot’s guests in chapter 19 is the culminating expression of a comprehensive moral collapse, of which the sexual dimension is one symptom among many. The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah becomes the Old Testament’s paradigmatic image of divine judgment — cited throughout the prophets (Isa. 1:9; Amos 4:11) and by Jesus himself (Matt. 10:15; Luke 17:29).

The theological center of the chapter is verse 29: “God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out.” Lot is saved not because of his own righteousness but because of Abraham’s intercession. He lingered (v.16) — hesitating to leave even as the city was about to be destroyed — and the angels had to physically drag him and his family to safety (“the LORD being merciful to him”). Salvation always comes from outside; it is always the merciful hand of God dragging us from the city we are unwilling to leave.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — The Destruction of Sodom and the Rescue of Lot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 19 is one of the most sobering chapters in the Old Testament. The wickedness of Sodom — described with harrowing specificity in the attempted assault on the two angels — demonstrates beyond any doubt that the city's destruction is just. Lot's compromised position (sitting in the gate, married into the city, with sons-in-law who mock the warning) shows the full cost of his earlier choice. The deliverance of Lot, his wife, and his daughters is accomplished by divine mercy against Lot's own hesitation; but the salvation is incomplete — Lot's wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt, and the chapter ends with Lot hiding in a cave, his daughters engineering the continuation of his line through incest.
verseByVerse.theology: The theological weight of chapter 19 is distributed between judgment and mercy. The judgment on Sodom is comprehensive and irreversible — fire and sulfur from heaven, the same imagery used in Revelation for final judgment. The mercy toward Lot is remarkable precisely because it is undeserved: Lot hesitated, his wife disobeyed, his sons-in-law laughed, and only the angels' physical intervention ('they seized his hand and the hand of his wife and the hands of his two daughters, the LORD being merciful to him,' v.16) moved him out of the city. Lot's salvation is entirely by divine seizure, not by his own faith. Peter calls him 'righteous Lot' (2 Pet. 2:7) — righteous by faith, not by behavior.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus refers to the destruction of Sodom as a type of the final judgment (Luke 17:28–30), and the 'remember Lot's wife' warning (Luke 17:32) is among his most sobering: she was physically outside the city but her heart was still inside it. The sin of Sodom — defined in Ezekiel 16:49–50 as pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease while neglecting the poor — is a warning to every comfortable, prosperous society, not merely a condemnation of sexual sin. The chapter's terrible conclusion — Lot's daughters with their father — is presented without editorial comment, but the resulting nations (Moab and Ammon) will be Israel's persistent adversaries, and the episode is the final fruit of Lot's choice to live in Sodom.

verseByVerse.quote: The two angels came to Sodom in the evening, and Lot was sitting in the gate of Sodom. When Lot saw them, he rose to meet them and bowed himself with his face to the earth and said, "My lords, please turn aside to your servant's house and spend the night and wash your feet. Then you may rise up early and go on your way." They said, "No; we will spend the night in the town square." But he pressed them strongly; so they turned aside to him and entered his house. And he made them a feast and baked unleavened bread, and they ate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Lot was sitting in the gate of Sodom." The gate was where the city's business was done and its elders sat — the courthouse, the market and the council chamber in one. The man who once pitched his tent towards Sodom now holds office in it. Three chapters have taken him from the edge of the valley to a seat among its magistrates.

To his credit, he does what Abraham did in the previous chapter: rises, bows, presses hospitality on the strangers. And there is one telling difference. The angels say they will spend the night in the square, and Lot "pressed them strongly." He knows what happens in that square after dark, and he will not let them find out.

Which is the shape of a compromised life. He is not comfortable here; Peter says Lot was "greatly distressed" and that his righteous soul was tormented day after day by what he saw and heard (2 Pet. 2:7–8). He knows exactly what the place is, and he lives in it, and he has raised his family in it. A man can be genuinely miserable about the world he has chosen and still not leave.

verseByVerse.quote: But before they lay down, the men of the city, the men of Sodom, both young and old, all the people to the last man, surrounded the house. And they called to Lot, "Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us, that we may know them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But before they lay down, the men of the city, the men of Sodom, both young and old, all the people to the last man, surrounded the house." The narrator piles up the phrases so that nobody can read this as the work of a criminal fringe. Young and old. All the people. To the last man. It is the whole city.

"Bring them out to us, that we may know them." The verb is the ordinary Hebrew euphemism for sexual relations, as in 4:1, and the demand is for gang rape of strangers who are guests under a roof.

What was Sodom's sin? The question is live and both halves of the Bible's answer belong on the page. Ezekiel names pride, excess of food, prosperous ease, and refusing to help the poor and needy — and then adds that "they were haughty and did an abomination before me" (Ezek. 16:49–50). Jude says they "indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire" (Jude 7). Neither statement cancels the other, and this scene contains both: a comfortable, arrogant city whose response to a stranger at the gate is to assault him.

And there is the measure of what God had told Abraham. The outcry had reached heaven (18:20); here is what was making the noise.

verseByVerse.quote: Lot went out to the men at the entrance, shut the door after him, and said, "I beg you, my brothers, do not act so wickedly. Behold, I have two daughters who have not known any man. Let me bring them out to you, and do to them as you please. Only do nothing to these men, for they have come under the shelter of my roof."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lot goes out, shuts the door behind him, and calls the mob "my brothers." He has enough courage to put his own body between the visitors and the crowd, and enough compromise to address a lynch mob as family.

Then he says the worst sentence in the chapter. "Behold, I have two daughters who have not known any man. Let me bring them out to you, and do to them as you please."

Genesis records it and does not defend it. No appeal to ancient hospitality codes makes this acceptable, and the book is not asking anyone to admire him. He offers his own children to be raped by a mob in order to protect his guests, and weighs the two as though it were a reasonable trade.

Take the measure of what a chosen environment does to a person over time. It does not merely surround him; it forms him. Peter calls Lot righteous, and Peter is right — but this righteous man has been in Sodom long enough that in a crisis he reaches instinctively for Sodom's arithmetic, in which some people's bodies are expendable. Nobody drifts into a place like that in one evening. And the daughters he offers here will be at the centre of the chapter's last, terrible scene.

verseByVerse.quote: But they said, "Stand back!" And they said, "This fellow came to sojourn, and he has become the judge! Now we will deal worse with you than with them." Then they pressed hard against the man Lot, and drew near to break the door down. But the men reached out their hands and brought Lot into the house with them and shut the door. And they struck with blindness the men who were at the entrance of the house, both small and great, so that they wore themselves out groping for the door.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"This fellow came to sojourn, and he has become the judge!" The mob's answer is the oldest one there is: who are you to tell us anything? And they are not entirely wrong about him. He has lived among them for years, married his daughters into their families, taken a seat in their gate — and now, on one night, he wants to be their conscience. Moral influence is built slowly and it cannot be produced on demand.

"Then they pressed hard against the man Lot, and drew near to break the door down." He is about to be torn apart. Everything he had built in that city — the house, the standing, the seat in the gate — buys him nothing at all when the city turns.

"But the men reached out their hands and brought Lot into the house with them and shut the door." He does not rescue himself. He is pulled inside, and the same verb will be used again in verse 16 when the angels drag him out of the city altogether. Twice in one night this man is saved by somebody else's hands.

"And they struck with blindness the men who were at the entrance... so that they wore themselves out groping for the door." It is a grim picture: blind, exhausted, and still feeling along the wall for the handle. Sin does not stop being wanted merely because it has become impossible to reach, and a judgment that removes the opportunity has not touched the appetite.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men said to Lot, "Have you anyone else here? Sons-in-law, sons, daughters, or anyone you have in the city, bring them out of the place. For we are about to destroy this place, because the outcry against its people has become great before the LORD, and the LORD has sent us to destroy it." So Lot went out and said to his sons-in-law, who were to marry his daughters, "Up! Get out of this place, for the LORD is about to destroy the city." But he seemed to his sons-in-law to be jesting.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Have you anyone else here? Sons-in-law, sons, daughters, or anyone you have in the city, bring them out of the place." The angels widen the rescue as far as Lot can take it. Whoever he can persuade may come.

"For we are about to destroy this place, because the outcry against its people has become great before the LORD." Judgment is announced with its grounds attached, exactly as it was to Abraham. God does not strike without telling anyone why.

"So Lot went out and said to his sons-in-law... 'Up! Get out of this place, for the LORD is about to destroy the city.' But he seemed to his sons-in-law to be jesting."

There is the harvest of a compromised life, and it is the saddest verse in the chapter. The one night Lot tells the plain truth about the judgment of God, the young men who have known him for years laugh in his face. He had lived so much like them for so long that when it mattered they could not take him seriously. Nobody in Sodom is persuaded by Lot. Not one person leaves the city because of him.

That is a sobering thing for anyone whose Christian testimony rests on being liked. A witness that has never cost anything cannot buy anything either — and the children and in-laws are usually the first to know which it is.

verseByVerse.quote: As morning dawned, the angels urged Lot, saying, "Up! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, lest you be swept away in the punishment of the city." But he lingered. So the men seized him and his wife and his two daughters by the hand, the LORD being merciful to him, and they brought him out and set him outside the city. And as they brought them out, one said, "Escape for your life. Do not look back or stop anywhere in the valley. Escape to the hills, lest you be swept away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"As morning dawned, the angels urged Lot... 'Up! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, lest you be swept away.'"

"But he lingered." Three words, and they are the most extraordinary in the chapter. The city is hours from destruction. There are angels standing in his hall. He has just been told the place is finished — and Lot cannot make himself walk out of the door. Whatever he had built in Sodom had its hooks in him, and it held on right up to the last morning.

"So the men seized him and his wife and his two daughters by the hand, the LORD being merciful to him, and they brought him out and set him outside the city."

Read that slowly. He is not persuaded, not convinced, not even willing. He is taken by the wrist and pulled out of a burning city against the drag of his own heart, and the reason is stated in the middle of the sentence: the LORD being merciful to him.

Everybody who is ever saved is saved like this. Not one person walked out of the condemned city under his own steam because the argument was finally compelling enough. The hand that closes on the wrist is the whole doctrine of grace, and Lot is its first illustration in Scripture — a man dragged out lingering, saved entirely by mercy, with nothing whatever to be proud of.

"Escape for your life. Do not look back or stop anywhere in the valley." Three commands: run, do not look, do not stop. Remember all three; two of them are about to be broken.

verseByVerse.quote: And Lot said to them, "Oh, no, my lords. Behold, your servant has found favor in your sight, and you have shown me great kindness in saving my life. But I cannot escape to the hills, lest the disaster overtake me and I die. Behold, this city is near enough to flee to, and it is a little one. Let me escape there—is it not a little one?—and my life will be saved!" He said to him, "Behold, I grant you this favor also, that I will not overthrow the city of which you have spoken. Escape there quickly, for I can do nothing till you arrive there." Therefore the name of the city was called Zoar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dragged out of a burning city by angels, Lot begins to negotiate. "Oh, no, my lords... I cannot escape to the hills." He has just been given his life and he argues about the destination.

His reasoning is almost comic: the hills are too dangerous, the little town is nearer, "is it not a little one?" He has been told the whole valley is going up, and he asks to stop just inside it because the walk is too far. Fear makes people choose the near thing over the safe thing, every time.

And God grants it. "Behold, I grant you this favor also, that I will not overthrow the city of which you have spoken." A town is spared because one reluctant man did not want to climb a hill. Its name becomes Zoar, which means Little — a place on the map named after an excuse.

"Escape there quickly, for I can do nothing till you arrive there." Let that stand as it is written. The judgment of two cities waits on the safe arrival of one argumentative, lingering, thoroughly unimpressive man. God will not let the fire fall until his own are clear of it (cf. 2 Pet. 2:9).

verseByVerse.quote: The sun had risen on the earth when Lot came to Zoar. Then the LORD rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the LORD out of heaven. And he overthrew those cities, and all the valley, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and what grew on the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The sun had risen on the earth when Lot came to Zoar. Then the LORD rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the LORD out of heaven." Not one minute before he was safe.

The valley that Lot had looked at and thought was "like the garden of the LORD" (13:10) burns to the ground, along with "all the valley, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and what grew on the ground." The best-watered land in Canaan becomes the wasteland at the bottom of the Dead Sea.

Every New Testament writer who mentions this treats it as a fixed and literal warning about a judgment still to come. Jesus set it beside the flood and said, "so will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed" (Luke 17:28–30). Peter says God made them "an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly" (2 Pet. 2:6). Jude calls them "an example by undergoing a punishment of eternal fire" (Jude 7). This is not a story Scripture grows out of, and a gospel that cannot say so has quietly stopped believing the Bible it preaches from.

verseByVerse.quote: But Lot's wife, behind him, looked back, and she became a pillar of salt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But Lot's wife, behind him, looked back, and she became a pillar of salt."

Nine words. And the Lord Jesus, teaching about the day of his return, reduced them to three: "Remember Lot's wife" (Luke 17:32). Of all the sentences in Genesis he might have quoted, he chose this one, and he attached it to a warning about the man on the housetop who goes back down for his things.

She was not idly curious. The text says she was behind him — lagging, falling back, already at the rear of the little group — and the looking is the end of a process, not a moment of weakness. She had a house in that town, and friends, and married daughters she was walking away from. Her feet were on the road and her heart was still at her own front door.

And that is exactly why Jesus used her. The question his warning puts is not whether you have crossed the city line. It is where you are looking. It is entirely possible to be outwardly out of something — the habit given up, the relationship ended, the old life formally left behind — and to spend years looking over your shoulder at it with regret. Genesis marks the spot with a pillar of salt and does not tell us her name.

"No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God" (Luke 9:62). The plough and the pillar are making the same point.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abraham went early in the morning to the place where he had stood before the LORD. And he looked down toward Sodom and Gomorrah and toward all the land of the valley, and he looked and, behold, the smoke of the land went up like the smoke of a furnace. So it was that, when God destroyed the cities of the valley, God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow when he overthrew the cities in which Lot had lived.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And Abraham went early in the morning to the place where he had stood before the LORD." He goes back to where he prayed. He wants to see what came of it, and what he sees is "the smoke of the land went up like the smoke of a furnace."

There were not ten righteous men in Sodom. The intercession failed on its own terms, and Abraham stands on a ridge at dawn looking at the answer. Scripture lets that stand without softening it, because it is honest about prayers that are not granted in the form they were prayed.

Then the narrator tells us what Abraham could not see from the hillside: "So it was that, when God destroyed the cities of the valley, God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow." The rescue in verse 16 had a cause, and the cause was a conversation on a hill the night before.

Neither man knew it. Lot never learned that he was pulled out of Sodom because of his uncle's praying, and Abraham, standing there watching the smoke go up, did not know that his prayer had saved anybody at all.

If you have prayed for years for someone and watched the situation burn anyway, this verse is for you. God's answer may be happening entirely out of your sight, in a form you did not ask for, and the person you prayed for may never know, and you may not either — until the day everything is told.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The final episode of Genesis 19 is the darkest in the Lot narrative: hiding in a cave after the destruction of Zoar, Lot's daughters conclude that there are no men left to continue their family line and engineer pregnancies through their father. The resulting children — Moab and Ammon — are the ancestors of Israel's eastern neighbors and persistent adversaries. The episode is presented without editorial comment, but its horror is obvious and its consequences long-lasting.
verseByVerse.theology: The theological question of the episode is not whether what Lot's daughters did was right (it was not) but why it is included and what it means. The daughters' belief that all the men of the earth have been destroyed is implausible — they saw Zoar's inhabitants — but may reflect the psychological trauma of witnessing Sodom's total destruction. Their action, however misguided, reflects the same concern for covenant continuity that drove Sarai to provide Hagar (ch.16): the fear that the line will end and the promise will fail. Both actions are human attempts to solve a perceived covenant crisis through morally compromised means.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes that the Moab-Ammon origin story is told here to explain Israel's complicated relationship with these peoples throughout the Old Testament — kinship combined with conflict, compassion combined with judgment. Ruth the Moabitess will become an ancestor of David and of Jesus, demonstrating that even the fruit of Lot's cave can be redeemed by the grace that runs through the covenant line. The darkness of Genesis 19's ending is not the Bible's last word about these nations or their descendants.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Lot went up out of Zoar and lived in the hills with his two daughters, for he was afraid to live in Zoar. So he lived in a cave with his two daughters. And the firstborn said to the younger, "Our father is old, and there is not a man on earth to come in to us after the manner of all the earth. Come, let us make our father drink wine, and we will lie with him, that we may preserve offspring from our father." So they made their father drink wine that night. And the firstborn went in and lay with her father. He did not know when she lay down or when she arose. The next day, the firstborn said to the younger, "Behold, I lay last night with my father. Let us make him drink wine tonight also. Then you go in and lie with him, that we may preserve offspring from our father." So they made their father drink wine that night also. And the younger arose and lay with him, and he did not know when she lay down or when she arose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lot ends in a cave. He had begged for Zoar and now he is "afraid to live in Zoar" — the man who could not be got out of Sodom cannot now settle anywhere at all. He has lost his wife, his home, his standing, his sons-in-law and his nerve, and he is living in a hole in the hills with two daughters.

"Our father is old, and there is not a man on earth to come in to us after the manner of all the earth." That is despair talking, and it is not even true — there were people in Zoar a few miles away. But these are girls raised in Sodom, betrothed to Sodomites, offered to a mob by their own father and now shut in a cave with a broken man, and they have concluded that the future has to be manufactured by any means available.

So they get him drunk on two consecutive nights and conceive by him. Genesis reports it without one syllable of approval, and every element of the scene grows out of something earlier in the story: the wine is the anaesthetic of a ruined man, the scheme is the reasoning of women who learned in Sodom that a body is a tool, and the father is twice too far gone to know what is happening to him.

It is the last we see of the man who once lifted up his eyes and chose the best-watered land in the country. He chose by sight, and this is where sight took him.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus both the daughters of Lot became pregnant by their father. The firstborn bore a son and called his name Moab. He is the father of the Moabites to this day. The younger also bore a son and called his name Ben-ammi. He is the father of the Ammonites to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The firstborn bore a son and called his name Moab... The younger also bore a son and called his name Ben-ammi." Moab and Ammon: two nations who will harass Israel for a thousand years, hire Balaam against her, and drag her into Baal worship — born in a cave, out of incest and despair, to the daughters of a righteous man.

Genesis lets the genealogy be the verdict and adds nothing. The reader who started at 13:10, watching Lot look at the green valley, has now been shown the whole arc: the choice by sight, the drift towards the city, the seat in the gate, the compromised household, the rescue by the wrist, and the cave.

And yet. Four hundred years later a widow of Moab stood on a road and said to her Israelite mother-in-law, "Your people shall be my people, and your God my God" (Ruth 1:16). Ruth the Moabitess married Boaz, and bore Obed, who fathered Jesse, who fathered David — and Matthew puts her name in the opening paragraph of the New Testament (Matt. 1:5).

So the line that begins in that cave runs to Bethlehem. God did not merely tolerate an ancestry like this; he chose to bring his own Son through it, and he had the whole story written down so that nobody could ever pretend otherwise. No one is disqualified by where they came from. Grace is not embarrassed by the worst paragraph in a family's history — it goes and gets a bride out of it.

19.theology:
Divine Judgment. The destruction of Sodom establishes that God’s patience with corporate wickedness is real but not infinite. The outcry against Sodom was “great” (18:20) — the accumulated weight of injustice toward the vulnerable, pride and contempt for the weak, and violence against the stranger. When that weight reaches the tipping point, judgment falls. The New Testament does not soften this: “it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10:31). The gospel does not abolish judgment; it provides the only refuge from it — the one who bore the fire of judgment so that those in him would not be consumed by it.

Saved Through Another’s Intercession. Lot’s salvation by virtue of Abraham’s intercession (v.29) is one of Genesis’s clearest prefigurations of the gospel: we are not saved by our own righteousness but by the righteousness and advocacy of another. Romans 5:10 — “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” — is Lot’s story told at universal scale. We were lingering in the city of destruction, and the Son came not to condemn but to drag us out.
19.examples:
Then: The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah left a lasting mark on the ancient Near East’s cultural memory — archaeological evidence suggests a dramatic destruction event in the region of the Dead Sea in the Middle Bronze Age. For Israel, Sodom was the paradigmatic destroyed city: the prophets regularly invoked it as the standard of total divine judgment (Isa. 1:9; Jer. 49:18; Amos 4:11). The warning was not abstract; it was a geographic reality their ancestors had witnessed.

Now: The chapter speaks to the danger of cultural accommodation — the Lot who moved toward Sodom gradually, integrated fully, and then found himself unable to leave freely. The church in every generation faces the temptation to integrate so thoroughly with the surrounding culture that its distinctiveness is lost and, when the moment of choice comes, it finds itself lingering. And “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke 17:32) is the perpetual warning against half-hearted discipleship: grace that drags you out of destruction also requires that you face the direction of your salvation, not the city you were rescued from.

20.title: Abraham and Abimelech
20.text: <sup>1</sup>From there Abraham journeyed toward the territory of the Negeb and lived between Kadesh and Shur; and he sojourned in Gerar.<sup>2</sup>And Abraham said of Sarah his wife, "She is my sister." And Abimelech king of Gerar sent and took Sarah.<sup>3</sup>But God came to Abimelech in a dream by night and said to him, "Behold, you are a dead man because of the woman whom you have taken, for she is a man's wife."<sup>4</sup>Now Abimelech had not approached her. So he said, "Lord, will you kill an innocent people?<sup>5</sup>Did he not himself say to me, 'She is my sister'? And she herself said, 'He is my brother.' In the integrity of my heart and the innocence of my hands I have done this."<sup>6</sup>Then God said to him in the dream, "Yes, I know that you have done this in the integrity of your heart, and it was I who kept you from sinning against me. Therefore I did not let you touch her.<sup>7</sup>Now then, return the man's wife, for he is a prophet, so that he will pray for you, and you shall live. But if you do not return her, know that you shall surely die, you and all who are yours."<sup>8</sup>So Abimelech rose early in the morning and called all his servants and told them all these things. And the men were very much afraid.<sup>9</sup>Then Abimelech called Abraham and said to him, "What have you done to us? And how have I sinned against you, that you have brought on me and my kingdom a great sin? You have done to me things that ought not to be done."<sup>10</sup>And Abimelech said to Abraham, "What did you see, that you did this thing?"<sup>11</sup>Abraham said, "I did it because I thought, 'There is no fear of God at all in this place, and they will kill me because of my wife.'<sup>12</sup>Besides, she is indeed my sister, the daughter of my father though not the daughter of my mother, and she became my wife.<sup>13</sup>And when God caused me to wander from my father's house, I said to her, 'This is the kindness you must do me: at every place to which we come, say of me, "He is my brother."'"<sup>14</sup>Then Abimelech took sheep and oxen, and male servants and female servants, and gave them to Abraham, and returned Sarah his wife to him.<sup>15</sup>And Abimelech said, "Behold, my land is before you; dwell where it pleases you."<sup>16</sup>To Sarah he said, "Behold, I have given your brother a thousand pieces of silver. It is a sign of your innocence in the eyes of all who are with you, and before everyone you are vindicated."<sup>17</sup>Then Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech, and also healed his wife and female slaves so that they bore children.<sup>18</sup>For the LORD had closed all the wombs of the house of Abimelech because of Sarah, Abraham's wife.
20.overview:
Genesis 20 is the second occurrence of Abraham’s “she is my sister” deception (the first was in Egypt, ch.12) — a repeat failure that reveals both the persistent weakness of the patriarch and the relentless protection of the covenant promise. The child of promise has not yet been born; if Sarah is taken into another man’s household, the covenant line is in jeopardy. God intervenes, this time not with plagues (as in Egypt) but with a direct divine warning to Abimelech in a dream.

The episode contains a theological surprise: Abimelech the Philistine king acts with more integrity than Abraham the covenant patriarch. God himself acknowledges this (v.6: “I know that you have done this in the integrity of your heart”) and attributes Abimelech’s not-sinning to divine restraint rather than human virtue (“it was I who kept you from sinning against me”). The general revelation of conscience, operating in a pagan king, produces behavior that the special-revelation recipient fails to match. This is not comfortable for any theology that too easily equates covenant membership with moral superiority.

The chapter ends with Abraham praying for Abimelech — the prophet who failed to protect his wife now interceding for the king he deceived. Grace is full of these inversions: the one who sinned becomes the instrument of healing for the one who was sinned against. This is the gospel logic: the sinner restored becomes the intercessor.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — Abraham and Abimelech: The Sister-Wife Repeated
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 20 records Abraham's second deception about Sarah's identity — this time with Abimelech king of Gerar. Coming immediately after the destruction of Sodom and the rescue of Lot, the episode is sobering: the covenant patriarch, the man through whom all nations will be blessed, repeats his Egypt lie in a new setting. The repetition is not a duplicate tradition but a deliberately repeated test of the same weakness. Abraham learned from Egypt that God protects Sarah; he has not learned to trust that protection.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter's theological complexity is considerable. God appears to Abimelech in a dream and acknowledges that Abimelech has acted in integrity — 'Yes, I know that you have done this in the integrity of your heart' (v.6). God prevents Abimelech from sinning, speaks to him in a dream, and protects Sarah through the Philistine king's moral integrity rather than through Abraham's faith. The pagan king again behaves more honorably than the covenant patriarch. Yet God's protection of Sarah is ultimately not for Abimelech's sake but for the covenant: 'he is a prophet, and he will pray for you' (v.7).
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham on Genesis 20: the episode serves several theological functions. It demonstrates that God's covenant purposes are not thwarted by the covenant man's failures. It introduces Abraham as a prophet — the first use of the word 'prophet' (nabi) in Scripture. It shows Abimelech as a model of the just ruler who responds to divine correction — a positive portrait of a Gentile king that prepares for the treaty of chapter 21. And it reveals Abraham's stated reason for the deception (v.11–13), which while inadequate, shows that Abraham was not cynically lying but acting from deep fear in a world he perceived as godless.

verseByVerse.quote: From there Abraham journeyed toward the territory of the Negeb and lived between Kadesh and Shur; and he sojourned in Gerar. And Abraham said of Sarah his wife, "She is my sister." And Abimelech king of Gerar sent and took Sarah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And Abraham said of Sarah his wife, 'She is my sister.'" He has done this before, in Egypt, twenty-five years earlier (12:13), and it went badly then. He does it again.

The timing could hardly be worse. God has just told him, by name and with a date, that Sarah will bear the covenant son within the year (17:21; 18:10). Abraham hands her to a foreign king anyway. The mother of the promise is in another man's house, months before Isaac is due, and the whole plan of redemption is standing in a harem because a hundred-year-old man was frightened.

Two things about besetting sins are on the page here. They come back — a fault dealt with once is not a fault dealt with — and they come back under the same conditions. It is the same trigger every time: a new place, an unfamiliar ruler, and a fear about his own skin. Every believer has a particular door he goes through when he is afraid, and knowing exactly where that door is does not, by itself, keep him out of it.

verseByVerse.quote: But God came to Abimelech in a dream by night and said to him, "Behold, you are a dead man because of the woman whom you have taken, for she is a man's wife." Now Abimelech had not approached her. So he said, "Lord, will you kill an innocent people? Did he not himself say to me, 'She is my sister'? And she herself said, 'He is my brother.' In the integrity of my heart and the innocence of my hands I have done this."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But God came to Abimelech in a dream by night." The pagan king gets a personal visit from God; the prophet gets nothing. God's initiative does not run along the lines of who deserves it.

"Behold, you are a dead man because of the woman whom you have taken, for she is a man's wife." No preamble and no softening. Note in passing what it assumes: adultery is a capital matter before God even in Gerar, where nobody has the law of Moses, because some things are written into the world rather than into a statute (cf. Rom. 2:14–15).

And Abimelech's reply is the honest protest of a man who has been lied to. "Lord, will you kill an innocent people? Did he not himself say to me, 'She is my sister'? And she herself said, 'He is my brother.'"

She herself said. Sarah went along with it. She had done it once in Egypt and she does it again here, and Genesis names her part in it rather than making her purely a victim of her husband's cowardice. A conspiracy needs two people.

verseByVerse.quote: Then God said to him in the dream, "Yes, I know that you have done this in the integrity of your heart, and it was I who kept you from sinning against me. Therefore I did not let you touch her. Now then, return the man's wife, for he is a prophet, so that he will pray for you, and you shall live. But if you do not return her, know that you shall surely die, you and all who are yours."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God's answer makes two distinctions, and both should be carried away.

First: "Yes, I know that you have done this in the integrity of your heart." God grants the man's plea, in so many words. Motive matters in God's court, and a person who acts on a deception he had no way of detecting is not judged as though he had schemed. That should settle a good deal of needless self-torment among Christians about things they did in genuine ignorance.

Second, and more startling: "it was I who kept you from sinning against me. Therefore I did not let you touch her." Abimelech's clean hands are not Abimelech's achievement. God restrained him.

Sit with that, because it changes the way a person reads his own record. The sins you did not commit last year are not all evidence of your strong character. Some number of them — and you have no way of knowing how many — are evidence of a God who arranged an interruption, delayed a journey, sent someone into the room, or simply made you ill on the wrong afternoon. Every honest believer will discover one day how much of his integrity was somebody else's doing.

"Now then, return the man's wife, for he is a prophet, so that he will pray for you, and you shall live." God calls Abraham a prophet — the first use of the word in the Bible — in the middle of the chapter where he behaves worst, and sends the injured party to ask the liar to pray for him. God's commitment to his covenant man is not a running commentary on his conduct.

verseByVerse.quote: So Abimelech rose early in the morning and called all his servants and told them all these things. And the men were very much afraid. Then Abimelech called Abraham and said to him, "What have you done to us? And how have I sinned against you, that you have brought on me and my kingdom a great sin? You have done to me things that ought not to be done." And Abimelech said to Abraham, "What did you see, that you did this thing?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"So Abimelech rose early in the morning and called all his servants and told them all these things. And the men were very much afraid." He believes the dream immediately and acts on it before breakfast, and the fear of God spreads through a Philistine court in a morning.

"Then Abimelech called Abraham and said to him, 'What have you done to us? And how have I sinned against you, that you have brought on me and my kingdom a great sin? You have done to me things that ought not to be done.'"

For the second time in Genesis a pagan king stands over the father of the faithful and gives him a lecture on integrity, and there is no answer to it. Pharaoh did it in chapter 12; Abimelech does it here, and adds a stinging phrase: things that ought not to be done. He does not need the law of God to know that.

There is a particular shame in being corrected by an outsider on a point of plain decency, and Scripture puts it on the page without covering for its hero. The world is quite capable of noticing when a Christian has behaved badly, and it is generally right.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham said, "I did it because I thought, 'There is no fear of God at all in this place, and they will kill me because of my wife.' Besides, she is indeed my sister, the daughter of my father though not the daughter of my mother, and she became my wife. And when God caused me to wander from my father's house, I said to her, 'This is the kindness you must do me: at every place to which we come, say of me, "He is my brother."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham's defence comes in three parts, and it is the anatomy of most of our excuses.

"I did it because I thought, 'There is no fear of God at all in this place.'" An assumption, not an investigation. He had decided in advance what these people were like, and the chapter has just demonstrated that Abimelech feared God rather more than Abraham did that week. The believer who assumes the worst about outsiders regularly ends up behaving worse than they do — and then defends it on the grounds of the danger he had imagined.

"Besides, she is indeed my sister, the daughter of my father though not the daughter of my mother." True, and irrelevant. A half-truth told in order to create a false impression is a lie with better paperwork, and the fact that it would survive cross-examination is exactly what makes it useful.

"And when God caused me to wander from my father's house, I said to her, 'This is the kindness you must do me: at every place to which we come, say of me, "He is my brother."'"

This is the most revealing thing he says, and it slips out at the end. It was not a panic. It was a policy — a standing arrangement made at the very start of the journey, at the moment God called him out of Haran, and never once revoked in twenty-five years. He left home with a promise from God in one hand and a contingency plan in the other, and he had been quietly running the contingency plan all along. Most people's worst failures are not sudden. They are a long-standing arrangement finally coming to light.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abimelech took sheep and oxen, and male servants and female servants, and gave them to Abraham, and returned Sarah his wife to him. And Abimelech said, "Behold, my land is before you; dwell where it pleases you." To Sarah he said, "Behold, I have given your brother a thousand pieces of silver. It is a sign of your innocence in the eyes of all who are with you, and before everyone you are vindicated."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abimelech returns Sarah and gives Abraham sheep, oxen, servants and the run of his country. The liar leaves richer than he arrived, for the second time in his life, and Genesis simply reports it without comment or approval.

Then the king turns to Sarah, and what he says is unexpectedly kind. The thousand pieces of silver are "a sign of your innocence in the eyes of all who are with you, and before everyone you are vindicated." He is making certain that nobody in the camp can whisper about her afterwards — a public, expensive, documented clearing of her name.

A pagan king spends a fortune protecting the reputation of a woman whose own husband had put it at risk to save himself. Genesis sets the two men side by side and lets the reader do the arithmetic.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech, and also healed his wife and female slaves so that they bore children. For the LORD had closed all the wombs of the house of Abimelech because of Sarah, Abraham's wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech, and also healed his wife and female slaves so that they bore children."

The man in the wrong prays for the man he wronged, and the prayer is answered. There is no recorded repentance in this chapter — Scripture does not narrate one — and Abraham is restored to his office and used. Which is not an argument for taking sin lightly; it is a statement about who is holding the relationship together. It was never Abraham.
