"For the LORD had closed all the wombs of the house of Abimelech because of Sarah, Abraham's wife." The last verse tells us what has been happening off-stage, and it explains the urgency of the whole chapter. God shut every womb in Gerar.

Consider the timing. Within months Sarah will conceive the son of promise. God arranges that in the kingdom where she has just spent time as another man's property, there is not one competing pregnancy — not a single child conceived in Gerar during those weeks. Nobody would ever be able to raise a question about who Isaac's father was.

So the chapter, read whole, is not about Abraham at all. It is about a God who sends a dream, restrains a king, protects a woman's name, closes and opens wombs, and answers the prayer of the man who caused the trouble — because a promise had been made and a child was coming, and nothing, least of all the failure of the man carrying it, was going to get in the way.

20.theology:
Common Grace and Moral Conscience. Abimelech’s integrity in chapter 20 demonstrates what Reformed theology calls “common grace” at work in the moral realm: the image of God, though distorted by sin, still functions as a moral compass in unregenerate humanity. Abimelech acted with integrity not because he had the Torah but because God had written the basic moral law on the human heart (Rom. 2:14–15) and personally restrained him from sin (v.6). The church has no monopoly on moral conscience; it has the unique gift of the Spirit who enables what conscience alone cannot sustain.

The Irrevocability of Calling. God calls Abraham “a prophet” (v.7) immediately after Abraham has failed as a husband and as an honest man. The calling is not contingent on the immediate moral performance. Paul makes this explicit for the new covenant: “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Rom. 11:29). This is both comfort (our failures do not revoke our calling) and warning (our calling does not excuse our failures). The cracked vessel is still in the Potter’s hands.
20.examples:
Then: The episode with Abimelech reflects the political vulnerability of a patriarch traveling through Philistine territory with a beautiful wife. In the power dynamics of the ancient Near East, a foreign woman was effectively unprotected — a king could take her with impunity. Abraham’s deception was pragmatic cowardice, not irrational fear. But God’s protection of Sarah through a Philistine king’s conscience demonstrates that divine providence operates through unexpected moral actors.

Now: The repeat failure of Abraham (same sin as chapter 12) speaks to every Christian who has been mortified to discover that they are still vulnerable to sins they thought they had put behind them. The specific, persistent sin does not disqualify from covenant relationship or from prophetic calling — but it does need to be addressed, confessed, and brought repeatedly to the God who holds his people not by their grip on him but by his grip on them. And Abimelech’s integrity should keep the church humble: God works through moral conscientiousness in unexpected places, and the covenant community has no exclusive claim on ethical seriousness.

21.title: God Has Made Laughter for Me
21.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did to Sarah as he had promised.<sup>2</sup>And Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age at the time of which God had spoken to him.<sup>3</sup>Abraham called the name of his son who was born to him, whom Sarah bore him, Isaac.<sup>4</sup>And Abraham circumcised his son Isaac when he was eight days old, as God had commanded him.<sup>5</sup>Abraham was a hundred years old when his son Isaac was born to him.<sup>6</sup>And Sarah said, "God has made laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh over me."<sup>7</sup>And she said, "Who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? And she departed and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba.<sup>15</sup>When the water in the skin was gone, she put the child under one of the bushes.<sup>16</sup>Then she went and sat down opposite him a good way off, about the distance of a bowshot, for she said, "Let me not look on the death of the child." He lived in the wilderness and became an expert with the bow.<sup>21</sup>He lived in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother took a wife for him from the land of Egypt.<sup>22</sup>At that time Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army said to Abraham, "God is with you in all that you do.<sup>23</sup>Now therefore swear to me here by God that you will not deal falsely with me or with my descendants or with my posterity, but as I have dealt kindly with you, so you will deal with me and with the land where you have sojourned."<sup>24</sup>And Abraham said, "I will swear."<sup>25</sup>When Abraham reproved Abimelech about a well of water that Abimelech's servants had seized,<sup>26</sup>Abimelech said, "I do not know who has done this thing; you did not tell me, and I have not heard of it until today."<sup>27</sup>So Abraham took sheep and oxen and gave them to Abimelech, and the two men made a covenant.<sup>28</sup>Abraham set seven ewe lambs of the flock apart.<sup>29</sup>And Abimelech said to Abraham, "What is the meaning of these seven ewe lambs that you have set apart?"<sup>30</sup>He said, "These seven ewe lambs you will take from my hand, that this may be a witness for me that I dug this well."<sup>31</sup>Therefore that place was called Beersheba, because there both of them swore an oath.<sup>32</sup>So they made a covenant at Beersheba. Then Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army rose up and returned to the land of the Philistines.<sup>33</sup>Abraham planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba and called there on the name of the LORD, the Everlasting God.<sup>34</sup>And Abraham sojourned many days in the land of the Philistines.
21.overview:
Chapter 21 is one of the most joyful chapters in Genesis: “The LORD visited Sarah as he had said” (v.1). The promise of decades, the waiting of chapters, the laughing and doubting and wandering — all of it comes to its appointed end in the simplest possible way: God did what he said he would do. Isaac is born. Sarah laughs — not the incredulous laugh of 18:12 but the laughter of fulfilled promise: “God has made laughter for me” (v.6). The name Isaac (he laughs) is now the permanent memorial to the joy of impossible-promise-kept.

The chapter does not remain in this joy for long. The conflict between Ishmael and Isaac erupts at the weaning feast, and Hagar and Ishmael are sent away — a painful episode that troubles modern readers and troubled Abraham greatly (v.11: “the thing was very displeasing to Abraham on account of his son”). But God provides for Hagar and Ishmael in the wilderness, meeting them again as he had in chapter 16, and promising that Ishmael too will become a great nation (v.18). The God who keeps his promises to Isaac is also the God who hears the voice of Ishmael (v.17: “God heard the voice of the boy” — Ishmael means “God hears”).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Birth of Isaac and the Expulsion of Hagar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 21 opens with the long-awaited birth of Isaac — the covenant child, born at the appointed time to a 90-year-old mother and a 100-year-old father. The laughter that greeted the promise (17:17; 18:12) becomes the laughter of fulfilled joy: 'God has made laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh over me.' The impossible has happened. But the joy of Isaac's birth immediately creates a crisis: Ishmael, now a young teenager, is seen 'laughing' (mocking) at the weaning feast, and Sarah demands his expulsion. Abraham is torn; God instructs him to comply; and Hagar and Ishmael are sent into the wilderness, where God provides for them a second time.
verseByVerse.theology: The expulsion of Hagar and Ishmael is one of the most pastorally sensitive episodes in Genesis. Hagar and Ishmael are victims of the consequences of Abraham and Sarah's impatience, and yet God's instruction to Abraham (v.12) and God's care for Hagar in the wilderness (vv.17–20) establish that their expulsion is not divine abandonment but divine re-routing. Paul uses the Hagar-Sarah typology typologically in Galatians 4:21–31 — the child of the slave woman and the child of the free woman, the covenant of law and the covenant of grace — but the typology must not be used to dismiss Hagar and Ishmael as merely symbolic. They are real people, and God's tender care for them in the wilderness is real grace.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller on Genesis 21: the birth of Isaac is the fulfillment of the promise that seemed most impossible. When God fulfills a promise that has been waiting 25 years, the fulfillment is not underwhelming — it is more than the waiting could have imagined. Sarah's laughter of incredulity (18:12) becomes the laughter of joy and wonder (21:6) — the same response to the same God, transformed by the encounter with his faithfulness. This transformation of incredulous laughter into joyful laughter is the pattern of faith's journey: what we could not believe, we learn to celebrate.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did to Sarah as he had promised. And Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age at the time of which God had spoken to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did to Sarah as he had promised... at the time of which God had spoken to him." Three times in two verses the narrator says the same thing in different words. He is not padding. He is hammering.

Count what those twenty-five years contained: a famine, a lie in Egypt, a split with Lot, a war, a shortcut with Hagar, thirteen years of silence, a laugh at the promise, and a second lie about his wife three months ago. Not one of them moved the date by a day.

The word translated visited is used elsewhere of God stepping into a situation to act — he "visited" Hannah, and she conceived (1 Sam. 2:21). It is not a social call. After a quarter of a century of nothing, God turns up and does the thing.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham called the name of his son who was born to him, whom Sarah bore him, Isaac. And Abraham circumcised his son Isaac when he was eight days old, as God had commanded him. Abraham was a hundred years old when his son Isaac was born to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Abraham called the name of his son... Isaac. And Abraham circumcised his son Isaac when he was eight days old, as God had commanded him." Both details are exact obedience to chapter 17 — the name God chose (17:19) and the day God specified (17:12). The old man is now doing everything precisely on time.

"Abraham was a hundred years old when his son Isaac was born to him." The number is given because it is the whole argument. Paul builds on this: Abraham "considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah's womb" — and God did it anyway. That, says Paul, is exactly why the promise "depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed" (Rom. 4:16–21).

If Isaac had been born to a fertile couple in their thirties, someone could have said the covenant ran on human capability. God waited until it plainly could not, and then gave the child. He still tends to work that way, and the reason is not cruelty but clarity about who did it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Sarah said, "God has made laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh over me." And she said, "Who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? Yet I have borne him a son in his old age."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"God has made laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh over me."

Sarah laughed behind a tent flap in unbelief and was caught at it, and denied it, and was told plainly that she had (18:12–15). Now she laughs again, and this time she says God made the sound.

The Hebrew has an edge she must have felt. Laughing over someone can mean laughing with them or laughing at them, and she has been the subject of camp talk for decades — the barren wife, the standing sadness of the household. What people said behind their hands has been turned into something they will celebrate.

"Who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children?" Nobody. That is her point, and she is enjoying it. There was not a person on earth who would have predicted this.

God did not merely keep the promise; he redeemed the laugh. The same sound that came out of her in disbelief is now her son's name, and she will say it out loud a hundred times a day for the rest of her life. He is not in the habit of holding our worst moment against us. He has been known to name the blessing after it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the child grew and was weaned. And Abraham made a great feast on the day that Isaac was weaned. But Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Abraham, laughing. So she said to Abraham, "Cast out this slave woman with her son, for the son of this slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac." And the thing was very displeasing to Abraham on account of his son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The weaning feast — a child was typically weaned at two or three — turns sour. "Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Abraham, laughing." The word is a form of the same root that gives Isaac his name, and given the seventeen-year age gap and the inheritance at stake, mockery is the likely sense. Paul, who knew the passage well, calls it persecution (Gal. 4:29).

"Cast out this slave woman with her son, for the son of this slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac." Sarah's tone is ugly. She uses neither name — only "this slave woman" and "her son" — against "my son Isaac." Fourteen years earlier she had personally handed Hagar to her husband. Now she wants her gone. The person who arranges a shortcut is very often the one who ends up hating the result of it, and the hatred is usually loudest where the guilt is.

"And the thing was very displeasing to Abraham on account of his son." Whatever else is true of him, Abraham loves this boy. Sarah's demand is about property; his grief is about a child he has raised for seventeen years. Genesis does not ask us to take sides in the tent. It shows us a household that a shortcut has poisoned beyond repair.

verseByVerse.quote: But God said to Abraham, "Be not displeased because of the boy and because of your slave woman. Whatever Sarah says to you, do as she tells you, for through Isaac shall your offspring be named. And I will make a nation of the son of the slave woman also, because he is your offspring."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God's answer holds both halves. "Whatever Sarah says to you, do as she tells you, for through Isaac shall your offspring be named." The covenant line must be unambiguous, and two heirs in one camp would have made it anything but. God endorses the outcome without endorsing Sarah's spirit — a distinction he makes rather often, and one we should be slow to claim for ourselves.

"And I will make a nation of the son of the slave woman also, because he is your offspring." In the same breath as the hard word comes a promise about the boy being sent away, and the reason given is Abraham's own paternity. God has not forgotten whose son Ishmael is.

Paul takes the two sons as a picture of two covenants — one born "according to the flesh," the product of human contrivance, and one born "through promise" — and tells the Galatians that they are children of the promise, like Isaac (Gal. 4:21–31). What human effort produces cannot inherit alongside what God gives. That is not a comment on Ishmael personally; it is the difference between a religion of achievement and the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: So Abraham rose early in the morning and took bread and a skin of water and gave it to Hagar, putting it on her shoulder, along with the child, and sent her away. And she departed and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba. When the water in the skin was gone, she put the child under one of the bushes. Then she went and sat down opposite him a good way off, about the distance of a bowshot, for she said, "Let me not look on the death of the child." And as she sat opposite him, she lifted up her voice and wept.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"So Abraham rose early in the morning and took bread and a skin of water and gave it to Hagar, putting it on her shoulder, along with the child, and sent her away."

It is a bleak sentence, and the details do not flatter him. The richest man in the region sends the mother of his firstborn into the desert with a loaf and a waterskin. He rises early, which he also does on the morning of chapter 22 — this man does hard things promptly — but there is no escaping how small the provision is.

"When the water in the skin was gone, she put the child under one of the bushes. Then she went and sat down opposite him a good way off, about the distance of a bowshot, for she said, 'Let me not look on the death of the child.' And as she sat opposite him, she lifted up her voice and wept."

A bowshot away, so that she would not have to watch him die, and not one step further, because she could not leave him. There is no more desolate picture of a mother anywhere in Scripture. She has been used, resented, driven out once already, and now she is watching the end of everything in a wilderness with no one to appeal to.

Genesis is not embarrassed to record that God's covenant family did this to her. The Bible has never been a promotional brochure for the people in it.

verseByVerse.quote: And God heard the voice of the boy, and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven and said to her, "What troubles you, Hagar? Fear not, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is. Up! Lift up the boy, and hold him fast with your hand, for I will make him into a great nation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And God heard the voice of the boy." Not hers — his. She is the one weeping out loud; the text says God heard the child. And the name says why: Ishmael means God hears, and the boy has carried that sentence in his name since before he was born (16:11). What was promised to Hagar at a spring seventeen years ago is being paid out in a desert.

"What troubles you, Hagar? Fear not, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is."

Three words that have carried a great many people through a bad night. Not where he ought to be. Not where you had hoped he would be by now. Not in church, not doing well, not safe, not sorted. Where he is — under a bush, in a desert, dying, outside the covenant household, nowhere near an altar. God heard him there.

Anyone praying for a child who has gone a long way off should stop on that clause. God does not require a person to get back to the right place before he will listen to them. He hears them where they are, which is the only place any of us has ever been heard from.

"Up! Lift up the boy, and hold him fast with your hand, for I will make him into a great nation." God does not merely comfort her; he gives her something to do, and it is to pick her son up. Grief that has sat down is often helped most by one concrete instruction.

verseByVerse.quote: Then God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. And she went and filled the skin with water and gave the boy a drink. And God was with the boy, and he grew up. He lived in the wilderness and became an expert with the bow. He lived in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother took a wife for him from the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water."

The well was already there. It did not appear; her eyes were opened. She had been sitting a bowshot from her dying son within reach of the water that would save him, and could not see it for exhaustion and grief.

Know that about despair, because it is one of its standard effects. It narrows the field of vision to the disaster and edits out everything else — the help that is available, the person who would come if asked, the provision that is already in place. God's answer here is not a new supply. It is sight.

"And God was with the boy, and he grew up." Twice now God has met this woman in a wilderness (16:7–13), and both times she was the person nobody in Abraham's camp was looking after. The God of Abraham is emphatically the God of the people Abraham's household failed, and he goes out to find them.

Ishmael becomes an archer in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother — an Egyptian — finds him an Egyptian wife. The line goes its own way, blessed and outside the covenant, exactly as God said.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–34 — The Covenant with Abimelech at Beersheba
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of Genesis 21 records Abraham's covenant with Abimelech at Beersheba — a political treaty that establishes Abraham's standing among the peoples of Canaan. Abimelech approaches Abraham not as a king condescending to a foreigner but as an equal seeking a binding agreement: 'God is with you in all that you do' (v.22). The recognition by the Philistine king that Abraham's prosperity is divinely given is a form of covenant blessing (12:3): the nations are acknowledging the covenant God through his servant.
verseByVerse.theology: The well at Beersheba becomes the site of covenant ratification: Abraham gives Abimelech seven ewe lambs as witness to his ownership of the well, and the place is named Beersheba ('well of the oath' or 'well of seven'). The planting of a tamarisk tree and calling on the name of the LORD establish Beersheba as a place of covenant worship — Abraham is marking the land with the worship of his God, consecrating the sites of his sojourn to the LORD.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes that the Beersheba covenant with Abimelech is the clearest example of the promise of 12:3 in action within the patriarchal period: the nations recognizing and seeking covenant relationship with the man God has blessed. The political treaty that results is not a compromise of the covenant but a fulfillment of it: in Abraham, a Philistine king finds the blessing of divine favor that he seeks.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army said to Abraham, "God is with you in all that you do. Now therefore swear to me here by God that you will not deal falsely with me or with my descendants or with my posterity, but as I have dealt kindly with you, so you will deal with me and with the land where you have sojourned." And Abraham said, "I will swear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"God is with you in all that you do." That is Abimelech speaking — the same king Abraham lied to in the previous chapter. Whatever damage the lie did, this man has watched Abraham for a year or two and drawn a conclusion about his God.

Then he asks for a treaty, and the wording has a point on it: "swear to me here by God that you will not deal falsely with me." Everybody in the tent knows why he is asking that particular thing of that particular man. A reputation, once dented, gets quoted back to you in every negotiation for years afterwards, and Abraham has no grounds for taking offence.

"And Abraham said, 'I will swear.'" No protest, no wounded dignity. He accepts the terms his own conduct made necessary, which is what genuine repentance looks like in practice long after the apology.

verseByVerse.quote: When Abraham reproved Abimelech about a well of water that Abimelech's servants had seized, Abimelech said, "I do not know who has done this thing; you did not tell me, and I have not heard of it until today."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When Abraham reproved Abimelech about a well of water that Abimelech's servants had seized." In that country a well was survival, and this is a serious grievance. Watch how he handles it, because it is a small masterclass.

He does not brood on it. He does not retaliate by quietly taking something else. He does not discuss it with everyone in the camp except the man concerned. He raises it with Abimelech directly, at the moment they are making a covenant, and he raises it plainly.

And Abimelech's answer is the reason it needed raising: "I do not know who has done this thing; you did not tell me, and I have not heard of it until today." He had no idea. His servants had done it and nobody had said a word.

That is Matthew 18:15 four thousand years early — if your brother sins against you, go and tell him, between you and him alone. An enormous proportion of what people carry for years as a settled grievance is something the other party has simply never been told, and would deal with in five minutes if they were.

verseByVerse.quote: So Abraham took sheep and oxen and gave them to Abimelech, and the two men made a covenant. Abraham set seven ewe lambs of the flock apart. And Abimelech said to Abraham, "What is the meaning of these seven ewe lambs that you have set apart?" He said, "These seven ewe lambs you will take from my hand, that this may be a witness for me that I dug this well." Therefore that place was called Beersheba, because there both of them swore an oath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The covenant is cut, and Abraham sets seven ewe lambs apart as a witness that he dug the well. The place is named Beersheba, which can mean the well of the oath or the well of seven, and the pun is deliberate. It becomes one of the fixed points of Israel's geography — the southern end of the phrase "from Dan to Beersheba."

It is a small commercial arrangement about water rights, and it matters more than it looks. Abraham has been promised this entire country by God, and here he is negotiating with a local king, paying livestock, and taking a receipt.

God's promises do not exempt his people from the ordinary work of getting on with neighbours, keeping agreements and settling disputes honestly and in writing. Faith in a future inheritance is no licence to be difficult about the present one, and a Christian who is careless with contracts because his real treasure is in heaven has misunderstood both.

verseByVerse.quote: So they made a covenant at Beersheba. Then Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army rose up and returned to the land of the Philistines. Abraham planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba and called there on the name of the LORD, the Everlasting God. And Abraham sojourned many days in the land of the Philistines.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Abraham planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba." A tamarisk is slow-growing, deep-rooted and very long-lived. A man well past a hundred does not plant one for his own shade. It is the act of somebody who intends his descendants to be standing here, and coming straight after the birth of Isaac, that is precisely what it means. He is planting for a boy who is barely walking.

"And called there on the name of the LORD, the Everlasting God." El Olam — the God of forever, the God of all the time there is. Of every title he might have used, this is the one he chooses now.

He has spent twenty-five years learning that God is never in a hurry and never late. The man who could not wait a decade and produced Ishmael stands at last under a sapling he will not live to see grown, and worships the God who does not run out of time.

21.theology:
The Children of Promise. Isaac’s birth is the pivot on which Paul’s theology of election turns in Romans 9: “it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring” (Rom. 9:8). Isaac’s birth establishes the principle that membership in God’s family is determined not by bloodline or merit but by the sovereign promise of God. Every believer is an Isaac — a child of the impossible, born of promise, belonging to a family constituted by grace from outside themselves.

The God Who Hears the Voiceless. The Hagar episode in chapter 21, like that of chapter 16, demonstrates that the God who chose Abraham is also the God who hears Ishmael (“God hears”) and sees Hagar (El Roi, “the God who sees”). The particular election of the covenant line does not exhaust God’s care for those outside it. The widow, the orphan, the foreign slave-woman abandoned in the wilderness — all are the special concern of the God whose covenant people are meant to embody that same concern for the overlooked.
21.examples:
Then: The birth of Isaac after decades of waiting would have resonated deeply with Israel’s own experience of long waiting for covenant fulfillment — the four hundred years in Egypt, the forty years in the wilderness, the centuries of waiting for the Davidic king. God’s faithfulness to Sarah was the paradigm and the promise of his faithfulness to Israel. What seemed impossible — a son for a ninety-year-old woman — was the same kind of impossible as redemption from Egypt or return from Babylon.

Now: The laughter of Sarah (v.6) is the appropriate response to every fulfilled promise of God — the joy that should characterize the Christian life, which is a life of accumulated “as he had said” and “as he had promised.” The church gathers weekly to celebrate the fulfilled promise: the seed of Abraham, the Son of promise, has come, has died, has risen. The weaning feast of Isaac is the distant shadow of the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9) — the celebration of the fulfilled promise that will make every previous joy look small.

22.title: The LORD Will Provide
22.text: <sup>1</sup>After these things God tested Abraham and said to him, "Abraham!" And he said, "Here I am."<sup>2</sup>He said, "Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains of which I shall tell you."<sup>3</sup>So Abraham rose early in the morning, saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and his son Isaac. And he cut the wood for the burnt offering and arose and went to the place of which God had told him.<sup>4</sup>On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw the place from afar.<sup>5</sup>Then Abraham said to his young men, "Stay here with the donkey; I and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you."<sup>6</sup>And Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son. And he took in his hand the fire and the knife. So they went both of them together.<sup>7</sup>And Isaac said to his father Abraham, "My father!" And he said, "Here I am, my son." He said, "Behold, the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?"<sup>8</sup>Abraham said, "God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son." So they went both of them together.<sup>9</sup>When they came to the place of which God had told him, Abraham built the altar there and laid the wood in order and bound Isaac his son and laid him on the altar, on top of the wood.<sup>10</sup>Then Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son.<sup>11</sup>But the angel of the LORD called to him from heaven and said, "Abraham, Abraham!" And he said, "Here I am."<sup>12</sup>He said, "Do not lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him, for now I know that you fear God, seeing you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me."<sup>13</sup>And Abraham lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, behind him was a ram, caught in a thicket by his horns. And Abraham went and took the ram and offered it up as a burnt offering instead of his son.<sup>14</sup>So Abraham called the name of that place, "The LORD will provide"; as it is said to this day, "On the mount of the LORD it shall be provided."<sup>15</sup>And the angel of the LORD called to Abraham a second time from heaven<sup>16</sup>and said, "By myself I have sworn, declares the LORD, because you have done this and have not withheld your son, your only son,<sup>17</sup>I will surely bless you, and I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore. And your offspring shall possess the gate of his enemies,<sup>18</sup>and in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed, because you have obeyed my voice."<sup>19</sup>So Abraham returned to his young men, and they arose and went together to Beersheba. And Abraham lived at Beersheba.<sup>20</sup>Now after these things it was told to Abraham, "Behold, Milcah also has borne children to your brother Nahor:<sup>21</sup>Uz his firstborn, Buz his brother, Kemuel the father of Aram,<sup>22</sup>Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel."<sup>23</sup>(Bethuel fathered Rebekah.) These eight Milcah bore to Nahor, Abraham's brother.<sup>24</sup>Moreover, his concubine, whose name was Reumah, bore Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah.
22.overview:
Genesis 22 — the Akedah, the binding of Isaac — is universally recognized as one of the most profound texts in all of human literature. God commands Abraham to take his only beloved son to Moriah and offer him as a burnt offering. Isaac is not merely Abraham’s son; he is the son of promise, the child through whom God had declared all his covenant purposes would be fulfilled. To sacrifice Isaac is to sacrifice the future, the covenant, and the promise itself. The command appears to contradict everything God has done and said for the past twenty-five years.

Abraham obeys. Hebrews 11:17–19 gives us the theological interpretation: “By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac... He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead.” Abraham’s obedience is grounded not in resignation but in resurrection faith: God had said the covenant would continue through Isaac; God had commanded the sacrifice of Isaac; therefore God would raise Isaac from the dead. He did not know how, but he knew who.

The theological weight of this chapter is immense. It is the most luminous prefiguration of Calvary in the Old Testament: a father, a son, a mountain (Moriah — the site of Solomon’s temple and, in Christian tradition, adjacent to Golgotha), a three-day journey, wood laid on the son’s back, the question “where is the lamb?”, and the divine provision of a substitute. The ram caught in the thicket dies in Isaac’s place; the lamb of God dies in ours. But unlike the story of Moriah, there is no angel’s hand to hold back the Father’s. The true Moriah is accomplished.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 22 is the theological summit of the Abraham narrative and one of the most profound passages in all of Scripture. God commands Abraham to offer Isaac as a burnt offering on Mount Moriah. Abraham obeys immediately and completely, proceeding to the point of raising the knife, at which moment the angel of the LORD intervenes and provides a ram as a substitute. The passage is both history and type: it is a real event in the life of a real man, and it is the most detailed Old Testament foreshadowing of the cross, in which God himself provides the sacrifice his own justice requires.
verseByVerse.theology: The theological density of the Akedah is extraordinary. It tests and reveals the depth of Abraham's faith — a faith that held the promise of resurrection (Heb. 11:19) against the command to sacrifice the promise-bearer. It establishes the principle of substitutionary atonement — a substitute provided at the moment of judgment, taking the place of the one who was condemned. It names the location 'the LORD will provide' (Yahweh Yireh), making the theology of divine provision into a permanent geographical testimony. And it is the context in which God swears the most comprehensive form of the covenant promise, now grounded in the oath of God himself.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller on Genesis 22: the Akedah is the passage in which Abraham's faith reaches its fullest expression — and also the passage in which the reader begins to see the shape of the gospel most clearly. The father who takes his beloved son, the three-day journey that culminates in a death-and-resurrection pattern, the wood carried by Isaac, the substitutionary ram — all these details are too specific and too theologically freighted to be coincidental. They are the shadow cast by the cross, moving backward through history. Calvin says of this passage that it is impossible to read it without being moved: a father, a son, a mountain, a knife — and a God who sees, who provides, who does not spare what is most precious.

verseByVerse.quote: After these things God tested Abraham and said to him, "Abraham!" And he said, "Here I am." He said, "Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains of which I shall tell you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"After these things God tested Abraham." The narrator tells the reader at the outset what Abraham will not learn for three days. This is a test, not a sentence; God has no intention of taking the boy. Genesis gives us that information deliberately, and Abraham climbing the mountain does not have it. Neither, usually, do we.

James is careful about the vocabulary: God tempts no one (James 1:13). A temptation is designed to make a man fall; a test is designed to show what is there. God is not fishing for information he lacks. He is bringing something in Abraham out into the open where it can be seen — by Abraham, by his household, by every reader since.

Then the command, and it is delivered with a cruelty of precision that no reader can miss. "Take your son" — he has two, and God is going to narrow it. "Your only son" — the only one that counts for the covenant. "Isaac" — the name is said out loud. "Whom you love" — the first appearance of the word love in the Bible, and it is used to sharpen a knife. Four phrases, each one closing an escape route, each one making it more impossible.

And the verb is lek-leka — go, get yourself out — the rare imperative God used only once before, at 12:1, when he told this man to leave his father's house. The two great commands of Abraham's life are tied together by one unusual word. The first cost him his past. This one asks for his future.

"To the land of Moriah... on one of the mountains of which I shall tell you." Not even the mountain is named yet. He is to set out for a region and be told the rest on the way, exactly as he set out from Haran for a land he had not been shown.

One thing must be said plainly, because the passage is sometimes used badly. God is not commending child sacrifice; he detests it, and says so in the strongest terms in the law that follows (Lev. 18:21; Deut. 12:31), and the whole point of this chapter is that he stops it. What is being asked is whether Abraham will hold anything back from the God who gave him everything he has — and the answer, in the end, is given by God himself on the same range of hills.

verseByVerse.quote: So Abraham rose early in the morning, saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and his son Isaac. And he cut the wood for the burnt offering and arose and went to the place of which God had told him. On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw the place from afar. Then Abraham said to his young men, "Stay here with the donkey; I and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"So Abraham rose early in the morning." There is no argument recorded. No counter-offer, no bargaining — and this is the man who haggled with God six times over Sodom (18:23–33). For a city of strangers he negotiated. For his own son he saddles the donkey before dawn.

Watch what he does with his hands: saddles the donkey, takes two young men, takes Isaac, cuts the wood. He cuts the wood himself, at home, before setting out. There would be trees on Moriah. A man who intends to obey does the preparation early and does not leave himself room to fail later for want of kindling.

"On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw the place from afar." Three days. Roughly fifty miles, walking, beside the boy, in silence. Whatever this cost him, it was not the cost of a moment's heroism. It was three days and two nights of lying awake next to his son with the knife in the pack.

"Stay here with the donkey; I and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you." Read the last four words. And come again to you. Not I will come again — we. He is not lying to the servants and he is not deceiving himself, because Hebrews tells us exactly what he was thinking: "He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back" (Heb. 11:19).

That is the hinge of his faith and it should be said plainly. Abraham had two certainties that could not both stand: God had said this boy was the covenant line (21:12), and God had said kill him. He did not resolve it by deciding God had not really meant one of them. He concluded that God would have to raise the dead — and he had no precedent for that whatever, because nobody in the history of the world had yet been raised. He invented resurrection faith on a fifty-mile walk, out of nothing but the reliability of God's word.

And he calls it worship. "I and the boy will go over there and worship." The hardest thing he will ever do is given the same name as the thing he does at an altar on an ordinary morning.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son. And he took in his hand the fire and the knife. So they went both of them together. And Isaac said to his father Abraham, "My father!" And he said, "Here I am, my son." He said, "Behold, the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?" Abraham said, "God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son." So they went both of them together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son." The son carries the wood for his own sacrifice up the hill. Christians have never been able to read that sentence without seeing another man carrying his own cross out of the same city (John 19:17), and the connection is not fanciful: the place is Moriah, and 2 Chronicles 3:1 says Solomon built the temple on Mount Moriah, which is Jerusalem.

"So they went both of them together." The phrase appears twice, here and at the end of verse 8, framing the only conversation between them that Scripture records. It is a phrase about companionship, and it is unbearable in the context.

"My father!" ... "Here I am, my son." That answer is the third time in this chapter Abraham says Here I am — to God in verse 1, to his son here, to the angel in verse 11. He is entirely available to God and entirely present to the boy at the same moment, which is a harder thing than either alone.

"Behold, the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?" Isaac has done the arithmetic. He is old enough to carry a load of firewood up a hill, which makes him a young man rather than a small child, and he has noticed the one thing missing.

"God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son." It is the truest sentence Abraham ever spoke and he did not know how true it was. Grammatically it can be read as an answer to the question or as an answer to the boy — God will provide the lamb, my son; or, God will provide the lamb: my son. Both readings hurt.

And it was not a ram that God finally provided for himself. Two thousand years later a man stood on a riverbank, saw Jesus walking towards him, and said, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" (John 1:29). Abraham's answer was left standing for twenty centuries and then paid in full.

verseByVerse.quote: When they came to the place of which God had told him, Abraham built the altar there and laid the wood in order and bound Isaac his son and laid him on the altar, on top of the wood. Then Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When they came to the place of which God had told him, Abraham built the altar there and laid the wood in order and bound Isaac his son and laid him on the altar, on top of the wood."

The verbs slow the scene down and make the reader watch every stage. Built. Laid in order. Bound. Laid on the altar. There is no way to hurry through those four actions, and Genesis does not let us.

The binding gives the passage its Jewish name — the Akedah, the binding — and it raises the question nobody asks. Isaac is a strong young man; his father is around a hundred and fifteen. If Isaac had not consented, there would have been no altar. Somewhere on that summit, off the page, a son agreed to be tied. The old covenant's clearest picture of the cross has a willing son in it as well as a giving father (cf. John 10:18).

"Then Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son." The sentence stops one word short. Everything up to the last possible instant has been done, and God's own verdict in the next verse is that it was as good as done: you have not withheld your son.

Obedience is tested at the point where it becomes irreversible. It is possible to intend a great deal and to be stopped, quite comfortably, by the fact that nobody ever required the last step. Abraham took the knife.

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel of the LORD called to him from heaven and said, "Abraham, Abraham!" And he said, "Here I am." He said, "Do not lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him, for now I know that you fear God, seeing you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But the angel of the LORD called to him from heaven and said, 'Abraham, Abraham!'" The doubled name is used in Scripture when the matter is urgent — Moses, Moses; Samuel, Samuel; Saul, Saul; Simon, Simon. It is God stopping a man mid-movement.

"Do not lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him." The prohibition is total and it is instant. Whatever else this chapter is about, God did not want the child dead, and every reader who has ever felt the horror of verse 10 is meant to feel the relief of verse 12.

"For now I know that you fear God, seeing you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me." God says now I know, and it does not mean he has learned something. Scripture is full of God speaking in the language of men — he smells an offering, he comes down to look at a tower. What has happened is that something real has been brought into the open. Abraham's fear of God was there before the mountain; now it has a history, a date and a witness, and it can never again be a matter of opinion.

That is what God does with tests. He does not run them to find out; he runs them to bring out — and generally what he brings out is stronger than the person being tested believed it was. Peter says the same of suffering: it is the testing of your faith, more precious than gold, and the point of it is that the genuine article should be found (1 Pet. 1:6–7).

verseByVerse.quote: And Abraham lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, behind him was a ram, caught in a thicket by his horns. And Abraham went and took the ram and offered it up as a burnt offering instead of his son. So Abraham called the name of that place, "The LORD will provide"; as it is said to this day, "On the mount of the LORD it shall be provided."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And Abraham lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, behind him was a ram, caught in a thicket by his horns." Behind him — where he had not been looking, where it had presumably been while he was building the altar. God's provision was already on the mountain before it was needed, and it was out of sight until the moment the knife went up.

"And Abraham went and took the ram and offered it up as a burnt offering instead of his son." There is the word the whole Bible turns on: instead. One life in the place of another, the innocent for the condemned, at the last possible moment, provided by God and not by the worshipper. Every sacrifice in Leviticus is a footnote to that phrase, and the whole doctrine of substitution is in it.

"So Abraham called the name of that place, 'The LORD will provide'" — Yahweh Yireh. The verb means to see; the sense is that God sees to it, God looks out the need and meets it. And note the tense he chooses: not the LORD provided, past, though he has just been rescued — but the LORD will provide. He names the place for the future.

"As it is said to this day, 'On the mount of the LORD it shall be provided.'" Moses, writing centuries later, records that the saying was still current. People were still repeating it, on that hill, waiting for the rest of it — and what was finally provided on the mount of the LORD was not a ram in a thicket. It was a Son who was not spared, on a hill outside the walls of the city built on that same range. Paul says it in the language of this chapter: God "did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all" (Rom. 8:32).

Abraham was stopped. God was not.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel of the LORD called to Abraham a second time from heaven and said, "By myself I have sworn, declares the LORD, because you have done this and have not withheld your son, your only son, I will surely bless you, and I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore. And your offspring shall possess the gate of his enemies, and in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed, because you have obeyed my voice." So Abraham returned to his young men, and they arose and went together to Beersheba. And Abraham lived at Beersheba.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"By myself I have sworn, declares the LORD." God swears an oath, and there is nothing higher to swear by, so he swears by himself. Hebrews makes a great deal of this precise moment: because God wanted to show "the unchangeable character of his purpose," he guaranteed it with an oath, so that "by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement" (Heb. 6:13–18). The promise and the oath are the two things. This verse is the oath.

The promise itself is not new — offspring like the stars, all the nations blessed — but it is enlarged (as the sand on the seashore) and it is now irrevocable. And notice the ground given: "because you have obeyed my voice." That does not make the covenant a wage. It was announced free in 12:1–3 and cut unilaterally in chapter 15 while Abraham slept. What obedience does here is what James says it does: it completes the faith and shows what it was (James 2:21–23). The tree is not the root, and the root is not in doubt when the fruit appears.

"And in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed." Paul puts his finger on the singular noun and says: that offspring "is Christ" (Gal. 3:16). Every Gentile who has ever come to God through Jesus arrived on the strength of a sentence spoken on a mountain to a shaking old man with a knife in his hand.

"So Abraham returned to his young men, and they arose and went together to Beersheba." Isaac is not mentioned. The narrative never brings him back down the hill in so many words, and the two of them are never recorded speaking to each other again. Whatever passed between father and son on Moriah, Genesis leaves it where it happened.

What the reader is left with is a hill, an altar, a substitute, and an oath — and a name for a place that is a promise in the future tense. On the mount of the LORD it shall be provided.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter concludes with a brief genealogical notice about Abraham's brother Nahor and his family. The list is not incidental; it serves the narrative purpose of introducing Rebekah (v.23, 'Bethuel fathered Rebekah') — the woman who will become Isaac's wife in chapter 24. The genealogy bridges the Akedah and the search for Isaac's wife: from the mountain of divine provision to the family that God has been preparing as the provision for Isaac's covenant continuity.
verseByVerse.theology: The placement of this genealogy immediately after the Akedah reflects the narrative logic of Genesis: the test that seemed to threaten the covenant promise is immediately followed by the report of a family that will carry the promise forward. God's provision of the ram at Moriah is followed by God's provision of a wife for Isaac — both provisions arranged before they are needed. The same divine foreknowledge that prepared the ram prepares Rebekah.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes that the genealogy of Nahor's family serves the structural function of transitioning from Abraham's great test (ch.22) to Sarah's death and burial (ch.23) to Isaac's marriage (ch.24) — the three episodes that will occupy the final years of Abraham's active role in the narrative. The covenant promise moves forward not through Abraham's dramatic interventions but through the ordinary biological and social processes of family life: birth, death, marriage.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after these things it was told to Abraham, "Behold, Milcah also has borne children to your brother Nahor: Uz his firstborn, Buz his brother, Kemuel the father of Aram, Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel." (Bethuel fathered Rebekah.) These eight Milcah bore to Nahor, Abraham's brother. Moreover, his concubine, whose name was Reumah, bore Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the highest point in the book of Abraham, a family newsletter. "Behold, Milcah also has borne children to your brother Nahor" — eight sons and four more by a concubine, in a household four hundred miles away in Mesopotamia.

Genesis does not put this here to change the subject. It is here for one clause, tucked in a bracket where a careless reader will miss it: "(Bethuel fathered Rebekah.)"

Abraham has just been promised offspring like the stars, and he has one unmarried son and a wife about to die. The obvious next question is where a wife for Isaac is going to come from — and before the question is asked, the answer has been born, named and reported by a passing traveller. She is a hundred and fifty miles up the road and neither she nor Abraham has any idea.

God's provision does not begin when we notice it. While Abraham was climbing Moriah, the girl who would carry the covenant into the next generation was growing up in Nahor's household, and the message about her arrives on the same page as the ram. He sees to it — Yahweh Yireh — and he has generally seen to it long before we look up.

22.theology:
Substitutionary Atonement. Genesis 22 is the Old Testament’s clearest picture of substitutionary atonement: the ram dies in the place of Isaac, who deserved death as a member of fallen humanity. The pattern is the scaffolding on which the entire sacrificial system is built and which is finally dismantled at the cross, where the scaffold is replaced by the reality it always pointed toward. The Lamb of God does not merely provide a substitute; he is the substitute, offered by the Father, provided by himself (“God will provide for himself the lamb”).

Resurrection Faith. Hebrews 11:19 identifies the theological ground of Abraham’s obedience as resurrection faith: he “considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.” Abraham did not understand what would happen on Moriah; he trusted the character of the God who had made the impossible promise and who could be trusted to keep it even through death. This is the faith that justifies: not certainty about outcomes but trust in the character of God, who is the God of resurrection.
22.examples:
Then: Moriah is identified in 2 Chronicles 3:1 as the site where Solomon built the temple — the same mountain where Abraham offered Isaac became the place of the permanent altar of Israel’s worship. The geography is theological: the place of the ultimate act of faith became the place of the ongoing memorial of that faith, and in Christian tradition the same hill of Moriah overlooks Golgotha, where the ultimate sacrifice was offered. The mountain carries the whole weight of redemptive history on its slopes.

Now: The Akedah asks every generation the same question: is there anything you love so much that you would not give it back to God? Keller identifies this as the test of the “Isaac” in every life — the person, career, dream, or relationship that has quietly moved from gift to god. The willingness to hold even the most precious things with open hands, trusting the God who gives and takes away, is the maturity that the Akedah both requires and produces. And for the preacher, Genesis 22 is the Old Testament text that most nakedly anticipates the cross — the Father’s love that withholds nothing, the Son who carries the wood, the Lamb who is provided.

23.title: A Burial Place for Sarah
23.text: <sup>1</sup>Sarah lived 127 years; these were the years of the life of Sarah.<sup>2</sup>And Sarah died at Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan, and Abraham went in to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her.<sup>3</sup>And Abraham rose up from before his dead and said to the Hittites,<sup>4</sup>"I am a sojourner and foreigner among you; give me property among you for a burying place, that I may bury my dead out of my sight."<sup>5</sup>The Hittites answered Abraham,<sup>6</sup>"Hear us, my lord; you are a prince of God among us. Bury your dead in the choicest of our tombs. None of us will withhold from you his tomb to hinder you from burying your dead."<sup>7</sup>Abraham rose and bowed to the Hittites, the people of the land.<sup>8</sup>And he said to them, "If you are willing that I should bury my dead out of my sight, hear me and entreat for me Ephron the son of Zohar,<sup>9</sup>that he may give me the cave of Machpelah, which he owns; it is at the end of his field. For the full price let him give it to me in your presence as property for a burying place."<sup>10</sup>Now Ephron was sitting among the Hittites, and Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham in the hearing of the Hittites, of all who went in at the gate of his city,<sup>11</sup>"No, my lord, hear me: I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it. In the sight of the sons of my people I give it to you. Bury your dead."<sup>12</sup>Then Abraham bowed down before the people of the land.<sup>13</sup>And he said to Ephron in the hearing of the people of the land, "But if you will, hear me: I give the price of the field. Accept it from me, that I may bury my dead there."<sup>14</sup>Ephron answered Abraham,<sup>15</sup>"My lord, listen to me: a piece of land worth four hundred shekels of silver, what is that between you and me? Bury your dead."<sup>16</sup>Abraham listened to Ephron, and Abraham weighed out for Ephron the silver that he had named in the hearing of the Hittites, four hundred shekels of silver, according to the weights current among the merchants.<sup>17</sup>So the field of Ephron in Machpelah, which was to the east of Mamre, the field with the cave that was in it and all the trees that were in the field, throughout its whole area, was made over<sup>18</sup>to Abraham as a possession in the presence of the Hittites, before all who went in at the gate of his city.<sup>19</sup>After this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah east of Mamre (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan.<sup>20</sup>The field and the cave that is in it were made over to Abraham as property for a burying place by the Hittites.
23.overview:
Genesis 23 is the first death in the patriarchal narrative and the first property transaction in the promised land. It is given extraordinary detail — the negotiation, the cultural conventions, the precise legal transfer — because it is theologically significant, not merely biographical. Abraham buys a cave and a field at Machpelah to bury Sarah: the first piece of the promised land becomes a burial ground. The covenant people enter their inheritance through death before they enter through life.

The chapter is a study in grief and faith held together. Abraham mourns and weeps for Sarah (v.2) — genuine, public, unashamed grief. He does not spiritualize or suppress his sorrow; he enters it fully. Then he rises and negotiates for a burial place — grief that acts, that makes provision, that refuses to be paralyzed. Biblical mourning is honest emotion followed by purposeful response. The Psalms of lament follow this same pattern.

The purchase of the cave of Machpelah becomes the family tomb: Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Leah will all be buried there (49:29–32). It is a small plot, purchased at considerable expense, in a land still occupied by others. But it is the first concrete installment on the promise — the first piece of Canaan held in Abraham’s name. Every burial in the cave of Machpelah is an act of faith: the patriarchs choose to be buried in the promised land rather than returning to Mesopotamia, because they believe the promise of the land will be fulfilled even for their bones.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Death of Sarah and the Purchase of Machpelah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 23 records the death of Sarah at 127 years and Abraham's purchase of the cave of Machpelah as a burial site — the first piece of the Promised Land that Abraham actually owns. The transaction is conducted with elaborate courtesy and formal legal precision, and its lengthy narration signals its importance: the purchase of Machpelah is both an act of mourning and an act of faith. Abraham insists on paying full price rather than accepting the land as a gift, creating an irrefutable legal record of his ownership of at least this piece of the land God has promised.
verseByVerse.theology: The theological significance of the Machpelah purchase is twofold. First, it is Abraham's most tangible act of faith in the land promise: he invests his own wealth in the promised land, purchasing a burial site in the land that is not yet his but will be. The purchase says, in the most concrete possible terms: I believe that my family will be here long enough to need burial land; I believe the promise enough to invest in its location. Second, the burial of Sarah in Machpelah establishes the patriarchs' permanent connection to the land: Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah, and Jacob will all be buried there (49:29–32), making it the physical anchor of the covenant family's connection to the land of promise.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes that the elaborate Hittite negotiation scene — with its offers of free land, its counter-insistence on purchase, its precise enumeration of the price and witnesses — reflects authentic ancient Near Eastern legal practice. The narrator's care to record every detail of the transaction is not pedantry but theology: the purchase is legally unassailable, and the legal precision is the point. When Israel returns to Canaan after Egypt, they will have clear legal title to at least this piece of land, purchased by their ancestor at full price in the presence of witnesses.

verseByVerse.quote: Sarah lived 127 years; these were the years of the life of Sarah. And Sarah died at Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan, and Abraham went in to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Sarah lived 127 years; these were the years of the life of Sarah." She is the only woman in the Bible whose age at death is recorded, and the sentence is deliberately formal, the way a stone is inscribed.

"And Abraham went in to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her." Two verbs, and the second is not the same as the first. Mourning was the public, formal business of a funeral in that world; weeping is what a man does. Genesis puts them side by side and lets the second one stand.

Take that as permission, if you have ever been told that strong faith means composure at a graveside. The father of the faithful, who had climbed Moriah without an argument and had God's own oath in his ears, sat down and cried for his wife. Grief is not a failure of trust. Jesus wept at a tomb he was about to empty (John 11:35).

They had been married the best part of a century, through Ur and Haran and Canaan, through Egypt and Gerar, through the tent and the barrenness and the laughter. Peter holds her up as an example to Christian women (1 Pet. 3:5–6), and Hebrews puts her in the roll of faith (Heb. 11:11). The last thing said about her in Genesis is that her husband wept.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abraham rose up from before his dead and said to the Hittites, "I am a sojourner and foreigner among you; give me property among you for a burying place, that I may bury my dead out of my sight." The Hittites answered Abraham, "Hear us, my lord; you are a prince of God among us. Bury your dead in the choicest of our tombs. None of us will withhold from you his tomb to hinder you from burying your dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I am a sojourner and foreigner among you; give me property among you for a burying place." He has lived in this country for sixty-two years and he still describes himself as a resident alien with no legal standing. He was promised the whole land; he owns none of it.

Hebrews takes those exact words as the key to the man: "he went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, living in tents... For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God" (Heb. 11:9–10). And it is the word the New Testament then hands to every Christian — "sojourners and exiles" (1 Pet. 2:11). A believer's discomfort in this world is not a sign that something has gone wrong. It is the correct sensation of somebody with a permanent address somewhere else.

"You are a prince of God among us. Bury your dead in the choicest of our tombs." The Hittites are warm and generous, and they offer him the free use of any grave he likes. Notice what that offer actually is: a loan, not a title. He would be burying Sarah in somebody else's ground, as a guest.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham rose and bowed to the Hittites, the people of the land. And he said to them, "If you are willing that I should bury my dead out of my sight, hear me and entreat for me Ephron the son of Zohar, that he may give me the cave of Machpelah, which he owns; it is at the end of his field. For the full price let him give it to me in your presence as property for a burying place." Now Ephron was sitting among the Hittites, and Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham in the hearing of the Hittites, of all who went in at the gate of his city, "No, my lord, hear me: I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it. In the sight of the sons of my people I give it to you. Bury your dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham bows — twice in this chapter, to men who are not his equals in anything except legal standing — and asks for one specific thing: the cave of Machpelah at the end of Ephron's field. And he uses a phrase he will repeat: "For the full price let him give it to me in your presence as property for a burying place."

He wants a purchase, in public, at the going rate, with the whole town at the gate as witnesses. Nothing about this is careless. He is buying a title that cannot later be disputed by anyone's heirs.

"No, my lord, hear me: I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it." Ephron offers it as a gift, loudly, in front of everybody — and adds a detail Abraham had not asked for. Abraham wanted the cave. Ephron offers the cave and the field, which in that culture carried a larger tax and feudal obligation with it. This is bargaining, and it is very smooth.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abraham bowed down before the people of the land. And he said to Ephron in the hearing of the people of the land, "But if you will, hear me: I give the price of the field. Accept it from me, that I may bury my dead there." Ephron answered Abraham, "My lord, listen to me: a piece of land worth four hundred shekels of silver, what is that between you and me? Bury your dead." Abraham listened to Ephron, and Abraham weighed out for Ephron the silver that he had named in the hearing of the Hittites, four hundred shekels of silver, according to the weights current among the merchants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I give the price of the field. Accept it from me." Abraham refuses the gift for the second time, and Ephron finally names his number: "a piece of land worth four hundred shekels of silver, what is that between you and me?"

It was a great deal, as it happens. Jeremiah later bought a field for seventeen shekels (Jer. 32:9), and David paid fifty for the threshing floor of Araunah (2 Sam. 24:24). Four hundred, tossed off as a trifle between friends, is a price that assumes the buyer will not haggle because he is burying his wife.

"Abraham listened to Ephron, and Abraham weighed out for Ephron the silver that he had named... four hundred shekels of silver, according to the weights current among the merchants." He pays it without a word of protest, in full, in public, weighed by the merchants' standard so that nobody could dispute the measure.

He has just been overcharged by a smiling man and he does not argue. There is a kind of strength in that which has nothing to do with weakness: he had decided what mattered, and it was not the money. A man who knows what he is buying does not always need to win the negotiation.

verseByVerse.quote: So the field of Ephron in Machpelah, which was to the east of Mamre, the field with the cave that was in it and all the trees that were in the field, throughout its whole area, was made over to Abraham as a possession in the presence of the Hittites, before all who went in at the gate of his city. After this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah east of Mamre (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan. The field and the cave that is in it were made over to Abraham as property for a burying place by the Hittites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The conveyance is recorded with the precision of a deed — the field, the cave in it, all the trees within its boundaries, made over in the presence of the Hittites, before all who went in at the gate of the city. Genesis spends four verses on the paperwork of one grave.

And here is why. This is the only piece of the promised land Abraham ever owns. He walked its length and breadth on God's instruction (13:17), he was told it would belong to his offspring for ever, and the sum total of his estate at the end of his life is a burial plot bought at an inflated price from a man who smiled while he named it.

So the purchase is an act of faith, and a public one. He could have taken Sarah's body back to Haran, where the family tomb was. He could have accepted the loan of a Hittite grave and kept his options open. Instead he buys ground in Canaan, at cost, with witnesses, and puts his wife in it — because his descendants are going to live here, and the deed says so.

Machpelah becomes the family grave. Abraham is buried there (25:9), and Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah, and Jacob, who makes his sons swear to carry his body four hundred miles out of Egypt to lie in it (49:29–32; 50:13). Four generations insisted on being buried in a field they did not otherwise own, in a country they did not yet possess.

That is what faith in a promise looks like when it comes to the practical arrangements. They were staking their bones on a word from God, and the only land any of them ever held was the piece they were laid in — waiting, as Hebrews says, for a better country and a city with foundations.

23.theology:
Grief and Faith. Genesis 23 refuses to separate genuine grief and genuine faith. Abraham mourns and weeps; he also rises and acts. The Psalms of lament demonstrate the same integration: honest expression of pain before God, followed by the refrain of trust. The New Testament does not eliminate grief but frames it differently: “we do not grieve as others do who have no hope” (1 Thess. 4:13). The hope of resurrection does not suppress the tears of loss; it gives them a horizon. Weeping now is real; the resurrection morning will be realer.

The Pilgrim Posture. Abraham’s self-description as “sojourner and foreigner” (v.4) becomes the defining identity of the people of God throughout Scripture. 1 Peter 2:11: “I urge you as sojourners and exiles to abstain from the passions of the flesh.” The pilgrim posture produces a particular kind of freedom: those who know they are passing through are not paralyzed by the conditions of their temporary residence. They can be generous because they are not accumulating; they can be bold because they are not protecting a permanent stake; they can love their neighbors without needing them to be their home.
23.examples:
Then: The elaborate negotiation protocol of Genesis 23 reflects the legal customs of ancient Hittite land transactions, which required public witnesses at the city gate and a formal oral and physical transfer of property. The legal precision was necessary to establish permanent ownership rather than leasehold rights. Abraham’s insistence on purchasing rather than accepting the land as a gift (vv.11–13) was strategic: a gift could be reclaimed, but a legal purchase could not. He was securing the first installment of the promise in the most durable form available.

Now: The chapter speaks to a culture that struggles with death. The modern West has largely removed death from public view, medicalized it, and deprived it of both the honest grief and the faith-framework that Genesis 23 models. Abraham mourns openly and specifically (he weeps for Sarah, not for death-in-general), then acts with faith-grounded purpose (buying a burial place in the promised land). The church that recovers the practice of honest, faith-framed grief for particular people will serve its culture better than one that either suppresses grief with spiritual clichés or drowns in it without hope.

24.title: A Wife for Isaac
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Abraham was old, well advanced in years. And the LORD had blessed Abraham in all things. <sup>2</sup>And Abraham said to his servant, the oldest of his household, “Put your hand under my thigh, <sup>3</sup>that I may make you swear by the LORD, the God of heaven and God of the earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I dwell, <sup>4</sup>but will go to my country and to my kindred, and take a wife for my son Isaac.” <sup>26</sup>The man bowed his head and worshiped the LORD <sup>27</sup>and said, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who has not forsaken his steadfast love and his faithfulness toward my master.” <sup>67</sup>Then Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother and took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her. And Isaac was comforted after his mother’s death.
24.overview:
Genesis 24 is the longest single narrative in Genesis — sixty-seven verses devoted to the search for Isaac’s wife. The length signals the importance: the covenant must continue through the right marriage, and the right marriage requires divine guidance, faithful obedience, and patient waiting. The servant’s mission is a model of what it looks like to seek God’s leading in a specific, practical, consequential decision.

The chapter is saturated with the language of divine providence. The servant prays for a specific sign (vv.12–14), receives the sign immediately (vv.15–20), interprets it as divine guidance (v.26), gives thanks (v.27), and reports it all to Rebekah’s family as God’s own doing (vv.48–49). The word “steadfast love” (hesed) appears in verse 27 — God’s covenant faithfulness, his loyal love, his unfailing commitment — as the theological explanation for what has just happened: the right woman at the right well at the right time is not coincidence but hesed.

The chapter also contains one of the Bible’s most tender ending lines: “Isaac... took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her. And Isaac was comforted after his mother’s death” (v.67). Love and comfort in a single sentence, grief resolved in grace. This is how God works: covenant purposes fulfilled, human hearts healed, the future secured through a love that is itself a gift of hesed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Abraham's Commission to His Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 24 is the longest chapter in Genesis and one of the most carefully crafted narratives in the entire Old Testament. Its subject is the finding of a wife for Isaac — the third link in the covenant chain (after Abraham and Isaac) — and its method is the providence of God operating through the faithful prayer and discernment of an unnamed servant. The chapter is both a wonderful story of answered prayer and a theological meditation on how God guides his people through ordinary human means: conversation, hospitality, gifts, and the quiet recognitions of a seeking heart.
verseByVerse.theology: Abraham's commission to his servant is structured as a covenant charge: the servant swears by the LORD, God of heaven and earth, that he will not take a wife for Isaac from the Canaanites but will go to Abraham's kin in Mesopotamia. The two negative conditions (no Canaanite wife, Isaac must not return to Mesopotamia) establish the parameters within which divine providence must work. The covenant bride must come from the covenant family; the covenant son must remain in the covenant land. These constraints are not arbitrary but theological: the purity of the covenant line and the centrality of the promised land are both at stake.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller on Genesis 24: the narrative of the servant's mission is one of the Bible's great stories of answered prayer. The servant prays specifically and experimentally — he asks God for a sign involving a specific action (offering water to the camels) — and the answer arrives before he has finished praying. The story teaches that specific prayer, prayed in faith, receives specific answers. It also teaches that God's guidance often operates through the recognition of his hand in ordinary events: the servant recognizes Rebecca's character through her hospitality before he knows who she is.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Abraham was old, well advanced in years. And the LORD had blessed Abraham in all things. And Abraham said to his servant, the oldest of his household, who had charge of all that he had, "Put your hand under my thigh,
verseByVerse.commentary: Abraham is old — the covenant patriarch has reached the end of his active ministry. "The LORD had blessed Abraham in all things" — a summary of the entire covenant journey: every area of life has received the covenant blessing. The servant who receives this commission is the most trusted member of the household, the one who has charge of all Abraham has — likely Eliezer of Damascus (15:2), the servant whose potential heirship had motivated Abraham's question to God in chapter 15. Now the servant's mission is to secure the true heir's future. "Put your hand under my thigh" — the most solemn form of ancient Near Eastern oath: the hand placed near the organ of generation, invoking the covenant of procreation and the future of the family line. To swear by Abraham's thigh is to swear by the covenant promise of offspring. Waltke notes that the oath-gesture is appropriate to the mission: the servant swears by the covenant sign (procreation) to serve the covenant purpose (a wife for the covenant heir).

verseByVerse.quote: that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell, but will go to my country and to my kindred, and take a wife for my son Isaac."
