When the men of the place asked him about his wife, he said, “She is my sister,” for he feared to say, “My wife,” thinking, “lest the men of the place should kill me because of Rebekah,” because she was attractive in appearance. ... And Isaac sowed in that land and reaped in the same year a hundredfold. The LORD blessed him, and the man became rich, and gained more and more until he became very wealthy. ... And Isaac dug again the wells of water that had been dug in the days of Abraham his father, which the Philistines had stopped after the death of Abraham. ... And the LORD appeared to him the same night and said, “I am the God of Abraham your father. Fear not, for I am with you and will bless you and multiply your offspring for my servant Abraham’s sake.”
26.overview:
Genesis 26 is the only chapter in Genesis focused solely on Isaac, and it reads as a concentrated echo of his father Abraham’s story. The same covenant is confirmed, the same famine tests, the same wife-sister deception recurs, the same wells are contested. The repetitions are not literary laziness but theological design: the blessing of Abraham passes to Isaac not through Isaac’s moral superiority but through divine faithfulness alone.

Isaac’s failures mirror Abraham’s almost exactly. He lies about his wife, just as Abraham did twice. Yet God protects Rebekah, corrects Abimelech, and continues the covenant without condition. Grace runs not through the perfection of the patriarchs but through the faithfulness of God. Keller observes that God’s persistent commitment to these flawed men is the ground of all hope for equally flawed readers.

The re-digging of Abraham’s wells is rich with symbolic weight. Isaac does not pioneer new territory; he recovers what his father had opened. The wells are named Esek (contention), Sitnah (accusation), and finally Rehoboth (“God has made room for us”). The Christian life is often this—recovering grace already available, moving through conflict and opposition toward the spaciousness that God promises. The covenant confirmed to Isaac at Beersheba (“I am with you”) is the foundation of all blessing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Isaac and Abimelech: The Covenant Repeated
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 26 is the only chapter in Genesis devoted primarily to Isaac — the middle patriarch, sandwiched between the towering figures of Abraham and Jacob. The chapter is structurally parallel to several key moments in Abraham's life: famine drives Isaac toward Egypt, God redirects him to Gerar, Isaac deceives Abimelech about Rebekah (as Abraham deceived him about Sarah), Isaac prospers greatly, and a dispute over wells leads to a covenant at Beersheba. The parallels are deliberate: Isaac is presented as the faithful carrier of the covenant promises, living out his father's story in his own generation.
verseByVerse.theology: The theological center of chapter 26 is God's renewal of the covenant with Isaac in vv.2–5 and again in vv.23–25. The repetition of the promise — offspring like stars, all nations blessed — reassures the reader that the covenant has not died with Abraham but continues with the same vigor and the same divine commitment through the next generation. Isaac is not a lesser Abraham but the covenant's continuation: the same God, the same promise, the same land, the same pattern of divine guidance through ordinary life.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller on Genesis 26: Isaac's story is the story of faithfulness in the middle. He is not the founding patriarch who left everything (Abraham) or the wrestler who became Israel (Jacob). He is the man who received the covenant, held it, and passed it on. The covenant does not always require dramatic encounters; sometimes it requires steady faithfulness in the ordinary — digging wells, resolving disputes, worshiping in the places your father worshiped. Isaac's quiet fidelity is as necessary to the covenant story as Abraham's dramatic obedience.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a famine in the land, besides the former famine that was in the days of Abraham. And Isaac went to Gerar to Abimelech king of the Philistines. And the LORD appeared to Isaac and said, "Do not go down to Egypt; dwell in the land of which I shall tell you.
verseByVerse.commentary: A second famine in the land — the first drove Abraham to Egypt (ch.12), and Isaac naturally moves toward Gerar, perhaps intending to go further south to Egypt. God intervenes before he reaches Egypt: "do not go down to Egypt." The command is specific and immediate: Isaac must stay in the land of promise, even when the land is failing. The divine prohibition does not explain itself; it simply redirects. Trust, not explanation, is what the covenant moment requires. "Dwell in the land of which I shall tell you" — the same open-ended guidance that characterized Abraham's original call (12:1: "go to the land that I will show you"). Isaac is being asked to do the same thing his father did: obey an open-ended divine directive without knowing the destination in full detail. Waltke notes that God's prohibition of Egypt preserves the covenant principle that the promised land is the place of promise, even when it is the place of hardship.

verseByVerse.quote: Sojourn in this land, and I will be with you and will bless you, for to you and to your offspring I will give all these lands, and I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham your father. I will multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and will give to your offspring all these lands. And in your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed,
verseByVerse.commentary: The covenant is renewed to Isaac in full: divine presence ("I will be with you"), blessing, land for Isaac and his offspring, and the oath sworn to Abraham now applied explicitly to Isaac. The three elements of the Abrahamic covenant — land, offspring, blessing to all nations — are all present. "I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham your father" — the covenant with Isaac is not a new covenant but the continuation of the old one. Isaac has inherited the promise exactly as it was given, not a derivative version. The stars-of-heaven promise extends to Isaac's offspring, and the all-nations blessing that Paul identifies as the gospel (Gal. 3:8) passes through Isaac to the world. Wenham notes that the divine speech to Isaac in vv.2–5 is the most comprehensive renewal of the Abrahamic covenant in the patriarchal period, deliberately echoing the oaths sworn to Abraham at Moriah (22:16–18).

verseByVerse.quote: because Abraham obeyed my voice and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws." So Isaac settled in Gerar.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Because Abraham obeyed my voice" — the continuation of the covenant in Isaac's generation is grounded in Abraham's faithfulness. This is not works-salvation for Isaac; it is the covenant logic of inherited blessing: the obedience of the founder creates the inheritance for the heirs. Abraham kept God's charge, commandments, statutes, and laws — the language is remarkably Mosaic (Deut. 11:1 uses the same fourfold formulation), as if the narrator is showing that Abraham, centuries before Sinai, lived by the spirit of the covenant that would be formally codified there. Isaac settles in Gerar: the covenant son, redirected from Egypt, dwelling in Philistine territory at God's direction. Kidner notes that the grounding of Isaac's blessing in Abraham's obedience is a reminder that faithfulness in one generation creates inheritance for the next — a principle that cuts both ways in the larger biblical narrative.

verseByVerse.quote: When the men of the place asked him about his wife, he said, "She is my sister," for he feared to say, "My wife," thinking, "lest the men of the place should kill me because of Rebekah," because she was attractive in appearance. When he had been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines looked out of a window and saw Isaac laughing with Rebekah his wife.
verseByVerse.commentary: The same deception — same location, same king's name, same fear, same exposure — that Abraham practiced twice (12:13; 20:2) is now practiced by Isaac. The repetition is pointed: the covenant heir has inherited his father's faith but also his father's fear. The fear is understandable (Rebekah is beautiful and could attract dangerous attention) but the deception is not faithful. "Laughing with Rebekah" — the Hebrew (metsaheq, playing, laughing) is the same root as Isaac's name (yitzhaq) and as Ishmael's provocative action (21:9); here it likely indicates intimate play, the behavior of a husband with his wife, not of a brother with his sister. Abimelech's observation through a window exposes the lie. Wenham notes that Isaac's deception of Abimelech is presented more briefly and with less theological elaboration than Abraham's, suggesting that the narrator is cataloging a pattern rather than celebrating a moment of great faith.

verseByVerse.quote: So Abimelech called Isaac and said, "Behold, she is your wife. How then could you say, 'She is my sister'?" Isaac said to him, "Because I thought, 'Lest I die because of her.'" Abimelech said, "What is this you have done to us? One of the people might easily have lain with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us."
verseByVerse.commentary: Abimelech confronts Isaac directly and Isaac's explanation is honest but incomplete: he feared death. Abimelech's rebuke is the same as his rebuke of Abraham (20:9): you endangered us, you nearly brought guilt on us through no fault of our own. The moral high ground occupied by the pagan king over the covenant patriarch is one of the most uncomfortable recurring patterns in Genesis. Abimelech's concern — guilt — reflects his own moral seriousness; he does not want to sin inadvertently. Isaac's deception has put the entire Philistine community in moral jeopardy. Waltke notes that the rebuke pattern (pagan king rebuking covenant patriarch for endangering him through deception) appears three times in Genesis (12:18; 20:9; 26:9) — a pattern that should produce repentance in both the characters and the readers who recognize themselves in the pattern.

verseByVerse.quote: So Abimelech warned all the people, saying, "Whoever touches this man or his wife shall surely be put to death." And Isaac sowed in that land and reaped in the same year a hundredfold. The LORD blessed him,
verseByVerse.commentary: Abimelech protects Isaac and Rebekah with a royal decree — the same protective response Abraham received (20:6–7). The protection is effective and immediate. Then: Isaac sows in Gerar and reaps a hundredfold. The covenant blessing on Isaac is expressed in agricultural abundance: hundredfold return in a famine year is miraculous. Jesus will use the hundredfold return as the image of fruitful reception of the word (Mark 4:20). "The LORD blessed him" — the narrator's theological summary of what is about to be described in detail: the blessing of the covenant God is the explanation for the inexplicable prosperity. Kidner notes that the sequence — deception exposed, protected by pagan king, then blessed with miraculous harvest — is characteristic of Genesis's pattern: human failure does not void divine blessing, but divine blessing does not endorse human failure.

verseByVerse.quote: and the man became rich, and gained more and more until he became very wealthy. He had possessions of flocks and herds and many servants, so that the Philistines envied him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The prosperity accumulates progressively: rich, then very wealthy, then possessing flocks, herds, and servants on a scale that provokes Philistine envy. The envying of the covenant patriarch by the surrounding nations is the fulfillment of the covenant promise (12:2: "I will make your name great") and the beginning of the covenant conflict (12:3: "whoever curses you I will curse"). Isaac's wealth is not inherited from Abraham (though he received all Abraham had, 25:5) but generated in his own generation by divine blessing on his own labor. The hundredfold harvest and the growing flocks are the result of the same covenant blessing on the work of Isaac's hands that operated on the work of Abraham's hands. Waltke notes that the Philistines' envy is the geopolitical expression of the covenant blessing: nations notice the prosperity of the covenant people and react with a mixture of recognition and resentment.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Philistines had stopped up and filled with earth all the wells that his father's servants had dug in the days of Abraham his father. And Abimelech said to Isaac, "Go away from us, for you are much mightier than we."
verseByVerse.commentary: The Philistines fill Abraham's wells with earth — an act of territorial aggression and covenant hostility. Wells in the Negev are life itself; destroying wells is destroying the possibility of habitation. The filling of Abraham's wells attempts to erase the previous generation's presence in the land — to make it as if Abraham had never been there. Abimelech's expulsion request is simultaneously an acknowledgment of Isaac's power ("you are much mightier than we") and a response to the covenant threat his prosperity represents. The king who protected Isaac from his own people now asks him to leave because Isaac has become too strong. Wenham notes that the filling of the wells and the expulsion request together represent the first extended conflict between the covenant family and the peoples of the land — a conflict that will recur throughout the patriarchal and conquest periods.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–35 — Wells, Beersheba, and the Covenant with Abimelech
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaac leaves Gerar and camps in the Valley of Gerar, where he reopens Abraham's wells and digs new ones. The Philistines dispute the first two wells — Esek (contention) and Sitnah (enmity) — but leave the third alone: Isaac names it Rehoboth, 'broad places,' declaring that God has made room for him. At Beersheba, God appears again and renews the covenant; Isaac builds an altar. Abimelech then comes to seek a treaty with Isaac, recognizing that the LORD is with him. The chapter ends with the report of Esau's Hittite wives, which causes grief to Isaac and Rebekah.
verseByVerse.theology: The well episodes are a quiet theology of perseverance and divine provision. Isaac does not fight for the disputed wells; he moves on. He does not claim the land by covenant right but waits for the space God opens. Rehoboth — 'broad places' — names what God does for those who trust him through conflict: he makes room, not by the covenant heir's aggression but by divine arrangement. The covenant with Abimelech, which mirrors Abraham's covenant in ch.21, confirms that Isaac's prosperity has the same divine origin and the same international recognition as his father's.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham on the well episodes: Isaac's willingness to yield the disputed wells rather than fight for them is a model of covenant patience. He invests labor in digging (three wells), loses the investment twice, and moves on rather than escalating. The third well — unopposed — is named for the room God has made. The pattern teaches that the covenant heir receives the land not through his own force but through God's provision of space. The wells are a parable of inheritance: dug by human labor, contested by human opposition, and ultimately given by divine arrangement.

verseByVerse.quote: So Isaac departed from there and encamped in the Valley of Gerar and settled there. And Isaac dug again the wells of water that had been dug in the days of Abraham his father, which the Philistines had stopped after the death of Abraham. And he gave them the names that his father had given them.
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaac leaves Gerar without resistance and camps in the Valley of Gerar. His first act is to reopen Abraham's wells — the very wells the Philistines had deliberately stopped up (v.15). The reopening of Abraham's wells is a covenant act: Isaac is reclaiming his father's presence in the land, restoring the infrastructure of covenant life. He gives them the same names Abraham gave them: continuity of memory, continuity of covenant. The covenant heir does not rename his inheritance but maintains the names of the father who established it. Waltke notes that the naming continuity is theologically significant: Isaac is not starting over but continuing — the same covenant, the same land, the same wells, the same names. His faithfulness is expressed through restoration rather than innovation.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Isaac's servants dug in the valley and found there a well of spring water, the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac's herdsmen, saying, "The water is ours." So he called the name of the well Esek, because they contended with him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaac's servants dig a new well — a well of spring water (living water, flowing water, not a cistern) — and immediately the Philistine herdsmen claim it: "the water is ours." The claim has no legal basis but it has practical force. Isaac's response is not legal argument or physical resistance but naming: he calls the well Esek (contention) and moves on. The naming is important: Isaac is not forgetting the injustice or pretending it did not happen. He is marking it — recording the contention in the well's name — and leaving it to God's assessment. The covenant heir who was promised the land does not take the land by force but waits for God to give it in his own way. Kidner notes that Isaac's naming of the disputed wells rather than fighting for them reflects the same covenant patience that characterized Abraham at his best.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they dug another well, and they quarreled over that also, so he called its name Sitnah. And he moved from there and dug another well, and they did not quarrel over it. So he called its name Rehoboth, saying, "For now the LORD has made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land."
verseByVerse.commentary: A second well, a second quarrel: Sitnah (enmity, the same root as the accuser, Satan). Then a third well — and the Philistines do not dispute it. Rehoboth: "broad places," the space God has made. "For now the LORD has made room for us" — Isaac attributes the absence of contention not to his own strategy or to Philistine goodwill but to divine action: God has made room. The theological interpretation of circumstance is characteristic of covenant faith: ordinary events (an uncontested well) are read as evidence of divine provision. "We shall be fruitful in the land" — the covenant promise of fruitfulness (1:28; 12:2; 17:6) is anticipated in the opening of this space. Isaac's naming of Rehoboth is his theology in miniature: God makes room; covenant faithfulness waits for the room God makes. Waltke notes that the three-well sequence (Esek, Sitnah, Rehoboth) traces Isaac's spiritual journey from contention through enmity to the broad place of divine provision.

verseByVerse.quote: From there he went up to Beersheba. And the LORD appeared to him the same night and said, "I am the God of Abraham your father. Fear not, for I am with you and will bless you and multiply your offspring for my servant Abraham's sake."
verseByVerse.commentary: At Beersheba — the site of Abraham's covenant with Abimelech and his altar to El Olam (21:31–33) — God appears to Isaac at night. The location is significant: God meets Isaac where Abraham worshiped. "Fear not" — the covenant comfort given to Abraham (15:1) is given to the covenant heir. The basis of the blessing is stated explicitly: "for my servant Abraham's sake." The covenant commitment runs through Abraham to Isaac; Isaac's security rests on Abraham's faithfulness before God, just as the covenant's continuation rested on Abraham's obedience (26:5). This is not works-righteousness but covenant inheritance: the faithfulness of the founding member of the covenant family creates inheritance for the heirs. Wenham notes that God's appearance at Beersheba to Isaac completes the covenant geography: the place Abraham consecrated with worship now receives the divine confirmation that the covenant continues through his son.

verseByVerse.quote: So he built an altar there and called upon the name of the LORD and pitched his tent there. And there Isaac's servants dug a well. Abimelech went to him from Gerar with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his army.
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaac's response to the divine appearance is identical to Abraham's characteristic response: an altar, calling on the name of the LORD, pitching his tent. The tent marks temporary residence; the altar marks permanent worship. Isaac consecrates Beersheba as a site of covenant worship, continuing what Abraham began (21:33). Then Abimelech arrives from Gerar — the same king (or his successor) with his adviser and commander. The arrival of Philistine leadership at the moment Isaac is establishing covenant worship is a providential convergence: the nations are drawn to the place where the covenant God is honored. Kidner notes that the pairing of altar-building and Abimelech's arrival echoes the pattern of Abraham: covenant worship and international recognition arrive together, each confirming the other.

verseByVerse.quote: Isaac said to them, "Why have you come to me, seeing that you hate me and have sent me away from you?" They said, "We see plainly that the LORD is with you. So we said, let there be a sworn oath between us, between you and us, and let us make a covenant with you,
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaac's question is direct and honest: "you hate me and sent me away" — he names the history without bitterness but without pretense. Abimelech's answer is equally direct: "we see plainly that the LORD is with you." The Philistine king's recognition of divine favor on Isaac is the same recognition Abimelech showed toward Abraham (21:22: "God is with you in all that you do"). The nations see what the covenant heir himself may sometimes doubt: the LORD's visible accompaniment. The proposal for a covenant between equals is grounded entirely in Isaac's divine favor: not in his military power, not in his diplomatic skill, but in the LORD's evident presence with him. Waltke notes that Abimelech's request fulfills the covenant promise of 12:2–3: the nations seek relationship with the covenant people because of the God who is with them.

verseByVerse.quote: that you will do us no harm, just as we have not touched you and have done to you nothing but good and have sent you away in peace. You are now the blessed of the LORD." So he made them a feast, and they ate and drank.
verseByVerse.commentary: Abimelech frames the proposed covenant in terms of mutual non-harm and acknowledges that he has dealt well with Isaac (he did protect him, v.11, and did send him away in peace, v.16). "You are now the blessed of the LORD" — the declaratory sentence that confirms everything: Abimelech and his men have come because they recognize that Isaac's blessing is divine, not human. Isaac's response is covenant hospitality: a feast. He does not rehearse grievances (the filled wells, the expulsion); he hosts. The feast is both covenant ratification and covenant generosity: Isaac hosts the people who displaced him with the abundance that God gave him in the land they forced him to leave. Wenham notes that Isaac's feast for Abimelech is an act of magnanimous covenant faithfulness: receiving as a guest the man who expelled you is grace, not naivety.

verseByVerse.quote: In the morning they rose early and exchanged oaths. And Isaac sent them on their way, and they departed from him in peace. That same day Isaac's servants came and told him about the well that they had dug and said to him, "We have found water." He called it Shibah; therefore the name of the city is Beersheba to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The covenant is sworn in the morning — both parties rise early, exchange oaths, and part in peace. The early rising mirrors Abraham's pattern of early-morning covenant faithfulness (21:14; 22:3). The departure "in peace" (shalom) echoes the promise of 15:15 (Abraham will go to his fathers in peace) — the covenant produces peace between peoples as the expression of divine blessing. Then, the same day: the servants report finding water in the new well. The divine provision is immediate and specific: the covenant is sworn in the morning; water is found the same day. Waltke notes that the simultaneous arrival of covenant peace (with Abimelech) and water (from the new well) on the same day is the narrative's way of showing that God's blessing is comprehensive — reconciliation and provision arrive together.

Shibah ("oath") names the new well and reinforces the name of Beersheba ("well of the oath"). The city's name is confirmed and explained for the second time in Genesis (first in 21:31): the narrator anchors the present place-name in the covenant events of the patriarchal period, giving the reader a theological geography.

verseByVerse.quote: When Esau was forty years old, he took Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite to be his wife, and Basemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite, and they made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here the narrative turns toward the next generation's conflict: Esau at forty marries two Hittite women. The age mirrors Isaac's age at marriage (25:20) but the choice is opposite: Isaac married within the covenant family; Esau marries Canaanites, the forbidden alternative. Wenham notes that the contrast between Isaac's faithful marriage (following Abraham's explicit instruction) and Esau's Canaanite marriages is the narrative preparation for the covenant conflict that will drive the Jacob narrative.

The simple, devastating verdict: the Hittite wives made life bitter (the Hebrew is lit. "a bitterness of spirit") for Isaac and Rebekah. The household is divided by the marriages of the elder son: the covenant parents are grieved; the covenant future is threatened. This grief is the emotional and theological context for Rebekah's later preference for Jacob and her manipulation of the blessing (ch.27) — she is not merely playing favorites but protecting the covenant from the consequences of Esau's contempt for covenant values. The bitterness of Isaac and Rebekah over Esau's marriages parallels the bitterness that Esau's sale of his birthright created: a man who despised the birthright (25:34) also despised the covenant marriage requirement. Kidner notes that the final verse of chapter 26 is a quiet indictment: Esau's choices create suffering for those who love him — a pattern that covenant-contempt always follows.

26.theology:
Genesis 26 is a chapter about the transmission of grace. The Abrahamic covenant does not pass to Isaac because of Isaac’s righteousness; it passes because God is faithful to his word. The patriarchal narratives consistently resist the idea that God’s blessing tracks human virtue. Isaac repeats his father’s sin; God’s promise is repeated unchanged. This is the logic of sovereign grace—the covenant rests on the Giver, not the recipient.

Wenham notes that the sevenfold repetition of “bless/blessing” in this chapter is intentional. Blessing is the theological key. And the blessing flows despite sin, through sojourning, across contested wells, into Philistine recognition of divine favor. The nations around Isaac already see what Isaac himself is learning: the LORD is with this man. This anticipates Paul’s argument in Romans 4—Abraham’s descendants inherit not through law-keeping but through faith in the God who gives life to the dead (Rom 4:17).
26.examples:
The re-digging of wells speaks to spiritual renewal in every generation. Every generation of the church must re-excavate the wells of grace—the gospel, the Scriptures, the practices of prayer and worship—that previous generations opened but that can become stopped up by worldly pressure, compromise, or neglect. Reformation is not invention; it is recovery.

Isaac’s persistence through Esek and Sitnah to Rehoboth models the patience of faith. The promise of “room” is not immediate; it comes through sustained trust in the God who promised it. Keller preaches this as the shape of the Christian life: not a straight line upward, but a journey through opposition toward the spaciousness that only God provides.

27.title: Jacob Receives the Blessing
27.text: When Isaac was old and his eyes were dim so that he could not see, he called Esau his older son and said to him, “My son”; and he answered, “Here I am.” He said, “Behold, I am old; I do not know the day of my death. Now then, take your weapons, your quiver and your bow, and go out to the field and hunt game for me, and prepare for me delicious food, such as I love, and bring it to me so that I may eat, and my soul may bless you before I die.” ... Rebekah said to her son Jacob, “I heard your father speak to your brother Esau. ... Obey my voice as I command you. Go to the flock and bring me two good young goats, so that I may prepare from them delicious food for your father, such as he loves. And you shall bring it to your father to eat, so that he may bless you before he dies.” ... Then his father Isaac said to him, “Come near and kiss me, my son.” So he came near and kissed him. And Isaac smelled the smell of his garments and blessed him and said, “See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed!” ... When Esau heard the words of his father, he cried out with an exceedingly great and bitter cry and said to his father, “Bless me, even me also, O my father!”
27.overview:
Genesis 27 is the most morally complex chapter in the patriarchal narrative. Every major character fails: Isaac resolves to bless Esau against the divine oracle (25:23); Rebekah schemes; Jacob deceives his dying father with deliberate cruelty; Esau’s grief is real but comes too late. Yet through this tangle of human sin and family dysfunction, the divine purpose announced before the boys were born is accomplished. The blessing passes to Jacob.

The chapter is a study in how God works not by circumventing human sinfulness but through it and despite it. This does not excuse the participants. Keller notes that both Jacob and Rebekah suffer severely for this moment: Jacob flees and never sees his mother again; Rebekah never holds her favorite son again. Sin has consequences even when God overrules it for his purposes.

Theologically, the irrevocability of the spoken blessing carries enormous weight. Isaac says, “I have blessed him—yes, and he shall be blessed” (v.33). Words of covenant blessing, once given, cannot be recalled. This points forward to the irreversibility of God’s own word and promise. The New Testament will read Esau’s tears as the pattern of those who despise what is holy and later find “no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears” (Heb 12:17).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 27 is one of the most psychologically complex and theologically demanding chapters in Genesis. Isaac, old and nearly blind, intends to give the covenant blessing to Esau. Rebekah, having received the oracle that the elder would serve the younger (25:23), conspires with Jacob to deceive Isaac and secure the blessing for Jacob. Jacob receives the blessing through deception, Esau arrives too late and receives a subordinate word, and the chapter ends with Esau's murderous rage and Rebekah's plan to send Jacob away. No one in this chapter behaves well: Isaac ignores the divine oracle; Rebekah manipulates; Jacob lies repeatedly; Esau despises covenant values but grieves their loss.
verseByVerse.theology: The theological puzzle of Genesis 27 is that the right outcome — Jacob receiving the covenant blessing — is achieved through the wrong means: deception, manipulation, and betrayal. Reformed commentators have consistently noted that God's sovereign purpose is achieved not because of human scheming but in spite of it. The divine oracle of 25:23 would have been fulfilled regardless of Rebekah's intervention; her deception was unnecessary and its consequences (Jacob's long exile, Rebekah's permanent separation from her son) were painful. God's purposes cannot be frustrated — but human sin in the service of God's purposes is still sin, and it still has consequences.
verseByVerse.examples: Waltke on Genesis 27: the chapter is a study in the difference between God's sovereign will (which cannot be frustrated) and God's moral will (which human beings regularly violate). Rebekah knows the oracle; she acts to secure its fulfillment through deception rather than trusting God to accomplish it in his own way. Her deception succeeds in its immediate goal but fails in its larger purpose: she will never see Jacob again after he flees Esau's rage. The chapter is not a model of how to obtain the covenant blessing but a model of how not to: faith trusts the oracle without engineering the outcome.

verseByVerse.quote: When Isaac was old and his eyes were dim so that he could not see, he called Esau his older son and said to him, "My son"; and he answered, "Here I am." He said, "Behold, I am old; I do not know the day of my death.
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaac is old, dim-eyed, and aware of his mortality. His intention to give the blessing now — before he dies — is understandable; the fear of dying before arranging the succession is universal. But the blindness is not merely physical: Isaac knows the oracle of 25:23 ("the elder shall serve the younger") and is proceeding to bless Esau anyway. His attachment to Esau (25:28, "Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his game") has blinded him spiritually as well as physically. "Behold, I am old; I do not know the day of my death" — the existential awareness that death is approaching motivates the urgency but does not excuse the theological error. Waltke notes that Isaac's imminent-death framing is the psychological pressure that drives the entire chapter: the sense of finality creates urgency on all sides, preventing careful discernment and enabling deception.

verseByVerse.quote: Now then, take your weapons, your quiver and your bow, and go out to the field and hunt game for me, and prepare for me delicious food, such as I love, and bring it to me so that I may eat, that my soul may bless you before I die."
verseByVerse.commentary: The blessing is to follow a meal of game — the same game-based love that shaped Isaac's favoritism (25:28) now shapes the blessing ritual. The meal is Isaac's preparation for the blessing; it is also, inadvertently, his vulnerability: it is what Rebekah will exploit, providing goat meat instead of game. Isaac's request for delicious food "such as I love" is the human framing that opens the deception: the blessing will be given on the basis of a sensory experience (taste, smell, touch) — the very senses a blind old man uses to compensate for lost sight. Wenham notes that the detailed preparation Isaac requests — specific food, prepared in a specific way — creates the detailed conditions that Rebekah will have to replicate for the deception to succeed. The longer and more specific the preparation, the more elaborate the deception required.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Rebekah was listening when Isaac spoke to his father Esau. So when Esau went to the field to hunt for game and bring it, Rebekah said to her son Jacob, "I heard your father speak to your brother Esau,
verseByVerse.commentary: Rebekah overhears the plan — the narrator does not present this as accidental; she is listening. What she hears is a direct challenge to the oracle she received (25:23): Isaac intends to bless Esau, the elder, with the covenant blessing. Her intervention is motivated by covenant conviction (the oracle must be fulfilled) and maternal preference (she loves Jacob). The combination is explosive. "I heard your father speak to your brother Esau" — Rebekah uses the possessive pronouns carefully: "your father" (not "my husband"), "your brother" (not "my son Esau"). The distancing language signals that she is positioning this as Jacob's problem to solve with her guidance. Kidner notes that Rebekah's overheard knowledge puts her in possession of information she uses for manipulation rather than prayer — the road not taken is the road of asking God to fulfill his own oracle in his own way.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Bring me game and prepare for me delicious food, that I may eat it and bless you before the LORD before I die.' Now therefore, my son, obey my voice as I command you.
verseByVerse.commentary: Rebekah adds a detail Isaac may not have said: "before the LORD." Whether this is accurate or an addition, it heightens the stakes of what she is about to do: the deception will be not merely a domestic manipulation but a deception performed in the name of the LORD. "Obey my voice as I command you" — Rebekah issues a command to Jacob with the same authority with which God issues commands to the patriarchs. The language is deliberate and theologically freighted: what Rebekah is commanding Jacob to do is obedience to her rather than to God. The parallel is ironic: Jacob will receive the blessing meant for the obedient son through obedience to his mother's deceptive plan. Waltke notes that Rebekah's command to obey "my voice" replaces the proper object of obedience (God's voice) with her own — the same substitution that produces most of the moral disasters in Genesis.

verseByVerse.quote: Go to the flock and bring me two good young goats, so that I may prepare from them delicious food for your father, such as he loves. And you shall bring it to your father to eat, so that he may bless you before he dies."
verseByVerse.commentary: The plan is practical and specific: two goats, prepared as Isaac likes, brought before Isaac while Esau is still hunting. Rebekah knows her husband well enough to replicate what he craves. The substitution of goat meat for game has the practical advantage of speed — the goats are at hand, while Esau must hunt and return. Rebekah has thought through the logistics; the deception is premeditated and detailed. "That he may bless you before he dies" — the urgency of Isaac's mortality is now Rebekah's urgency too, but deployed differently: Isaac uses it to call Esau; Rebekah uses it to motivate Jacob to act before Esau returns. Wenham notes that the practical details of the plan — the goats, the timing, the preparation — are all calculated to exploit the specific vulnerabilities of a blind, hungry, elderly man waiting for his favorite food.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jacob said to Rebekah his mother, "Behold, my brother Esau is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man. Perhaps my father will feel me, and I shall seem to be mocking him and bring a curse upon myself and not a blessing."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jacob's objection is practical, not moral: not "this is wrong" but "this might not work." The moral concern he raises is the curse that might result from being exposed — not the wrongness of deception itself but the negative consequence for himself. This is the moral level at which Jacob operates in chapter 27: calculating risk, not discerning righteousness. The detail of his smooth skin versus Esau's hairiness is the practical obstacle that Rebekah will solve with goatskin. Jacob's objection reveals that he is considering the plan but worried about detection. Waltke notes that Jacob's failure to raise a moral objection to the deception is itself morally significant: the man who will become Israel begins his blessing-seeking through a scheme he does not refuse on principle but evaluates only on pragmatic grounds.

verseByVerse.quote: His mother said to him, "Let your curse be on me, my son; only obey my voice, and go, bring them to me." So he went and took them and brought them to his mother, and his mother prepared delicious food, such as his father loved.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Let your curse be on me" — Rebekah assumes full moral responsibility for the deception. Her willingness to bear the curse is a form of maternal love and covenant conviction, however misdirected: she is willing to sacrifice herself for the outcome she believes is right. The phrase echoes later biblical moments of redemptive substitution — Moses's offer to be blotted out for Israel (Exod. 32:32), Paul's wish to be cut off for his kindred (Rom. 9:3) — but Rebekah's substitution is in the service of deception rather than righteousness. Jacob complies without further objection: he goes, takes the goats, brings them. His obedience to his mother's deceptive plan is the same obedience he will later exercise toward God — only here the commanding voice is human. Kidner notes that Rebekah's "let your curse be on me" will be fulfilled literally: she will bear the curse of never seeing Jacob again after he flees.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Rebekah took the best garments of Esau her older son, which were with her in the house, and put them on Jacob her younger son. And the skins of the young goats she put on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck.
verseByVerse.commentary: Rebekah dresses Jacob in Esau's garments (the smell of the field is on them) and covers his smooth hands and neck with goatskin. The deception is now complete in three dimensions: taste (the goat meat prepared as game), smell (Esau's garments), and touch (the goatskin on his hands and neck). Isaac's remaining senses — the compensatory heightening of smell and touch in the absence of sight — have all been addressed. The thoroughness of the disguise reflects Rebekah's intelligence and her knowledge of Isaac's compensatory sensory strategies. She has prepared for every possible check. Wenham notes that the thoroughness of the preparation is also the thoroughness of the sin: no element of the deception is left to chance, and the careful planning makes the moral responsibility all the more deliberate.

verseByVerse.quote: And she put the delicious food and the bread that she had prepared into the hand of her son Jacob. Then he came to his father and said, "My father." And he said, "Here I am. Who are you, my son?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Rebekah equips Jacob fully and sends him in. Jacob's opening — "my father" — is innocent; the response — "here I am" — is the covenant response of attentiveness that Abraham and Isaac have used in their encounters with God (22:1, 7, 11). Isaac's immediate question — "who are you, my son?" — is either routine (he cannot see who has entered) or an intuition of something amiss. The question "who are you?" is the most important question in the chapter: it will be answered falsely four times (vv.19, 24, 32, 33) before the true answer finally emerges. Jacob's identity — who he is, what his name means — will be central to everything that follows: the flight, the wrestling at Peniel (32:27, "what is your name?"), the renaming as Israel. The chapter begins with the identity question that the rest of Jacob's life will answer. Waltke notes that Isaac's "who are you?" is the chapter's theological question as well as its narrative one.

verseByVerse.quote: Jacob said to his father, "I am Esau your firstborn. I have done as you told me; now sit up and eat of my game, that your soul may bless me." But Isaac said to his son, "How is it that you have found it so quickly, my son?" He answered, "Because the LORD your God granted me success."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jacob's first direct lie: "I am Esau your firstborn." The claim is total and specific — name and status. "I have done as you told me" is technically false (he was not told to do this) and morally false (he is deceiving, not obeying). Isaac's suspicion is immediate: the meal has come too quickly for a hunting expedition. Jacob's explanation — "the LORD your God granted me success" — is the most theologically offensive line in the chapter: he invokes the covenant God as the cover for his lie. Using the divine name to authenticate a deception is a profound form of irreverence. Kidner notes that Jacob's invocation of the LORD to explain the improbably quick return is the lowest point of the deception: lying in the name of God is worse than lying in one's own name, because it implicates the divine character in human sin.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaac said to Jacob, "Please come near, that I may feel you, my son, to know whether you are really my son Esau or not." So Jacob went near to Isaac his father, who felt him and said, "The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau."
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaac's suspicion deepens: he wants to feel Jacob. The voice — Jacob's smooth, domestic voice — does not match Esau's rougher character; Isaac notices the discrepancy. The touch check is meant to resolve it, and the goatskin does its work: "the hands are the hands of Esau." But Isaac's intuition about the voice is correct, and the narrator preserves it: "the voice is Jacob's voice" — recorded before the false conclusion of the touch. The chapter is honest about what Isaac correctly perceived and what the deception overcame. Wenham notes that Isaac's dual-sense check (voice vs. touch) is the chapter's way of showing that the deception was not easily accomplished: it required specific countermeasures (goatskin) to overcome Isaac's compensatory perception, and even so his voice-perception was correct. The deception succeeded against Isaac's intuition.

verseByVerse.quote: And he did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like his brother Esau's hands. So he blessed him. He asked, "Are you really my son Esau?" He said, "I am."
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaac does not recognize Jacob — the goatskin overcomes his tactile perception. He proceeds to bless him. But the narrator notes that he blessed him in a context where he still had a residual question: "are you really my son Esau?" The final identity check, the direct question, receives the direct lie: "I am." Jacob's repeated lies (vv.19, 20, 24) accumulate into a pattern of sustained, deliberate deception. He is not deceiving impulsively or reluctantly; each lie is chosen in response to a specific challenge. The moral weight of the deception increases with each layer. Waltke notes that the repeated identity questions and repeated lies create the impression of a character who is deeply committed to obtaining the blessing through deception — and that this commitment to obtaining what is covenant-right through covenant-wrong is the central contradiction that the rest of Jacob's life will have to resolve.

verseByVerse.quote: He said, "Bring it near to me, that I may eat of my son's game and bless you." So he brought it near to him, and he ate; and he brought him wine, and he drank. Then his father Isaac said to him, "Come near and kiss me, my son."
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaac eats, drinks, and then calls Jacob near for a kiss — the final sensory check and the intimate gesture of familial blessing. The meal has satisfied his taste; the wine has warmed him; the kiss will involve smell. Every sense Isaac has is engaged in the process of blessing, and every sense is being deceived. The hospitality of the meal — Jacob serving his father, his father eating — is a perverse parody of the covenant hospitality that Abraham showed to the three visitors (ch.18): the serving of a meal as the context for covenant communication. Here the meal is false from beginning to end, and yet the covenant communication that follows is real and irrevocable. Kidner notes that the intimacy of the kiss in this context — son to deceived father, right before the blessing — makes the scene one of the most uncomfortable in Genesis.

verseByVerse.quote: So he came near and kissed him. And Isaac smelled the smell of his garments and blessed him and said, "See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed! May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth and plenty of grain and wine.
verseByVerse.commentary: The smell of Esau's garments — the smell of the field — convinces Isaac. The final sensory check passes, and the blessing begins. The blessing itself is beautiful and comprehensive: dew of heaven (moisture in an arid land), fatness of earth (agricultural abundance), plenty of grain and wine (the two staples of covenant life in Canaan). These are the covenant blessings of the land, the material expressions of divine favor. Ironically, these blessings are what Isaac intended to give Esau — and they are now given to Jacob, the covenant heir God designated before birth. The blessing is right even though the means of obtaining it are wrong. Waltke notes that the agricultural richness of the blessing reflects the land promise of the covenant: the promised land flowing with grain and wine, watered by heaven's dew, is the physical expression of the covenant inheritance Isaac is conveying.

verseByVerse.quote: Let peoples serve you, and nations bow down to you. Be lord over your brothers, and may your mother's sons bow down to you. Cursed be everyone who curses you, and blessed be everyone who blesses you!" As soon as Isaac had finished blessing Jacob, when Jacob had scarcely gone out from the presence of Isaac his father, Esau his brother came in from his hunting.
verseByVerse.commentary: The political dimension of the blessing: dominion over peoples and nations, lordship over brothers, and the covenant curse-and-blessing formula (12:3: "whoever curses you I will curse, and whoever blesses you I will bless"). The blessing conveys covenant status: the promises given to Abraham and to Isaac are now given to Jacob. The last element — the curse-and-blessing formula — makes the blessing explicitly covenantal, identifying Jacob as the continuation of the covenant line. Then: "as soon as Isaac had finished... Esau came in." The timing is the narrative's most dramatic moment: the door between blessing and expulsion is measured in minutes. The writer lingers on the threshold: scarcely gone out, just coming in. The near-miss is deliberate: what God arranged through oracle, human scheming, and providential timing has been accomplished with the narrowest of margins. Kidner notes that the timing of Jacob's departure and Esau's arrival is Genesis's most precisely calibrated narrative moment.

verseByVerse.quote: He also prepared delicious food and brought it to his father. And he said to his father, "Let my father arise and eat of his son's game, that you may bless me." His father Isaac said to him, "Who are you?" He answered, "I am your son, your firstborn, Esau."
verseByVerse.commentary: Esau arrives with his game, prepared with care and love, and asks for the blessing. "Who are you?" — Isaac asks the identity question again, and this time Esau answers truthfully: "I am your son, your firstborn, Esau." The same words Jacob spoke falsely, Esau speaks truly — and the truth arrives too late. The juxtaposition of the false claim and the true claim, both using the same form, is the narrator's judgment on the deception: Jacob obtained through lies what Esau deserved through truth, and the reversal is permanent. Waltke notes that Esau's honest self-identification — the truth that should have secured the blessing — is now the statement that reveals the theft. The identity question that Jacob answered falsely, Esau answers truly; and the truth cannot undo what the lie accomplished.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaac trembled very violently and said, "Who was it then that hunted game and brought it to me, and I ate it all before you came, and I have blessed him? Yes, and he shall be blessed." As soon as Esau heard the words of his father, he cried out with an exceedingly great and bitter cry and said to his father, "Bless me, even me also, O my father!"
verseByVerse.commentary: "Isaac trembled very violently" — the Hebrew is emphatic: a great trembling seized him. The shock is not merely surprise but theological recognition: Isaac understands that the blessing has been given to Jacob and that the divine oracle (25:23) has been fulfilled in spite of his intention. "Yes, and he shall be blessed" — Isaac's confirmation is not resignation but recognition: what has been spoken in the LORD's name cannot be revoked. The irrevocability of blessing distinguishes it from a casual promise; a patriarch's blessing, spoken in the LORD's name, is as irrevocable as the divine word. Esau's cry — "exceedingly great and bitter" — is the most emotionally raw moment in the chapter. He does not argue; he begs. "Bless me, even me also" — the repetition is desperate and heartbreaking. Wenham notes that Esau's cry is the authentic grief of a man who has lost something he only now fully understands was precious.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said, "Your brother came deceitfully, and he has taken away your blessing." Esau said, "Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has cheated me these two times. He took away my birthright, and behold, now he has taken away my blessing." And he said, "Have you not reserved a blessing for me?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaac names the truth: "your brother came deceitfully." Esau names Jacob's character through his name: "Is he not rightly named Jacob?" — the heel-grabber, the supplanter — "he has cheated me twice." The birthright and the blessing: Esau recognizes that both transactions are connected, that he is dealing with a consistent pattern in his brother's character. What he does not acknowledge is his own role in the first transaction: he sold his birthright voluntarily for stew (25:33). The deception of the blessing was real and wrong; the "theft" of the birthright was a legal sale Esau made freely. Esau conflates both into a narrative of victimhood that obscures his own contempt for covenant values. Waltke notes that Esau's naming of Jacob's character is accurate as far as it goes — but it does not go far enough, because Esau does not name his own role in the history between them.

verseByVerse.quote: Isaac answered and said to Esau, "Behold, I have made him lord over you, and all his brothers I have given to him for servants, and with grain and wine I have sustained him. What then can I do for you, my son?" Esau said to his father, "Have you but one blessing, my father? Bless me, even me also, O my father." And Esau lifted up his voice and wept.
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaac's summary of what has been given to Jacob — lordship, servants, grain, wine — is the enumeration of the covenant blessing in full. "What then can I do for you?" — the patriarch is not withholding; he is acknowledging that the primary blessing is gone. Esau's question — "have you but one blessing?" — reveals his assumption: surely there is more. His weeping is genuine and moves Isaac to give what secondary blessing remains. Hebrews 12:17 will note that Esau "found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears" — the tears are real, but they are the tears of loss, not the tears of covenant repentance. He weeps not because he has despised the birthright and the covenant but because he has lost the material benefit he now recognizes. Kidner observes that Esau's tears are for what he has lost, not for what he has been.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his father Isaac answered and said to him: "Behold, away from the fatness of the earth shall your dwelling be, and away from the dew of heaven on high. By your sword you shall live, and you shall serve your brother; but when you grow restless, you shall break his yoke from your neck."
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaac's word to Esau is not a blessing in the covenant sense but a prophetic description of Esau's/Edom's future: a life in the dry hill country (away from the fatness of the earth, away from the dew of heaven), a life sustained by the sword rather than by agricultural abundance. "You shall serve your brother" — the oracle of 25:23 ("the elder shall serve the younger") is now formally stated in the blessing context. "But when you grow restless, you shall break his yoke from your neck" — the subordination is not permanent; Edom will periodically revolt against Israelite dominance (as historically in the days of Jehoram, 2 Kings 8:20–22). The word to Esau is honest, not cruel: Isaac describes what Esau's life will be. Wenham notes that the word to Esau reflects the covenant reality: he has received what was available after the covenant blessing was given, and it is a diminished but real future.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–46 — Esau's Rage and Jacob's Flight
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes with Esau's murderous intention (he will kill Jacob after Isaac's death), Rebekah's intervention (she sends Jacob to Laban before Esau can act), and Rebekah's cover story for Isaac (she sends Jacob to find a wife among her family). The flight that began with the oracle of 25:23 now becomes necessary; the deception that secured the blessing now produces the exile that will shape Jacob's character. Every element of the deception has a corresponding consequence: Rebekah loses her son permanently; Jacob loses his home; Esau loses his brother. The stolen blessing produces stolen years.
verseByVerse.theology: The theological irony of the chapter's ending is profound: Jacob has the blessing but loses the land. He holds the covenant promise but must flee the covenant territory. The man who schemes to secure his inheritance through deception is the man who must live as a fugitive in someone else's country for twenty years. God will fulfill the covenant promise — but Jacob will receive it through a long discipline of suffering rather than through the immediate enjoyment the stolen blessing seemed to promise.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller on Genesis 27:41–46: the consequences of Rebekah's deception are not a correction of a wrong outcome but a refinement of Jacob's character. God uses Esau's rage and Jacob's exile to do what the deception could not do: make Jacob into a man who can carry the covenant. The blessing obtained through lying produces a covenant heir who will need twenty years in the school of suffering before he is ready to be Israel. God's sovereign purposes are not frustrated by human sin; they are pursued through its consequences.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing with which his father had blessed him, and Esau said to himself, "The days of mourning for my father are not far off; then I will kill my brother Jacob." But the words of Esau her older son were told to Rebekah. So she sent and called Jacob her younger son and said to him, "Behold, your brother Esau comforts himself about you by planning to kill you.
verseByVerse.commentary: Esau's grief becomes murderous rage: he plans to wait for Isaac's death (so as not to destroy his father's last years) and then kill Jacob. The murder plan is not impulsive but calculated — he will wait for mourning to pass. This deliberateness makes the plan more threatening, not less. Rebekah hears of it — the narrator does not explain how — and acts immediately. Her action is again pragmatic and decisive: she does not confront Esau or appeal to Isaac but calls Jacob and tells him bluntly: "your brother comforts himself by planning to kill you." The directness is characteristic: Rebekah does not soften or theologize; she states the threat and prepares to act. Waltke notes that Esau's hatred of Jacob will become the founding conflict of the Edomite-Israelite relationship that runs through the entire Old Testament, reaching its most intense expression in the book of Obadiah.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore, my son, obey my voice. Arise, flee to Laban my brother in Haran and stay with him a while, until your brother's fury turns away—
verseByVerse.commentary: Rebekah's plan for Jacob's escape is Laban in Haran — her own brother, the man who calculated the value of Rebekah's jewelry before welcoming the servant (ch.24). Jacob will go to the household that has been both the source of covenant wives (Rebekah herself) and the home of the family's calculating nature. The instruction — "flee to Laban my brother in Haran" — sets up the entire Jacob-in-Mesopotamia narrative that follows. "A while" — Rebekah's assessment of how long the exile will last is tragically optimistic: she assumes days or weeks; the actual exile will be twenty years, and she will never see Jacob again. Kidner notes that Rebekah's "a while" is one of the most painful ironies in Genesis: the mother who sacrificed everything to secure Jacob's blessing will sacrifice their relationship to Esau's rage, and the sacrifice is permanent.

verseByVerse.quote: until your brother's anger turns away from you, and he forgets what you have done to him. Then I will send and bring you from there. Why should I be bereft of you both in one day?" Then Rebekah said to Isaac, "I loathe my life because of the Hittite women. If Jacob marries one of the Hittite women like these, one of the women of the land, what will my life be worth to me?"
verseByVerse.commentary: "Why should I be bereft of you both in one day?" — Rebekah's logic is sound: if Esau kills Jacob, she loses both sons — Jacob to death, Esau to the legal consequences of murder. Her cover story to Isaac is the complaint about Hittite wives (26:35): she uses the legitimate grievance (Esau's covenant-violating marriages) as the stated reason for sending Jacob to Haran. The cover story is not entirely false — finding a covenant wife from the covenant family is a genuine and important reason — but it conceals the real urgency. Rebekah is managing Isaac's knowledge as carefully as she managed his senses during the blessing deception. Wenham notes that Rebekah's cover story transforms an exile motivated by survival into a mission motivated by covenant faithfulness — not entirely dishonest, but not entirely honest either. This is Rebekah's final recorded speech in Genesis; she and Jacob will never speak again.

27.theology:
Genesis 27 forces readers to reckon with a disturbing doctrine: God accomplishes his purposes through human sin without thereby endorsing the sin. Jacob’s deception is never praised; its consequences are severe. Yet the blessing passes to Jacob, not Esau, exactly as God said. This is not divine determinism that removes moral responsibility; it is divine sovereignty that operates through human choice without annulling it.

Paul draws on Esau and Jacob in Romans 9 to argue that election does not depend on works or merit but on God who calls (Rom 9:11–12). The point is not that God is indifferent to morality but that God’s purpose is not hostage to human goodness. The heir of promise is not the more deserving son; he is the chosen one. This is the radical grace that the patriarchal narratives exist to demonstrate.

The irrevocability of the spoken blessing (v.33) anticipates the eternal security of the new covenant. God’s word, once given, stands. “The gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Rom 11:29). What God has blessed cannot be cursed by any human reversal.
27.examples:
Every reader of Genesis 27 recognizes the family dynamics: parents playing favorites, siblings competing for approval, schemes hatched in whispered conversation, irreversible words spoken in the heat of the moment. The patriarchal family is not an idealized portrait but a mirror. Its dysfunction is our dysfunction. Its grace—that God works through these broken families to accomplish redemption—is our grace.

Keller uses this chapter to address those who feel their past is too compromised for God to use. Jacob is not chosen because he is good; he is made good (eventually, after much suffering) because he is chosen. The same grace that overruled Jacob’s deception is available to every deceiver who comes to the God of Jacob in faith.

28.title: Surely the LORD Is in This Place
28.text: Jacob left Beersheba and went toward Haran. And he came to a certain place and stayed there that night, because the sun had set. Taking one of the stones of the place, he put it under his head and lay down in that place to sleep. And he dreamed, and behold, there was a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven. And behold, the angels of God were ascending and descending on it! And behold, the LORD stood above it and said, “I am the LORD, the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac. The land on which you lie I will give to you and to your offspring. Your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth, and you shall spread abroad to the west and to the east and to the north and to the south, and in you and your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed. Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, and will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.” Then Jacob awoke from his sleep and said, “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it.” And he was afraid and said, “How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.”
28.overview:
Genesis 28 is the pivot of the Jacob narrative. A fugitive from his own family, fleeing into the wilderness with a stone for a pillow, Jacob meets God. He has done nothing to deserve the vision; he has done much to deserve exile. But the God of Abraham and Isaac appears and renews the covenant with the deceiver. Grace finds Jacob in the wilderness.

The vision of the stairway (or ramp, sullam) with angels ascending and descending is one of the most iconic images in Genesis. Its theological meaning is clear: heaven and earth are connected; God’s realm interpenetrates the human. The LORD stands “above it” (or “beside him,” depending on the Hebrew syntax) and speaks the covenant words that have been spoken to Abraham and Isaac. The blessing is confirmed to a man who did not earn it.

Jesus himself applies this vision to his own person in John 1:51: “You will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.” Jacob’s ladder is not a permanent structure; it is a preview of the incarnation—the place where heaven and earth permanently meet, the one in whom God dwells bodily, the gate of heaven for all who come to the Father through him (John 14:6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Isaac's Blessing and Jacob's Dream at Bethel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 28 is a pivotal chapter in the Jacob narrative. Isaac sends Jacob to Paddan-aram with an explicit blessing — not the stolen blessing of chapter 27 but a deliberate, informed covenant blessing: the blessing of Abraham, the promise of land and offspring. Esau, overhearing that the Canaanite wives displeased his father, takes a wife from Ishmael's line — a belated and inadequate attempt to please his parents. Then Jacob encounters God at Bethel, in the most remarkable theophany since the burning bush: a stairway to heaven, angels ascending and descending, and God himself speaking the covenant promise to Jacob directly for the first time.
verseByVerse.theology: The Bethel dream is the moment when the covenant comes to Jacob personally. He has held the blessing (secured through deception) and the birthright (purchased through opportunism), but he has not yet encountered the covenant God face to face. At Bethel, alone and fleeing, Jacob receives what Abraham received at Ur and in Canaan: the God of the covenant addresses him by name, promises him land and offspring and blessing, and pledges his own presence on the journey. The encounter transforms the fugitive into the covenant heir.
verseByVerse.examples: Waltke on Genesis 28: the Bethel encounter is the covenant's own correction of the deception of chapter 27. Jacob has secured the blessing through human scheming; God now gives him the covenant directly, person to person, without human intermediary. The ladder to heaven and the divine presence at the bottom of it tell Jacob what he most needs to know: the God he is fleeing toward (in Haran) is already present here, at the very place of his flight. God is not geographically limited; his covenant presence goes with the covenant heir wherever he goes.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaac called Jacob and blessed him and directed him, "You shall not take a wife from the Canaanite women. Arise, go to Paddan-aram to the house of Bethuel your mother's father, and take as your wife from there one of the daughters of Laban your mother's brother.
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaac calls Jacob and blesses him explicitly — this time with full knowledge of who he is blessing. The blessing of chapter 27 was given under deception; this blessing is given in clarity. Isaac's instruction about marriage — no Canaanite wife, go to Laban's family — mirrors Abraham's instruction to his servant in chapter 24 (24:3–4). The covenant pattern of marriage within the covenant family is maintained across three generations: Abraham insisted on it, Isaac is now insisting on it, and it is grounded in the same covenant logic (the purity of the covenant line). The destination — Paddan-aram, to the house of Bethuel, to the daughters of Laban — is exactly the household from which Rebekah came. Jacob will return to the source of his mother to find the source of his children. Wenham notes that Isaac's formal blessing and instruction transform Jacob's flight from an escape into a mission: he goes as a fugitive, but with covenant purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: God Almighty bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you, that you may become a company of peoples. May he give you the blessing of Abraham, to you and to your offspring with you, that you may take possession of the land of your sojournings that God gave to Abraham!"
verseByVerse.commentary: "God Almighty" (El Shaddai) — the divine name that Abraham received when the covenant of circumcision was established (17:1): the God of overpowering provision, the God who can make fruitful what is barren. The blessing Isaac pronounces is the full Abrahamic blessing: fruitfulness ("a company of peoples"), the blessing of Abraham, and possession of the land. For the first time, Jacob receives the covenant promise from his father's lips — explicitly, formally, with the full weight of the patriarchal transmission. The stolen blessing of chapter 27 was real but compromised; this blessing is unambiguous. Isaac knows who he is blessing and what he is blessing him with. Waltke notes that El Shaddai is the appropriate name for Isaac's blessing: Jacob is going to a foreign land, and what he needs is the God who can make even a fugitive in someone else's country into a fruitful covenant heir.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Isaac sent Jacob away. And he went to Paddan-aram, to Laban, the son of Bethuel the Aramean, the brother of Rebekah, Jacob's and Esau's mother. Now Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him away to Paddan-aram to take a wife from there, and that as he blessed him he directed him, "You shall not take a wife from the Canaanite women,"
verseByVerse.commentary: Jacob departs with Isaac's blessing. The genealogical fullness of Laban's identification — son of Bethuel the Aramean, brother of Rebekah, Jacob's and Esau's mother — establishes the family relationship that will structure the next twenty years of Jacob's life. Then the narrator shifts to Esau's perspective: Esau observes what Isaac has done (sent Jacob with a blessing and a marriage commission) and draws conclusions. The contrast between the brothers is now measured not just in character but in comprehension: Esau begins to understand what covenant-shaped marriage looks like, but the understanding comes too late and is pursued in the wrong way. Wenham notes that the narrator's shift to Esau's perspective at this point creates a momentary sympathy for the elder son — he is trying, belatedly, to do what his father values.

verseByVerse.quote: and that Jacob had obeyed his father and his mother and gone to Paddan-aram. So when Esau saw that the Canaanite women did not please Isaac his father,
verseByVerse.commentary: "Jacob had obeyed his father and his mother" — the narrator's description of Jacob's departure as obedience (even though the primary motivation was survival) stands in ironic contrast to Esau's consistent pattern of covenant-disregard. Jacob, who deceived his father, is now departing in obedience to his father's explicit instruction; Esau, who never deceived his father, has consistently displeased him through his marriage choices. "The Canaanite women did not please Isaac his father" — Esau's dawning recognition that his marriages were wrong comes only now, after Jacob's departure has made the point unmistakable. Waltke notes that Esau's belated recognition of what pleased his father is one of the saddest moments in the chapter: the learning comes too late, the application will be inadequate, and the approval sought is now permanently beyond reach.

verseByVerse.quote: Esau went to Ishmael and took as his wife, besides the wives he had, Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael, Abraham's son, the sister of Nebaioth. Jacob left Beersheba and went toward Haran.
verseByVerse.commentary: Esau's solution to the Canaanite-wife problem is to take a third wife — from Ishmael's family, within the broader Abrahamic family but outside the specific covenant line. The choice reflects Esau's pattern: a belated, partial, and inadequate response to covenant requirements. He does not put away his Canaanite wives (which would have been the appropriate response); he adds an Ishmaelite wife. The addition cannot compensate for the existing problem. Jacob's simultaneous departure — "Jacob left Beersheba and went toward Haran" — is the covenant departure in the right direction, for the right reasons, at the right time. The two brothers diverge permanently: Esau stays and adds a wife; Jacob goes and will receive the covenant God's direct address. Kidner notes that the juxtaposition of Esau's third marriage and Jacob's covenant departure is the chapter's most pointed contrast: one man adjusts his marriage portfolio; the other encounters the living God.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came to a certain place and stayed there that night, because the sun had set. Taking one of the stones of the place, he put it under his head and lay down in that place to sleep. And he dreamed, and behold, there was a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven. And behold, the angels of God were ascending and descending on it!
verseByVerse.commentary: Jacob stops for the night at "a certain place" — a nondescript location that will become the most sacred site in Canaan. The stone for a pillow is the image of the solitary fugitive: no tent, no servants, no bed. Then the dream: a ladder (or stairway) set up from earth to heaven, with angels ascending and descending. The image is magnificent and theologically rich: heaven and earth are not separate realms but connected by a constant traffic of divine messengers. Jesus will apply this image to himself (John 1:51: "you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man") — he is the true ladder, the real connection between heaven and earth. Waltke notes that the ascending-and-descending sequence (ascending first, then descending) suggests the angels are already on earth, serving the covenant purposes of God in the world, and returning to heaven for further instruction.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, the LORD stood above it and said, "I am the LORD, the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac. The land on which you lie I will give to you and to your offspring. Your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth, and you shall spread abroad to the west and to the east and to the north and to the south, and in you and your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.
verseByVerse.commentary: "The LORD stood above it" — above the ladder, as its source and summit. The covenant is stated in the most direct form Jacob has yet received it: the God of Abraham and Isaac now identifies himself as Jacob's God. The three elements of the Abrahamic covenant are all present: land ("the land on which you lie I will give to you"), offspring (like the dust of the earth), and blessing to all families of the earth. The land promise is geographically vivid: west, east, north, south — all four directions from this spot. Jacob, lying on the ground that is the covenant land, is promised that everything he can see in every direction belongs to his offspring. The blessing formula — "in you and your offspring" — echoes 12:3 and 22:18: the covenant purpose of the patriarchal promise is the blessing of all humanity. Wenham notes that the Bethel divine speech is the most comprehensive direct statement of the covenant promise to any patriarch in Genesis.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, and will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you." Then Jacob awoke from his sleep and said, "Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it."
verseByVerse.commentary: "I am with you" — the covenant presence promise given to Isaac (26:3, 24) is now given to Jacob. The specific addition for Jacob's situation is the promise of return: "I will bring you back to this land." Jacob is leaving; God promises he will return. The promise of return is the covenant's acknowledgment of Jacob's exile: he is going, but he will come back. "I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised" — the unconditional commitment. Jacob wakes from the dream and his first response is theological recognition: "surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it." He did not choose this place for its sanctity; he stopped because the sun set. But God was there, and the encounter has made a nowhere-place into the house of God. Kidner writes that Jacob's "I did not know it" is one of the most important moments in his spiritual development: he is learning that God is present in places he did not expect, pursuing him in places he did not choose.

verseByVerse.quote: And he was afraid and said, "How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." So early in the morning Jacob took the stone that he had put under his head and set it up for a pillar and poured oil on top of it.
verseByVerse.commentary: Fear and awe: the appropriate responses to the presence of the holy. "How awesome is this place" — the Hebrew (nora, fearful, awesome) is the same word used of God in the psalms of divine majesty. "The house of God" (Bethel, which Jacob will name the place, v.19) and "the gate of heaven" — the place where earth and heaven meet, where the ladder stands, where God has spoken. Jacob's response is immediate and concrete: he takes the stone he slept on — the most ordinary object of the night — and sets it up as a pillar, anointing it with oil. The stone that was his pillow becomes a sacred monument. The most ordinary object of Jacob's sleep becomes the first act of covenant worship he performs. Waltke notes that Jacob's consecration of the stone reflects the same instinct that drove Abraham to build altars: the covenant response to divine encounter is the marking of holy space with a physical act of dedication.

verseByVerse.quote: He called the name of that place Bethel, but the name of the city was Luz at the first. Then Jacob made a vow, saying, "If God will be with me and will keep me in this way that I go, and will give me bread to eat and clothing to wear,
verseByVerse.commentary: Bethel — "house of God" — replaces the previous name Luz. The place is named for the encounter, as Moriah was named for divine provision (22:14) and Beersheba for the covenant oath (21:31; 26:33).
